Chapter 1

Introduction

1.1What this document is

A condensed study document for the Vibration and Noise 354 A2 assessment (the whole semester), organised by teaching week to match Weeks Content/.

  • Chapter 2 — what A2 asks: the layout, the 2020 and 2024 papers mapped to weeks, and a study plan.
  • Weeks 1–6 (term 3) and Weeks 7–12 (term 4) — one section per week, then exam technique and a mock A2 paper (10 questions, 80 marks).
  • Appendices — the formula sheet with what it omits (A) and the question index (B).

1.2How to use it

  1. Each week opens with This week in brief: the ideas to carry into the exam. Below it are the formulas (red where the sheet omits them), the traps, tables, figures and benches.
  2. The full explanations and derivations are still there, collapsed under Explanation and derivation. Open one when a result does not make sense, or when the exam asks for that derivation (marked).
  3. Worked examples are collapsed too. Try them first, then open.
  4. Do each week's practice questions with the memos hidden. Every question names its source and says what its memo was checked against.
  5. The night before: Appendix A (what the formula sheet will not give you) and the self-test in the exam-technique section.

Red text

Text in red is something you must know because the formula sheet (Admin Documents/Asessment_appendices.pdf, 2025) will not give it: a formula that is not on the sheet, or a small condition without which a problem cannot be set up (for example "isolation needs $r>\sqrt2$", "$k_n=10$ dB from 22:00 to 06:00", "a free string end has zero slope"). Everything in normal colour is on the sheet in some form. Where the sheet gives a formula in a different but equivalent form, it is not marked.

1.3Notation

Symbols are defined beside the equation that introduces them — equation on the left, the new symbols on the right. Standard ones you know from mechanics and mathematics ($m$, $k$, $c$, $x$, $t$, $F$, $\omega$, $g$, $E$, $I$, …) are not repeated. The notation follows the formula sheet and Inman, Engineering Vibration, 4th ed.

1.4Sources

  • Lecture notes and slides, Lectures 1–13, signal processing, EMA, condition monitoring and the noise lectures (Weeks Content/).
  • Inman, Engineering Vibration, 4th ed. (Admin Documents/).
  • Tutorials 1–5 with their solutions, Practicals 1–3, MATLAB Assignments 1–2.
  • Past papers: term-3 papers 2012 and 2020–2023, and the 2020 and 2024 A2 papers (Past Papers/).

Where a printed memo or tutorial solution disagrees with a recomputation, the question says so and gives the cause. Two notes on sources, as of 14 November 2026: the damping part of Week 1 was first written from Inman §1.3 and agrees with Lecture 2; the measurement part of Week 1 was written from Inman §1.6, Lecture 1 and Practical 1 and has not yet been cross-checked line by line against the Week 1 measurement notes.

Chapter 2

What the A2 paper asks, and where to find it

This chapter tells you what A2 looks like, where each part of the paper is taught in this document, and how the past papers map onto it.

2.1The paper

A2: Wednesday 18 November 2026, 14:00 (A3: 5 December 2026, 09:00 — the same format). A2 carries 45 % of the final mark, and A2/A3 contain the ECSA GA2 questions with a subminimum (module framework, 2026).

The lecturers' A2/A3 layout slide (shared 9 November 2026) gives:

BlockMarksWeeks here
Single degree of freedom: free vibration and EOM (viscous and Coulomb, Newton and energy), harmonic excitation, base excitation and rotating unbalance[10, 10]1–4
2DOF / MDOF: equations in matrix form, natural frequencies and mode shapes[10]5–6
Vibration suppression: isolation and absorption[10]8
Continuous systems: strings (rods/bars, shafts) and beams[10]9–10
Additional lectures / practicals: vibration measurement, signal processing, condition monitoring, experimental modal analysis[10, 10]1, 7, 10
Sound lectures[10]11–12

The same slide says 10 questions, 3 hours, full marks 80, on a question–answer paper (write in the spaces, hand in the paper). The listed blocks add up to eight 10-mark questions, not ten. The 2024 A2 had ten 10-mark questions. Expect either ten questions, some of them shorter, or eight questions of 10 marks. Plan for about 2.25 minutes per mark: about 20 minutes per 10-mark question, which leaves about 20 minutes for reading the paper and checking.

The formula sheet is the 2025 assessment appendix (Admin Documents/Asessment_appendices.pdf). Its SDOF section, MDOF section, vibration suppression, distributed-parameter and sound/noise sections are all examinable now. Appendix A lists what is on it and what is not.

2.3What the papers have in common

  • The tutorials are the paper. 2020 Q3, Q4 and Q8 are Tutorial 4 AP3, Tutorial 3 AP2 and Tutorial 5 Q21 almost word for word. Every tutorial "additional problem" in this document is marked with its source for that reason.
  • The octave-band weighting table appears in both papers (A in 2020, C in 2024), and so does a noise-rating calculation. Expect one of each.
  • Term-3 questions come back. The 2024 swing door is the 2020 term-3 paper's Q2; the 2024 energy method is question type B again (§2.5). Weeks 1–6 are half of A2.
  • The descriptive lectures are examined with short-answer questions (condition monitoring, signal-processing terms, SANS definitions, measurement practice). They are cheap marks if the lists are learned.
  • Continuous systems are asked as "find $\omega_n$ and sketch the modes" with unusual boundary conditions (pinned–free string in 2024; clamped–clamped and pinned–pinned beam in 2020). Know how to apply boundary conditions, not only the table.

Not in the readable past papers — do not skip

No readable A2 asks for the modal-coordinate free response (Week 6), longitudinal or torsional vibration of rods and shafts, isolator design with a damping choice, the PSD or windowing beyond definitions, or the Western Cape definitions in detail. That is a warning, not reassurance: the layout slide names rods/bars, shafts and isolation explicitly, and the 2024 Question 2 is missing.

2.4Study plan for the last four days

  1. Saturday–Sunday: Weeks 6, 8, 9 and 10 with their question sets (modal analysis, suppression, continuous systems: 30–40 marks of the paper). Then the 2020 A2 Q3 and Q4 timed.
  2. Monday: Weeks 11–12 (sound, 10 marks, very predictable) and Weeks 7 and 10 (signal processing, EMA, condition monitoring). Do every Tutorial 5 question.
  3. Tuesday: Weeks 1–6: the in brief boxes, then each week’s question set (most are term-3 paper questions, including the 2026 paper): the five SDOF/2DOF question types (§2.5), the swing door (Q 1.5) and the unbalance/beating question (Q 4.4). Then the Mock paper under exam conditions (3 hours), and mark it from the memos. Keep the 2024 A2 as a second timed paper if there is time.
  4. Wednesday morning: Appendix A — the red items — and the self-test in the exam-technique section.

2.5The five SDOF and 2DOF question types

The SDOF and 2DOF blocks of A2 draw on the same five question types that the term-3 papers used. The 2024 A2 Q1 is a term-3 question reused word for word.

Exam angle

Slots B, D and E have appeared in every conventional paper since 2012. Slot A has appeared as Question 1 in three of the last five conventional papers, and the 2021 and 2023 wordings are nearly identical — “Derive the forms of the solutions of the free responses of the system … It is not required to determine the amplitudes of the responses in terms of initial conditions.” That is 10 marks of pure, rehearsable bookwork. Rehearse it until you can write it in eight minutes.

2.6Term-3 papers, question by question

Show the term-3 papers, question by question (Table 2.2)

2.7Questions answered in words, not numbers

Show the questions answered in words

Roughly one mark in six is awarded for words or a sketch rather than a number. Past examples:

  • 2023 Q2(e): “If the disk were to slip on the mass, with a coefficient of friction $\mu$, would you still be able to use the energy method? Why or why not?” (Answer: no — friction is non-conservative, so $T+U\neq$ const; and slipping adds a second degree of freedom.)
  • 2023 Q3(c): “What is the significance of the DC offset observed in the acceleration measurement?” (A DC accelerometer measures gravitational as well as dynamic acceleration; the offset is the component of $g$ along the measurement axis.)
  • 2023 Q4(e) / 2022 Q4(c): “What action could the driver take to reduce vibration?” (Change speed, so as to move $r$ away from 1; here, speed up.)
  • 2012 Q1(c): “Explain the notions of degree of freedom and state.”
  • 2020 Q3(b): “If one of the natural frequencies were zero, what would this mean?” (Rigid-body mode: the whole system translates or rotates without straining any spring.)
  • Every base-excitation question: sketch $|X/Y|$ versus $r$ and mark the region where the passenger is isolated.

These are the cheapest marks on the paper and the most commonly left blank.

2.8Time budget

180 minutes for 80 marks is 2.25 minutes per mark. With eight 10-mark blocks that is about 20 minutes per question, leaving about 20 minutes to read the paper first and check at the end. When a question's time is up, move on: a half-finished question that sets up the method usually earns more than the last two marks of the one before it.

2.9The ECSA GA 2 question

The module framework states that A2 and A3 include questions with a subminimum requirement for ECSA Graduate Attribute 2: you must pass them to pass the module [2, 3]. The rubric has three criteria, each graded Fail / Marginal Fail / Marginal Pass / Pass:

Reference — ECSA GA 2 assessment rubric

Exam angle

Read the “OR” in the Pass definition carefully: an arithmetic slip does not fail you if the physics and the method are right and visible. The corollary is brutal — if you write only a final number with no free-body diagram, no stated law and no method, a wrong answer fails all three criteria. Always draw the FBD, always name the principle you are applying, always show the substitution. On a GA-assessed question this is worth more than the answer.

Week 1

Free vibration, damping and vibration measurement

Lectures 1–2 · Vibration measurement

This week in brief

  • Model every system as mass, spring and damper, with $x$ measured from static equilibrium. Gravity and the static spring force then cancel and drop out of the EOM.
  • Newton: draw the FBD in a displaced position, sum the forces (or moments about a fixed point) and write $m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=0$. Then $\omega_n=\sqrt{k/m}$ is the coefficient of $x$ divided by the coefficient of $\ddot x$.
  • The undamped free response is $x=A\sin(\omega_nt+\phi)$, with $A$ and $\phi$ from $x_0$ and $v_0$.
  • Damping: $\zeta=c/c_{cr}$ with $c_{cr}=2\sqrt{km}$. The four regimes are $\zeta=0$, $<1$, $=1$ and $>1$. Only the underdamped case oscillates, at $\omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$.
  • From a decay record: $\delta=\ln(x_1/x_2)$, then $\zeta=\delta/\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}$. With $k$ from a static test, this gives $m$ and $c$. This is Practical 1 and a regular exam question.
  • Measurement: know the sensors (accelerometer types and what a DC accelerometer reads), the ISO reference values, and the conversions between displacement, velocity and acceleration ($\times\omega$ per step).

1.1What vibration is

Definition (Lecture 1)

“Vibration is the sub-discipline of dynamics that deals with repetitive motion described by a frequency (in rad/s or Hz) and an amplitude (in displacement, velocity or acceleration).” — Bekker, VN354 Lecture 1 [4]
Explanation and derivation

Every SDOF problem in this module reduces to one of two questions:

  1. Free vibration. Disturb the system and let go. What does $x(t)$ look like, and at what frequency does it oscillate? (Week 2–2)
  2. Forced vibration. Shake it continuously at a frequency $\omega$. How big is the steady response, and how much of the input gets through? (Week 3–4)

1.2Degree of freedom, and state

Degree of freedom (asked verbatim in 2012 Q1(c))

A degree of freedom is the minimum number of independent coordinates required to specify the position of every part of a system at any instant.
The state of a system is the set of variables needed to specify the total energy stored in it at any instant. For a SDOF spring–mass system there are two energy stores — potential in the spring, kinetic in the mass — so two states are required: displacement $x$ and velocity $\dd x$.

Exam angle

2023 Q2(e) hangs on a related idea: if the disc slips on the mass, the constraint $x=r\theta$ is broken, so $x$ and $\theta$ become independent — the system gains a degree of freedom. Counting DOF is: (number of coordinates you could draw) $-$ (number of rigid kinematic constraints between them).
Explanation and derivation

The distinction matters. A SDOF system has one degree of freedom but two states; that is exactly why its equation of motion is second order and why you need two initial conditions $x_0$ and $v_0$.

1.3The three model elements

\begin{equation*} k\delta_{st} = mg \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \delta_{st} = \frac{mg}{k}. \end{equation*}(1.1)
$\delta_{st}$
static deflection of the spring under the weight
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x(t) + kx(t) = 0\;} \end{equation*}(1.2)

Rule

If $x$ is measured from the static equilibrium position, gravity and the static spring force cancel and never appear in the equation of motion again. If you measure from the unstretched spring position, you must carry both.

Exam angle

The energy method (§2.9) is the exception: when you write $U$ from the unstretched position you must include both the gravitational term and the full spring term, and then substitute the static-deflection relation at the end. 2021 Q4 and 2022 Q2 award explicit marks for the static-deflection step ($\theta_0=mg/6kr$ and similar). Skipping it loses those marks even if your final EOM is right.
Explanation and derivation

Every lumped system in this module is assembled from three idealised elements. Each is defined by the force it produces:

Inman describes the damper physically as a dashpot — a perforated piston in an oil-filled cylinder — and notes that the damping force is proportional to velocity and opposes the motion [1]. Figure 1.1 reproduces the standard schematic and free-body diagram; commit this FBD to memory, because it is the starting point of Question 1 in most years.

1.3.1Why $x$ is measured from static equilibrium

This is worth two minutes because it removes gravity from every subsequent equation.

Hang a mass $m$ on a vertical spring $k$. At rest the spring is stretched by the static deflection $\delta_{st}$, and a force balance gives

\begin{equation*} k\delta_{st} = mg \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \delta_{st} = \frac{mg}{k}. \end{equation*}(1.1)

Now let $x(t)$ be measured downwards from that rest position. The spring force is $f_k = k(\delta_{st}+x)$ and Newton's second law gives [4]

\begin{equation*} mg - k(\delta_{st}+x(t)) = m\ddd x(t). \end{equation*}

But $k\delta_{st}=mg$, so those two terms cancel exactly and

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x(t) + kx(t) = 0\;} \end{equation*}(1.2)

1.4The equation of motion by Newton's method

Method for any Newton-based EOM question

  1. Choose a coordinate and a positive direction. Draw it on the sketch.
  2. Draw the free-body diagram in a displaced position, not at rest.
  3. Write every force as a function of that coordinate ($f_k=kx$, $f_c=c\dd x$, $f_f=\mu N$).
  4. Apply $\sum F = m\ddd x$ or $\sum M_O = I_O\ddd\theta$.
  5. Collect terms as $m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx = F(t)$; identify $\wnn=\sqrt{k/m}$.
Explanation and derivation

Take the spring–mass system of Week 1, measure $x$ from static equilibrium, and apply $\sum F_x = m\ddd x$. Gravity cancels against the static spring force (Eq. (1.1)), leaving

\begin{equation*} m\ddd x(t) + kx(t) = 0 . \end{equation*}(1.3)

1.5Solving it: the observational approach

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\wnn = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\;}\qquad \text{[rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$]} \end{equation*}(1.4)
$\omega_n$
undamped natural frequency [rad/s]; $f_n=\omega_n/2\pi$ in Hz

Definition of natural frequency (2023 Q1(a), worth marks on its own)

The natural frequency is the frequency at which the system will vibrate if it is disturbed from its equilibrium position and no other periodic force acts on it [4]. Symbolically $\wnn=\sqrt{k/m}$ in rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$, or $f_n=\wnn/2\pi$ in Hz.
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;A = \frac{\sqrt{\wnn^2x_0^2+v_0^2}}{\wnn}\;}, \qquad \boxed{\;\phi = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{\wnn x_0}{v_0}\;} \end{equation*}(1.5)
$x_0,\ v_0$
initial displacement and velocity
$A$
amplitude of the free response
$\phi$
phase angle

Exam angle

This is the 2022 term-3 paper, Q1(b) in full, for 5 marks. The memo's mark scheme is: guess the solution, differentiate twice, substitute, obtain $\wnn$, apply both ICs, solve for $A$ and $\phi$, state the final $x(t)$. Seven visible steps. Write them as seven lines.
Explanation and derivation

Guess a periodic solution [4]:

\begin{align*} x(t) &= A\sin(\wnn t+\phi) \\ \dd x(t) &= \wnn A\cos(\wnn t+\phi) \\ \ddd x(t) &= -\wnn^2 A\sin(\wnn t+\phi) \end{align*}

Substituting into Eq. (1.3):

\begin{equation*} -m\wnn^2 A\sin(\wnn t+\phi) = -kA\sin(\wnn t+\phi) \end{equation*}

which is satisfied for all $t$ only if

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\wnn = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\;}\qquad \text{[rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$]} \end{equation*}(1.4)

1.5.1Fitting the initial conditions

With $x(0)=x_0$ and $\dd x(0)=v_0$:

\begin{align*} x_0 &= A\sin\phi \\ v_0 &= \wnn A\cos\phi \end{align*}(1.6)

Square and add Eqs. (1.6) and (1.7), then divide them:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;A = \frac{\sqrt{\wnn^2x_0^2+v_0^2}}{\wnn}\;}, \qquad \boxed{\;\phi = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{\wnn x_0}{v_0}\;} \end{equation*}(1.5)

so that the complete free response is

\begin{equation*} x(t) = \frac{\sqrt{\wnn^2x_0^2+v_0^2}}{\wnn}\, \sin\!\left(\wnn t + \tan^{-1}\frac{\wnn x_0}{v_0}\right). \end{equation*}(1.7)

1.6Solving it: the analytical approach

Three equivalent ways to write the same undamped free response

\begin{equation*} x(t)=A\sin(\wnn t+\phi) \;=\;A_1\sin\wnn t + A_2\cos\wnn t \;=\;a_1e^{j\wnn t}+a_2e^{-j\wnn t} \end{equation*}
All three appear on the formula sheet. Use the first for sketching, the second when fitting ICs by hand, the third when you need to carry the algebra through a damped or forced problem.
Explanation and derivation

The general method — the one that also works when damping is present — assumes an exponential:

\begin{equation*} x(t) = a e^{\lambda t}. \end{equation*}(1.8)

Substituting into Eq. (1.3) gives $m\lambda^2 ae^{\lambda t}+kae^{\lambda t}=0$. Since $ae^{\lambda t}\neq0$ for a non-trivial solution,

\begin{equation*} m\lambda^2 + k = 0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \lambda = \pm\sqrt{-\frac{k}{m}} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\,j = \pm\wnn j . \end{equation*}(1.9)

Two roots, so two solutions, summed linearly:

\begin{equation*} x(t) = a_1 e^{j\wnn t} + a_2 e^{-j\wnn t}. \end{equation*}(1.10)

This is the complex form. Converting it to a real form uses the Euler relations $2j\sin\theta = e^{j\theta}-e^{-j\theta}$ and $2\cos\theta = e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta}$ [4], giving

\begin{equation*} x(t) = (a_1+a_2)\cos\wnn t + j(a_1-a_2)\sin\wnn t = A_1\sin\wnn t + A_2\cos\wnn t \end{equation*}

with $A_1=(a_1-a_2)j$, $A_2=a_1+a_2$, and

\begin{equation*} A = \sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2}, \qquad \phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{A_2}{A_1}. \end{equation*}(1.11)

1.7Summary of Week 2

1.8Why the model needs a damper

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x(t) + c\dd x(t) + kx(t) = 0\;} \end{equation*}(1.12)
Explanation and derivation

Inman puts the motivation exactly right:

The damping force is

\begin{equation*} f_c = c\,\dd x(t), \end{equation*}(1.13)

with $c$ the damping coefficient in N$\cdot$s$\cdot$m$^{-1}$, or in strict SI base units, kg$\cdot$s$^{-1}$ [1]. Both appear in memos; they are the same thing.

Applying $m\ddd x = -f_c-f_k$ to the FBD of Figure 1.1 gives

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x(t) + c\dd x(t) + kx(t) = 0\;} \end{equation*}(1.12)

subject to $x(0)=x_0$, $\dd x(0)=v_0$.

1.9The characteristic equation

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\lambda^2 + c\lambda + k = 0\;} \qquad\text{(the \emph{characteristic equation})} \end{equation*}(1.14)
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;c_{cr} = 2\sqrt{km} = 2m\wnn\;} \qquad\text{[N$\cdot$s$\cdot$m$^{-1}$]} \end{equation*}(1.15)
$c_{cr}$
critical damping coefficient: the smallest $c$ that stops oscillation
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\zeta = \frac{c}{c_{cr}} = \frac{c}{2m\wnn} = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{km}}\;} \end{equation*}(1.16)
$\zeta$
damping ratio: $<1$ under-, $=1$ critically, $>1$ overdamped
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\lambda_{1,2} = -\zeta\wnn \pm \wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\;} \end{equation*}(1.17)

Exam angle

Steps 1–5 are the whole of a 5-mark part. Do not skip Step 3 (“for a solution to exist, $ae^{\lambda t}\neq0$”) — it carries a mark in every memo. The 2023 memo also awards a mark for explicitly stating the substitution $c_{cr}=2\sqrt{km}=2m\wnn$ and $\zeta = c/c_{cr}$ before writing Eq. (1.17).
Explanation and derivation — 2012, 2021 and 2023 Q1 ask this derivation

This is the derivation that has been Question 1 in 2012, 2021 and 2023, and it is worth writing out in full every single time.

Step 1 — assume an exponential solution:

\begin{equation*} x(t) = ae^{\lambda t}, \qquad \dd x(t) = a\lambda e^{\lambda t}, \qquad \ddd x(t) = a\lambda^2 e^{\lambda t}. \end{equation*}

Step 2 — substitute into Eq. (1.12):

\begin{equation*} \big(m\lambda^2 + c\lambda + k\big)ae^{\lambda t} = 0 . \end{equation*}

Step 3 — for a non-trivial solution $ae^{\lambda t}\neq0$, so:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\lambda^2 + c\lambda + k = 0\;} \qquad\text{(the \emph{characteristic equation})} \end{equation*}(1.14)

Step 4 — solve with the quadratic formula:

\begin{equation*} \lambda_{1,2} = -\frac{c}{2m} \pm \frac{1}{2m}\sqrt{c^2-4km} \end{equation*}(1.18)

Step 5 — non-dimensionalise. Everything now depends on the sign of the discriminant $c^2-4km$. Define the critical damping coefficient

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;c_{cr} = 2\sqrt{km} = 2m\wnn\;} \qquad\text{[N$\cdot$s$\cdot$m$^{-1}$]} \end{equation*}(1.15)

and the dimensionless damping ratio

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\zeta = \frac{c}{c_{cr}} = \frac{c}{2m\wnn} = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{km}}\;} \end{equation*}(1.16)

Substituting into Eq. (1.18) gives the form used throughout the module:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\lambda_{1,2} = -\zeta\wnn \pm \wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\;} \end{equation*}(1.17)

1.10The four regimes

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\wdd = \wnn\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\;}\qquad\text{[rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$]} \end{equation*}(1.19)
$\omega_d$
damped natural frequency: the frequency of the decaying oscillation
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;x(t) = Ae^{-\zeta\wnn t}\sin(\wdd t + \phi)\;} \end{equation*}(1.20)
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;x(t) = (a_1 + a_2 t)\,e^{-\wnn t}\;} \end{equation*}(1.21)

The whole of Question 1 in one box

\begin{align*} m\ddd x+c\dd x+kx&=0,\quad x=ae^{\lambda t} \;\Rightarrow\; m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_{1,2}=-\zeta\wnn\pm\wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\\[4pt] \zeta=0:&\quad x(t)=A\sin(\wnn t+\phi)\\ 0<\zeta<1:&\quad x(t)=Ae^{-\zeta\wnn t}\sin(\wdd t+\phi),\quad \wdd=\wnn\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\\ \zeta=1:&\quad x(t)=(a_1+a_2t)e^{-\wnn t}\\ \zeta>1:&\quad x(t)=e^{-\zeta\wnn t}\big(a_1e^{-\wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}t}+a_2e^{+\wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}t}\big) \end{align*}
Explanation and derivation

The sign of $\zeta^2-1$ determines everything.

1.10.1Undamped, $\zeta=0$

$c=0$, so $\lambda_{1,2}=\pm j\sqrt{k/m}=\pm j\wnn$. Two purely imaginary roots give pure, undecaying oscillation (Week 2).

1.10.2Underdamped, $0<\zeta<1$

The discriminant is negative. Factor out $(-1)$ to make the imaginary part explicit [1]:

\begin{equation*} \sqrt{\zeta^2-1} = \sqrt{(1-\zeta^2)(-1)} = \sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\;j, \end{equation*}

so

\begin{equation*} \lambda_{1,2} = -\zeta\wnn \pm \wnn\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\;j . \end{equation*}

Define the damped natural frequency

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\wdd = \wnn\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\;}\qquad\text{[rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$]} \end{equation*}(1.19)

The solution is then

\begin{equation*} x(t) = e^{-\zeta\wnn t}\big(a_1e^{j\wdd t} + a_2e^{-j\wdd t}\big) \end{equation*}

which, via the Euler relations, collapses to the real form

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;x(t) = Ae^{-\zeta\wnn t}\sin(\wdd t + \phi)\;} \end{equation*}(1.20)

An exponentially decaying sinusoid: the sine gives the oscillation, the exponential $Ae^{-\zeta\wnn t}$ is the decay envelope. This is by far the most common case in practice and in the exam.

The constants from the initial conditions [1]:

\begin{equation*} A = \frac{\sqrt{(v_0+\zeta\wnn x_0)^2 + (x_0\wdd)^2}}{\wdd}, \qquad \phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{x_0\wdd}{v_0+\zeta\wnn x_0} \end{equation*}(1.22)

Sanity check: setting $\zeta=0$ (so $\wdd=\wnn$) recovers Eq. (1.5) exactly.

1.10.3Overdamped, $\zeta>1$

The discriminant is positive, giving two distinct negative real roots $\lambda_{1,2}=-\zeta\wnn\mp\wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}$ and

\begin{equation*} x(t) = e^{-\zeta\wnn t}\left(a_1e^{-\wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\,t} + a_2e^{+\wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\,t}\right) \end{equation*}(1.23)

with [1]

\begin{equation*} a_1 = \frac{-v_0 + \big(-\zeta+\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\big)\wnn x_0}{2\wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}}, \qquad a_2 = \frac{v_0 + \big(\zeta+\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\big)\wnn x_0}{2\wnn\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}} . \end{equation*}

There is no oscillation. The mass returns to rest exponentially. Note it can cross zero at most once (if $v_0$ is large and opposite in sign to $x_0$).

1.10.4Critically damped, $\zeta=1$

The discriminant is zero; the roots are repeated, $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=-\wnn$. Repeated roots of a second-order ODE require the second solution to carry a factor $t$:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;x(t) = (a_1 + a_2 t)\,e^{-\wnn t}\;} \end{equation*}(1.21)

with $a_1=x_0$ and $a_2=v_0+\wnn x_0$.

Critical damping is the boundary between oscillatory and non-oscillatory motion, and it is the fastest possible return to equilibrium without overshoot. This is why door closers, instrument needles and vehicle dampers are designed near $\zeta\approx0.7$–$1$.

1.11Logarithmic decrement: getting $\zeta$ out of a measurement

\begin{equation*} \delta = \zeta\wnn\frac{2\pi}{\wnn\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}} = \frac{2\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\zeta = \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}}\;} \end{equation*}(1.24)
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\delta = \frac{1}{n}\ln\frac{x(t)}{x(t+nT)}\;} \end{equation*}(1.25)
$\delta$
logarithmic decrement
$T$
damped period, $2\pi/\omega_d$
$n$
number of whole periods between the two peaks used

From a decay record to $m$, $c$, $k$

  1. Period. $T_d = \dfrac{t_{\text{last peak}} - t_{\text{first peak}}}{N}$ where $N$ = number of intervals (peaks $-1$).
  2. Damped natural frequency. $\wdd = 2\pi/T_d$.
  3. Log decrement. $\delta = \dfrac1n\ln\dfrac{x_1}{x_{1+n}}$, using amplitudes measured from the settled/DC level, not from zero.
  4. Damping ratio. $\zeta = \dfrac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}}$.
  5. Natural frequency. $\wnn = \dfrac{\wdd}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}$.
  6. Mass (if $k$ known from a static test): $m = \dfrac{k}{\wnn^2}$.
  7. Damping coefficient. $c = 2\zeta\sqrt{km} = 2\zeta m\wnn$.

Exam angle

Two mistakes cost marks in this chain every year: (i) counting peaks instead of intervals — 10 peaks span 9 periods, not 10; (ii) forgetting to subtract the DC offset before taking the ratio. In the 2023 term-3 paper, Q3 the accelerometer signal has a $4.905$ m$\cdot$s$^{-2}$ offset, and the memo computes $\delta = \frac16\ln\frac{15.70-4.905}{8.16-4.905}$. Subtracting first is not optional — the ratio of raw values is not the ratio of the amplitudes.
Worked example — Term-3 paper 2023, Q3 — full system identification (this is Practical 1 on paper)
A mass slides on a frictionless inclined plane. A force–displacement test gives $F=250$ N at $x = 0.2$ m. A DC accelerometer records the free decay with a DC offset of $4.905$ m$\cdot$s$^{-2}$; peak 1 is at $t=0.40$ s with $15.70$ m$\cdot$s$^{-2}$ and peak 7 at $t=5.29$ s with $8.16$ m$\cdot$s$^{-2}$.

(a) Stiffness — static test, Hooke's law:

\begin{equation*} k=\frac{F}{x}=\frac{250}{0.2}=1250\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^{-1} \end{equation*}

(b) Mass and damping — the chain:

\begin{align*} T_d &= \frac{5.29-0.40}{6} = 0.815\ \text{s} &&\text{(7 peaks = 6 intervals)}\\ \wdd &= \frac{2\pi}{T_d} = 7.709\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\\ \delta &= \frac16\ln\!\left(\frac{15.70-4.905}{8.16-4.905}\right) = \frac16\ln(3.316) = 0.1998\\ \zeta &= \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}} = \frac{0.1998}{\sqrt{39.478+0.0399}} = 0.03179\\ \wnn &= \frac{\wdd}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}} = \frac{7.709}{0.99950} = 7.713\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\\ m &= \frac{k}{\wnn^2} = \frac{1250}{59.49} = 21.01\ \text{kg}\\ c &= 2\zeta\sqrt{km} = 2(0.03179)\sqrt{1250\times21.01} = 10.3\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} \end{align*}

(c) The DC offset — a DC accelerometer responds to static as well as dynamic acceleration. The constant offset is the component of gravity along the measurement axis (down the incline).

(d) Incline angle — from that interpretation:

\begin{equation*} g_{\text{meas}} = g\sin\theta \;\Rightarrow\; \theta = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4.905}{9.81}\right) = 30^\circ \quad\checkmark \end{equation*}

(e) Unstretched spring length — static force balance along the incline:

\begin{equation*} mg\sin\theta = k\Delta x \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta x = \frac{(21.01)(9.81)\sin30^\circ}{1250} = 0.08244\ \text{m} = 82.4\ \text{mm} \end{equation*}
so with a stretched length of 130 mm, $x_0 = 130 - 82.4 = 47.6$ mm.

Note the structure: one physical system, six sub-answers, each feeding the next. This is the single most valuable question type to rehearse, because an error in step (b) propagates into (d) and (e) — but if you show the method, the memo's “non-fundamental error” clause protects most of the marks.

Explanation and derivation

You cannot measure $c$ with a ruler. Inman is explicit: “Both mass and stiffness can be determined by static tests; however, damping requires a dynamic test to measure” [1]. The standard dynamic test is the free-decay record.

Because the envelope is $Ae^{-\zeta\wnn t}$, the ratio of any two peaks one period apart is a constant. Define the logarithmic decrement

\begin{equation*} \delta = \ln\frac{x(t)}{x(t+T)} . \end{equation*}(1.26)

Substituting the underdamped form and using $\wdd T = 2\pi$ (so the sine terms are equal):

\begin{equation*} \delta = \ln\frac{Ae^{-\zeta\wnn t}\sin(\wdd t+\phi)}{Ae^{-\zeta\wnn(t+T)}\sin(\wdd t+\wdd T+\phi)} = \ln e^{\zeta\wnn T} = \zeta\wnn T . \end{equation*}

Since $T$ is the damped period $2\pi/\wdd$,

\begin{equation*} \delta = \zeta\wnn\frac{2\pi}{\wnn\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}} = \frac{2\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\zeta = \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}}\;} \end{equation*}(1.24)

For better accuracy, use $n$ cycles instead of one — this is the form on the formula sheet:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\delta = \frac{1}{n}\ln\frac{x(t)}{x(t+nT)}\;} \end{equation*}(1.25)

1.11.1The identification chain

This chain is Slot C (Table 2.1) and appears in some form almost every year. Learn it as a sequence, because each step feeds the next:

1.12Sanity checks and typical magnitudes

Reference — Order-of-magnitude sense checks

Exam angle

Also note $\wdd \approx \wnn$ for small $\zeta$: at $\zeta=0.1$, $\wdd = 0.995\wnn$, a $0.5\%$ difference. If a question gives you $\zeta<0.1$ and asks for $\wnn$ from a measured period, you may quote $\wnn\approx\wdd$ provided you state the assumption. Do not do this when $\zeta>0.3$.
Explanation and derivation

If you compute $\zeta = 3$ for a car suspension, or $\zeta=0.0001$ for a rubber mount, you have made an arithmetic error — most often forgetting the factor 2 in $c_{cr}=2\sqrt{km}$.

1.13Why measurement matters

1.14Measuring the three parameters

Reference — How each model parameter is obtained experimentally

The sentence to quote

“Both mass and stiffness can be determined by static tests; however, damping requires a dynamic test to measure.” — Inman §1.6 [1]
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;J = \frac{gT^2r_0^2(m_0+m)}{4\pi^2 l} - J_0\;} \end{equation*}(1.27)

Exam angle

This inversion — measure a frequency, back out a material or geometric property — is a favourite. The 2020 term-3 paper's column question (Q1) is the same idea run forwards: given geometry and material, predict $\wnn$, then ask what change in mass or stiffness shifts it by 10%. Remember $\wnn\propto\sqrt{k/m}$, so a 10% change in $\wnn$ needs a 21% change in $k$ or a 17% change in $m$ ($1.1^2 = 1.21$; $1/1.1^2 = 0.826$).
Explanation and derivation

1.14.1Moment of inertia: the trifilar suspension

For an irregular object, hang a disk of known $J_0$, mass $m_0$ and radius $r_0$ on three wires of length $l$, place the object on it with its mass centre on the axis, and measure the torsional period $T$. Then [1]

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;J = \frac{gT^2r_0^2(m_0+m)}{4\pi^2 l} - J_0\;} \end{equation*}(1.27)

1.14.2Elastic modulus from a vibration test

Inman's Example 1.6.1 is a good template [1]. A steel beam of length $l = 1$ m and $I = 10^{-9}$ m$^4$ with a tip mass $m = 6$ kg oscillates with period $T=0.62$ s. Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ and $k=3EI/l^3$,

\begin{equation*} T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{ml^3}{3EI}} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad E = \frac{4\pi^2 ml^3}{3T^2I} = \frac{4\pi^2(6)(1)^3}{3(0.62)^2(10^{-9})} = 205\times10^9\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^{-2} \end{equation*}

1.15Sensors, and what a DC accelerometer actually reads

Reference — Accelerometer types and the DC-offset issue

Two consequences you must be able to state (2023 term-3 paper, Q3(c)–(d))

  1. The DC offset must be subtracted before computing amplitude ratios for the logarithmic decrement. The offset is not part of the vibration.
  2. The offset is itself useful information: if the sensitive axis lies along an incline of angle $\theta$, the offset is $g\sin\theta$, so $\theta = \sin^{-1}(g_{\text{meas}}/g)$. In 2023 an offset of $4.905 = 9.81\sin30^\circ$ proves the incline is $30^\circ$.

1.16Practical 1: the whole identification chain in the lab

Practical 1 method, and how it becomes an exam question

  1. $k$ statically. Add known masses, measure the deflection with the ruler, plot $F=mg$ against $x$. The slope is $k$. A straight line also confirms the spring is linear over the working range.
  2. Record a free decay with the accelerometer. Displace, release, capture.
  3. $T_d$ and $\wdd$ from the peak spacing.
  4. $\delta$ and $\zeta$ from the peak amplitudes (offset-corrected).
  5. $\wnn = \wdd/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$, then $m = k/\wnn^2$, then $c = 2\zeta\sqrt{km}$.
  6. Comment on the damping model: plot the peak amplitudes on a log scale against time. A straight line on a log plot confirms exponential decay, so viscous damping is appropriate. Curvature — especially a straight line on a linear plot — indicates Coulomb friction, and a viscous model would then be wrong.

Exam angle

The 2023 term-3 paper, Q3, is Practical 1 transcribed onto a question paper, with the plot and the peak table supplied. The full worked solution is in Week 1. Expect a variant. The “comment on the suitability of viscous damping” part is worth marks and needs the log-plot argument, not just an assertion.
Explanation and derivation

Practical 1 [13] gives you a ruler, an accelerometer, a data acquisition system, a computer, and known masses, and asks you to determine $k$, $m$ and $c$ for a SDOF rig — and then to comment on the suitability of modelling the damping as viscous.

1.17Quantifying a vibration signal

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\text{dB} = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{x_{\text{rms}}}{x_{\text{ref}}}\right)^{\!2} = 20\log_{10}\frac{x_{\text{rms}}}{x_{\text{ref}}}\;} \end{equation*}(1.28)
$x_{\text{rms}}$
rms value of the measured signal
$x_{\text{ref}}$
reference value (ISO 1683; reference table in Week 1)
Reference — ISO 1683:2015 reference values

Decibel rules of thumb

  • A factor of 2 in amplitude $= 20\log_{10}2 = \mathbf{6.02}$ dB.
  • A factor of 10 in amplitude $=\mathbf{20}$ dB.
  • A factor of $\sqrt2$ (the half-power point) $=\mathbf{3.01}$ dB.
The factor 20 (not 10) is because the reference is defined on the squared quantity — power goes as amplitude squared, and $10\log_{10}(x^2) = 20\log_{10}x$.
Explanation and derivation

Lecture 1 gives the three standard amplitude measures [4].

1.17.1Peak, mean and rms

\begin{align*} \text{Peak value:}\quad & x_{\text{peak}} = \max|x(t)|\\ \text{Mean value:}\quad & \bar x = \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T x(t)\,dt\\ \text{RMS value:}\quad & x_{\text{rms}} = \left[\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T x^2(t)\,dt\right]^{1/2} \end{align*}(1.29)

For a pure sinusoid of amplitude $A$: $\bar x = 0$, $x_{\text{rms}} = A/\sqrt2 = 0.707A$. The mean is useless for a zero-mean vibration, which is why rms is the standard measure — it is proportional to the square root of the average energy.

1.17.2The decibel scale

Vibration amplitudes span many orders of magnitude, so a logarithmic scale is used [4]:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\text{dB} = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{x_{\text{rms}}}{x_{\text{ref}}}\right)^{\!2} = 20\log_{10}\frac{x_{\text{rms}}}{x_{\text{ref}}}\;} \end{equation*}(1.28)

The reference values are set by ISO 1683:2015:

1.18Between frequencies: the conversion table

Reference — Frequency and period conversions

Exam angle

Watch for “wave height of 1 m (peak-to-trough)”. The amplitude $Y$ is half of a peak-to-trough figure. The 2022 term-3 paper, Q4, gives the wave height as 1 m, so $Y = 0.5$ m. Halving errors here propagate into every subsequent answer.

Practice questions — Week 1

Q 1.1Term-3 paper 2026, Question 1[8]

The single-DOF system in Figure 1.7 has the equation of motion $m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=f(t)$.

(a) Define the degree of freedom of a system. [2]
(b) Would there be a gravitational term in the equation of motion? Explain why or why not. [2]
(c) Describe the effect of damping on the free response of the system. There are four cases. [4]

For (b): where is $x=0$?
Step 1 — (a) Definition

The number of degrees of freedom is the minimum number of independent coordinates needed to describe the position of every mass of the system at any instant. Here it is one: $x$.

Step 2 — (b) Gravity

No. $x$ is measured from the static equilibrium position, where the spring already carries the weight: $k\delta_{st}=mg$. In the force balance $m\ddot x=mg-k(\delta_{st}+x)-c\dot x$ the terms $mg$ and $k\delta_{st}$ cancel. Gravity only shifts the equilibrium position; it is not a restoring force.

Step 3 — (c) Four damping cases
  • Undamped, $\zeta=0$: oscillates forever at $\omega_n$ with constant amplitude.
  • Underdamped, $0<\zeta<1$: oscillates at $\omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$ inside an exponentially decaying envelope $e^{-\zeta\omega_nt}$.
  • Critically damped, $\zeta=1$: does not oscillate; the fastest return to equilibrium without overshoot.
  • Overdamped, $\zeta>1$: does not oscillate; returns more slowly than the critically damped case.
Answer. (a) Minimum number of independent coordinates. (b) No — measured from static equilibrium, $mg$ cancels $k\delta_{st}$. (c) The four cases above; a sketch of each earns the marks quickly.

Matches the 2026 memo.

Q 1.2Term-3 paper 2021, Question 1(a)[8]

The equation of motion of a single-DOF system is $m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=f(t)$. Derive the forms of the free response for (i) undamped, (ii) underdamped, (iii) critically damped and (iv) overdamped systems. You need not find the constants from initial conditions.

Substitute $x=ae^{\lambda t}$ and look at the sign of $\zeta^2-1$.
Step 1 — Characteristic equation

With $f=0$, try $x=ae^{\lambda t}$: $(m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k)ae^{\lambda t}=0$. For a non-trivial solution $m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k=0$, so with $c=2\zeta m\omega_n$:

\[\lambda_{1,2}=-\zeta\omega_n\pm\omega_n\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\]Step 2 — The four cases

(i) $\zeta=0$: $\lambda=\pm j\omega_n$, so $x=a_1e^{j\omega_nt}+a_2e^{-j\omega_nt}=A\sin(\omega_nt+\phi)$.

(ii) $\zeta<1$: complex roots $-\zeta\omega_n\pm j\omega_d$ with $\omega_d=\omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$, so $x=Ae^{-\zeta\omega_nt}\sin(\omega_dt+\phi)$.

(iii) $\zeta=1$: repeated root $\lambda=-\omega_n$. The second solution is $te^{-\omega_nt}$, so $x=(a_1+a_2t)e^{-\omega_nt}$.

(iv) $\zeta>1$: two real negative roots, so $x=e^{-\zeta\omega_nt}\left(a_1e^{-\omega_n\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\,t}+a_2e^{\omega_n\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}\,t}\right)$.

Answer. The four forms above. Mind (iii): with a repeated root the solution is $(a_1+a_2t)e^{-\omega_nt}$.

Matches the 2021 memo, except case (iii): the memo prints $(a_1+a_2)e^{-\omega_nt}$, which has only one constant and cannot meet two initial conditions. The correct form has $a_2t$.

Q 1.3Term-3 paper 2026, Question 4[10]

A dynamic weighing system on a production line is a spring–mass–damper with known natural frequency $\omega_n=10$ rad/s (scale alone) and stiffness $k=1000$ N/m. The scale mass $m_1$ is unknown. A box of unknown mass $m_2$ falls onto it and the system oscillates. The measured acceleration is shown in Figure 1.8(b); the labelled peaks are:

PeakABCD
$t$ [s]0.572.113.655.19
$\ddot x$ [m/s²]15.849.485.673.39

(a) What type of damping is modelled? Explain from the response whether this is an appropriate choice. [3]
(b) Determine the box mass $m_2$. Show all calculations and assumptions. [7]

How many oscillations are there between two labelled peaks?
Step 1 — (a) Type of damping

Viscous damping (the dashpot $c$). It is appropriate: the peaks decay exponentially — the ratio between successive labelled peaks is constant (15.84/9.48 = 1.67, 9.48/5.67 = 1.67, 5.67/3.39 = 1.67). Coulomb damping would give a linear decay.

Step 2 — Scale mass

$m_1=k/\omega_n^2=1000/10^2=10$ kg.

Step 3 — Damped period — count the cycles

Between A and C there are four cycles (two between each labelled peak): $\omega_d=2\pi\cdot4/(3.65-0.57)=8.16$ rad/s.

Step 4 — Damping ratio

Acceleration decays with the same envelope as displacement, so $\delta=\frac14\ln(15.84/5.67)=0.257$ and $\zeta=\delta/\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}=0.0408$.

Step 5 — Total mass

$\omega_n=\omega_d/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}=8.17$ rad/s, so $m=k/\omega_n^2=1000/8.17^2=15.0$ kg and $m_2=15.0-10=4.99$ kg.

Answer. (a) Viscous, appropriate because the decay is exponential. (b) $m_2\approx5.0$ kg ($\zeta=0.041$, $\omega_d=8.16$ rad/s). Assumptions: $k$ unchanged by the box, the box stays on the scale and moves with it.

Labelled peaks are two cycles apart

Treating A–B as one period gives $\omega_d=4.08$ rad/s and $m=60$ kg — a 50 kg box. Count the oscillations on the plot before using the table.

Printed: $m_2=4.98$ kg ✓ (recomputed 4.99 kg; using A and D over six cycles gives the same). Recomputed in verify.py.

Q 1.4Term-3 paper 2021, Question 2[10]

Mass $m_1=1$ kg hangs from a spring $k=500$ N/m and a damper $c=50$ N·s/m. Mass $m_2=4$ kg is held to $m_1$ by a magnet (Figure 1.9). The system is at rest with the spring stretched by $\Delta_{m_1+m_2}$. The magnet releases and $m_2$ falls away. $x(t)$ is the motion of $m_1$, positive downward. Use $g=9.81$ m/s².

(a) What is $\Delta_{m_1}$, the rest position of $m_1$ after $m_2$ has detached? [1]
(b) Is the system under-, over- or critically damped? [1]
(c) Determine $x(t)$ if $\zeta$ were 0.2. [5]
(d) The damper is damaged if $m_1$ rises more than 30 mm above the unstretched-spring position (i.e. the spring is compressed by more than 30 mm) after $m_2$ detaches. Sketch $x(t)$. Is this threshold exceeded (with $\zeta=0.2$)? [3]

Measure $x$ from the equilibrium of $m_1$ alone; the start is then $x_0=m_2g/k$.
Step 1 — (a) New rest position

$\Delta_{m_1}=m_1g/k=9.81/500=19.6$ mm below the unstretched length.

Step 2 — (b) Damping

$\zeta=c/(2\sqrt{km_1})=50/(2\sqrt{500})=1.12>1$: overdamped. (Part (c) then asks "what if" with $\zeta=0.2$.)

Step 3 — (c) Response with ζ = 0.2

Measure $x$ from the new equilibrium. Initial conditions: $x_0=\Delta_{m_1+m_2}-\Delta_{m_1}=m_2g/k=78.5$ mm, $v_0=0$.

$\omega_n=\sqrt{500/1}=22.36$ rad/s, $\omega_d=22.36\sqrt{1-0.04}=21.91$ rad/s. With $x=Ae^{-\zeta\omega_nt}\sin(\omega_dt+\phi)$ and $v_0=0$:

\[\phi=\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_d}{\zeta\omega_n}=1.369\ \text{rad},\qquad A=\frac{x_0}{\sin\phi}=80.1\ \text{mm}\] \[x(t)=80.1\,e^{-4.47t}\sin(21.91t+1.369)\ \text{mm}\]Step 4 — (d) Maximum compression

The first extreme above equilibrium is at $\dot x=0$: $t=\pi/\omega_d=0.143$ s, where $x=-x_0e^{-\zeta\pi/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}=-41.3$ mm. That is 41.3 mm above the $m_1$ equilibrium, which is itself 19.6 mm below the unstretched length, so the spring is compressed by $41.3-19.6=21.7$ mm.

If you measured $x$ from the release position instead, the whole curve shifts by 78.5 mm; the extreme positions, and the verdict, are the same.

Sketch: starts at +78.5 mm with zero slope, swings to −41.3 mm at 0.143 s, then decays about zero at 21.9 rad/s.

Answer. (a) 19.6 mm. (b) Overdamped, $\zeta=1.12$. (c) $x=80.1e^{-4.47t}\sin(21.91t+1.369)$ mm. (d) Maximum compression 21.7 mm < 30 mm: the damper survives.

Printed: $\Delta_{m_1}=19.62$ mm ✓, $\zeta=1.118$ ✓, $A=0.080$ ✓, $\phi=1.372$ ✓, compression 22.1 mm (recomputed 21.7 mm; the memo prints $t_{max}=0.1414$ s where $\pi/\omega_d=0.1434$ s). Same conclusion. Recomputed in verify.py.

Q 1.5A2 2024, Question 1 (repeat of the 2020 term-3 paper, Question 2)[10]

A swing door (width $L=900$ mm, mass $m=60$ kg, $J=7.2$ kg·m² about its centroid, about an axis parallel to the hinges) hangs on vertical hinges at one edge and has a torsional spring $k=25$ N·m/rad (unstretched when the door is closed) and a torsional viscous damper. (a) Derive the equation of motion. (b) Find $\omega_n$. (c) What damping makes it critically damped? (d) Critically damped and closed, it is pushed violently (an impulse). What initial angular velocity opens it to at most 70°?

Which point does the door rotate about? Use the parallel-axis theorem before anything else.
(a) EOM about the hinge The door rotates about the hinge, not its centroid. Parallel-axis theorem: $J_O=J+m(L/2)^2=7.2+60(0.45)^2=19.35$ kg·m². Moments about the hinge: $J_O\ddot\theta+c\dot\theta+k\theta=0$. (b) $\omega_n=\sqrt{k/J_O}=\sqrt{25/19.35}=1.137$ rad/s. (c) $c_{cr}=2\sqrt{kJ_O}=2\sqrt{25\times19.35}=44.0$ N·m·s/rad. (d) Critically damped with $\theta_0=0$: $\theta(t)=\dot\theta_0\,t\,e^{-\omega_nt}$. Maximum where $\dot\theta=0$: $t=1/\omega_n=0.88$ s, so $\theta_{max}=\dot\theta_0/(\omega_ne)$. Then $\dot\theta_0=\theta_{max}\,\omega_n e=(70\pi/180)(1.137)(2.718)=3.77$ rad/s.
Answer. $J_O\ddot\theta+c\dot\theta+k\theta=0$ with $J_O=19.35$ kg·m²; $\omega_n=1.137$ rad/s; $c_{cr}=44.0$ N·m·s/rad; $\dot\theta_0=3.77$ rad/s (maximum at 0.88 s).

No 2024 memo. $J=7.2$ kg·m² is as given (a uniform 60 kg, 0.9 m slab would have 4.05); use the given value. Method checked against the 2020 term-3 memo, Q2 ($A=J+m(w/2)^2$, $\theta(t)=(A_1+A_2t)e^{-\omega_nt}$, $\dot\theta_0=\alpha e\omega_n$) ✓; numbers recomputed.

Week 2

Coulomb damping, modelling and the energy method

Lectures 3–4

This week in brief

  • Coulomb (dry friction) damping gives a linear decay: the amplitude drops by $4\mu mg/k$ per cycle. The frequency stays $\omega_n$, and motion stops inside the dead zone $|x|\le\mu mg/k$, usually not at zero.
  • Viscous damping decays exponentially and Coulomb damping linearly. Use the shape of the envelope to say which one a record shows.
  • Equivalent stiffness: springs in series add as reciprocals, in parallel directly. Beams and shafts act as springs, $k=$ force per deflection, and a spring at an angle contributes $k\cos^2\theta$.
  • Kinematic constraints (rolling, pulleys, rigid links) reduce a system to one coordinate. Write every displacement in terms of that coordinate before writing any energy.
  • Energy method: $T+U=$ constant, so $\frac{d}{dt}(T+U)=0$. Write $T=\tfrac12m_{eq}\dot x^2$ and $U=\tfrac12k_{eq}x^2$, then $\omega_n=\sqrt{k_{eq}/m_{eq}}$.
  • Trap: a disc rolling without slip has $T=\tfrac12m v^2+\tfrac12J\omega^2$. The rotational term is the one that gets forgotten.

2.1Why friction is different

Exam angle

Table 2.1 is the answer to 2012 Q5(a) and 2022 Q3(b) almost verbatim. Given two decay plots, look at the envelope: curved (exponential) $\Rightarrow$ viscous; straight $\Rightarrow$ Coulomb. Then look at where it stops: at zero, or offset.
Explanation and derivation

A viscous damper produces a force proportional to velocity. Dry friction produces a force of constant magnitude that always opposes the direction of motion. That single difference makes the equation of motion nonlinear and produces qualitatively different behaviour:

2.2The equation of motion

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x(t) + \mu N\operatorname{sgn}(\dd x(t)) + kx(t) = 0\;} \qquad \operatorname{sgn}(\dd x) = \begin{cases} -1 & \dd x<0\\ 0 & \dd x=0\\ +1 & \dd x>0 \end{cases} \end{equation*}(2.1)
$\mu$
kinetic friction coefficient
$N$
normal force on the sliding surface
$\operatorname{sgn}$
sign function: $+1$, $0$ or $-1$
Explanation and derivation

The friction force depends on the direction of motion [5]:

\begin{equation*} f_f = \begin{cases} -\mu N & \dd x(t) > 0\\ 0 \ldots \mu_s N & \dd x(t) = 0\\ +\mu N & \dd x(t) < 0 \end{cases} \end{equation*}(2.2)

where $\mu$ is the kinetic coefficient of friction and $\mu_s$ the static one. The equation of motion is therefore piecewise:

\begin{equation*} m\ddd x(t) + kx(t) = \begin{cases} -\mu N & \dd x(t) > 0\\ 0 \ldots \mu_s N & \dd x(t) = 0\\ +\mu N & \dd x(t) < 0 \end{cases} \end{equation*}(2.3)

which is written compactly using the signum function as

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x(t) + \mu N\operatorname{sgn}(\dd x(t)) + kx(t) = 0\;} \qquad \operatorname{sgn}(\dd x) = \begin{cases} -1 & \dd x<0\\ 0 & \dd x=0\\ +1 & \dd x>0 \end{cases} \end{equation*}(2.1)

For a horizontal surface $N = mg$; on an incline $N = mg\cos\alpha$; if a spring presses the mass against the surface, $N$ includes that too. Always state what $N$ is.

2.3Solving it, half cycle by half cycle

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;x(t) = \left(x_0-\frac{\mu N}{k}\right)\cos\wnn t + \frac{\mu N}{k}\;} \end{equation*}(2.4)
Explanation and derivation — term-3 papers ask the half-cycle solution

The trick is that within any half cycle the sign of $\dd x$ is fixed, so Eq. (2.3) is a linear ODE with a constant forcing term $\pm\mu N$. Solve it, then hand the end conditions to the next half cycle.

First half cycle. Release from rest at $x(0)=x_0>0$, so the mass starts moving left and $\dd x<0$:

\begin{equation*} m\ddd x + kx = \mu N . \end{equation*}

The solution is the homogeneous undamped solution plus a constant particular solution $x_p = \mu N/k$:

\begin{equation*} x(t) = A_1\cos\wnn t + B_1\sin\wnn t + \frac{\mu N}{k}. \end{equation*}

Applying $x(0)=x_0$ and $\dd x(0)=0$ gives $B_1=0$ and $A_1 = x_0-\mu N/k$, so for $0\le t\le\pi/\wnn$ [5]:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;x(t) = \left(x_0-\frac{\mu N}{k}\right)\cos\wnn t + \frac{\mu N}{k}\;} \end{equation*}(2.4)

The motion continues until $\dd x = 0$ again, which first happens at $t=\pi/\wnn$ — exactly half an undamped period.

Second half cycle. Now $\dd x>0$ and the sign flips: $m\ddd x + kx = -\mu N$. Using $x(\pi/\wnn) = 2\mu N/k - x_0$ and $\dd x(\pi/\wnn)=0$ as the new initial conditions,

\begin{equation*} x(t) = \left(x_0-\frac{3\mu N}{k}\right)\cos\wnn t - \frac{\mu N}{k}, \qquad \frac{\pi}{\wnn} < t < \frac{2\pi}{\wnn} \end{equation*}(2.5)

General $n$-th half cycle ($n = 0,1,2,\dots$):

\begin{equation*} x(t) = \left[x_0 - (2n+1)\frac{\mu N}{k}\right]\cos\wnn t + (-1)^n\frac{\mu N}{k} \end{equation*}(2.6)

2.4The three consequences

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\text{slope} = -\frac{2\mu N\wnn}{\pi k}\;} \qquad\text{[m$\cdot$s$^{-1}$]} \end{equation*}(2.7)
$\text{slope}$
rate at which the peak amplitude falls (the decay envelope is a straight line)
\begin{equation*} k|x| \le \mu_s N \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;|x_{\text{final}}| \le \frac{\mu N}{k}\;} \end{equation*}(2.8)
$\mu_s$
static friction coefficient
$x_{\text{final}}$
position where the mass comes to rest
Explanation and derivation

2.4.1Linear decay

Each half cycle the amplitude drops by exactly $2\mu N/k$, regardless of how big it is. Plotting peak amplitude against time therefore gives a straight line with slope

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\text{slope} = -\frac{2\mu N\wnn}{\pi k}\;} \qquad\text{[m$\cdot$s$^{-1}$]} \end{equation*}(2.7)

(derived by dividing the loss per half cycle, $2\mu N/k$, by the duration of a half cycle, $\pi/\wnn$) [5].

2.4.2The frequency is unchanged

Notice that $\wnn$ appears in Eq. (2.6), not some damped $\wdd$. Dry friction does not change the frequency of oscillation. This is a clean discriminator: if a measured decay has the same period as the undamped prediction $2\pi/\sqrt{k/m}$, the damping is Coulomb, not viscous.

2.4.3It stops, and not at zero

The oscillation stops when the spring force can no longer overcome static friction:

\begin{equation*} k|x| \le \mu_s N \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;|x_{\text{final}}| \le \frac{\mu N}{k}\;} \end{equation*}(2.8)

The band $|x|\le\mu N/k$ is called the dead zone or stiction band. The mass comes to rest somewhere inside it, not at $x=0$. Lecture 3 says it plainly: “Note that the mass does not come to rest at the position of static equilibrium” [5].

2.5Extracting $\mu$ from a measurement

\begin{equation*} \frac{x_b - x_a}{t_b - t_a} = -\frac{2\mu N\wnn}{\pi k} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\mu = -\frac{x_b-x_a}{t_b-t_a}\cdot\frac{\pi k}{2N\wnn}\;} \end{equation*}(2.9)
Worked example — Term-3 paper 2022, Q3(b)–(c) — classify and quantify two decays
Two systems, both $m=1$ kg and $k=10$ N$\cdot$m$^{-1}$. Six peaks are tabulated for each.

System F: $t = 0.389, 2.37, 4.36, \ldots$ s with $x = 0.309, 0.187, 0.114, \ldots$ m. The ratio of successive peaks is constant ($0.187/0.309 = 0.605$, $0.114/0.187=0.610$) — a geometric sequence, so an exponential envelope. Viscous, underdamped.

System G: $t = 0.391, 2.38, 4.36,\ldots$ s with $x = 0.325, 0.286, 0.247,\ldots$ m. The differences are constant ($0.325-0.286=0.039$, $0.286-0.247=0.039$) — an arithmetic sequence, so a linear envelope. Coulomb (friction).

System F, quantify: using the 1st and 6th peaks, $n=5$ intervals:

\begin{align*} \delta &= \frac15\ln\frac{x_1}{x_6}, \qquad \zeta = \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2+\delta^2}} \approx 0.0792,\\ c &= \zeta\cdot2\sqrt{km} = 0.0792\times2\sqrt{1\times10} = 0.501\ \text{N}\cdot\text{s}\cdot\text{m}^{-1} \end{align*}

System G, quantify: $\wnn=\sqrt{10/1}=3.162$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$, and using the first and last tabulated peaks,

\begin{equation*} \mu = -\frac{x_{\text{last}}-x_{\text{first}}}{t_{\text{last}}-t_{\text{first}}} \cdot\frac{\pi k}{2mg\wnn} \end{equation*}
with $N=mg=9.81$ N and the first and last peaks, $(0.391\text{ s},\,0.325\text{ m})$ and $(10.3\text{ s},\,0.129\text{ m})$:
\begin{equation*} \mu = \frac{0.325-0.129}{10.3-0.391}\cdot\frac{\pi(10)}{2(1)(9.81)(3.162)} = 0.01978\times0.5063 = 0.0100 \end{equation*}

Memo (2022 term-3 paper, Q3): $\zeta = 0.0792$, $c = 0.5$ kg/s, $\mu = 0.01$ ✓

The exam point: the classification (part b) is 2 marks for two words, and it decides which formula you use in part (c). Check whether the peaks form a geometric or an arithmetic sequence before you compute anything.

Explanation and derivation

Rearranging the linear-decay result gives the identification formula. If two peaks $n$ half cycles apart have amplitudes $x_a$ and $x_b$ measured at times $t_a$ and $t_b$, then over that span the peak envelope has fallen at the slope of Eq. (2.7):

\begin{equation*} \frac{x_b - x_a}{t_b - t_a} = -\frac{2\mu N\wnn}{\pi k} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\mu = -\frac{x_b-x_a}{t_b-t_a}\cdot\frac{\pi k}{2N\wnn}\;} \end{equation*}(2.9)

With $N=mg$ this is exactly the formula the 2022 memo uses.

2.6Coulomb damping in the presence of viscous damping

Reference — Key quantities for the MATLAB Assignment 1

Exam angle

In Simulink this is built with a Sign block feeding a gain of $\mu N/m$ into the acceleration summing junction. A conceptual question could ask you to sketch the block diagram or to explain why ode45 needs a reduced maximum step size near the sign switch (the derivative is discontinuous there, so the adaptive step estimator struggles).
Explanation and derivation

MATLAB Assignment 1 Task 2 (Inman Problem 1.128) combines both:

\begin{equation*} m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx + \mu N\operatorname{sgn}(\dd x) = 0 \end{equation*}(2.10)

with $m=250$ kg, $\mu=0.01$, $c=25$ N$\cdot$s$\cdot$m$^{-1}$, $k=3000$ N$\cdot$m$^{-1}$. This has no closed-form solution and must be integrated numerically (Week 4). Useful numbers for that system:

2.7Equivalent stiffness

\begin{equation*} F_1=F_2=F,\qquad x = x_1+x_2 = \frac{F}{k_1}+\frac{F}{k_2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{k_{\text{eff}}} = \frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{k_{\text{eff}} = \frac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}} \end{equation*}(2.11)
\begin{equation*} \boxed{k_{\text{eff}} = k_1+k_2} \end{equation*}(2.12)

Exam angle

2022 Q1(a) is exactly Eq. (2.11), derived, for 5 marks. The memo awards marks for stating $F_1=F_2=F$, for $x=x_1+x_2$, and for the algebra. Write the physical statement in words before the algebra.
Reference — Equivalent stiffnesses used in VN354

Use Inman's constants

The memoranda follow Inman's Table 1.2, so use steel $E = 2.0\times10^{11}$ Pa, $\rho = 7.8\times10^3$ kg$\cdot$m$^{-3}$, $G = 8.0\times10^{10}$ Pa, not the 207 GPa you may have used in Strength of Materials 143. The difference is $+3.5\%$ in $k$ and $+0.8\%$ in $\wnn$ — small, but it will not match the memo. Take $g = 9.81$ m$\cdot$s$^{-2}$.
\begin{equation*} k_{x} = k\cos^2\!\theta. \end{equation*}(2.13)
$\theta$
angle between the spring axis and the $x$-direction
$k_x$
stiffness the spring contributes in $x$
\begin{equation*} m_{\text{eff}} = \frac{33}{140}M + m, \qquad \wnn = \sqrt{\frac{k}{\frac{33}{140}M+m}}. \end{equation*}(2.14)
$M$
distributed mass of the beam or column
$m$
lumped mass at the tip
$m_{\text{eff}}$
equivalent lumped mass at the tip
Explanation and derivation

Real questions never hand you $k$. They hand you a beam, a rod, a cable, or two springs in an arrangement, and expect you to produce $k_{\text{eff}}$.

2.7.1Springs in series and parallel

Series — the same force passes through both springs, and the deflections add:

\begin{equation*} F_1=F_2=F,\qquad x = x_1+x_2 = \frac{F}{k_1}+\frac{F}{k_2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{k_{\text{eff}}} = \frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{k_{\text{eff}} = \frac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}} \end{equation*}(2.11)

Parallel — the same deflection, and the forces add:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{k_{\text{eff}} = k_1+k_2} \end{equation*}(2.12)

Series stiffness is always less than the smallest of the two; parallel is always more than the largest. Use that as a sanity check.

2.7.2Stiffness from geometry and material

These come straight from strength of materials. Inman collects them in Table 1.3.

Written out, with the ones VN354 actually uses:

For a solid circular section of diameter $d$: $I = \pi d^4/64$ and $J_P = \pi d^4/32 = 2I$. For a hollow circular section, $I = \frac{\pi}{64}(d_o^4-d_i^4)$.

2.7.3Resolving stiffness into the direction of motion

A cable or strut at an angle contributes only its component along the vibration direction, and the contribution goes as $\cos^2\!\theta$, not $\cos\theta$. The reason: the displacement along the cable is $x\cos\theta$, the resulting axial force is $kx\cos\theta$, and the component of that force back along $x$ is $kx\cos^2\!\theta$. Hence

\begin{equation*} k_{x} = k\cos^2\!\theta. \end{equation*}(2.13)

This is precisely the step in the 2020 term-3 paper, Q1: three stay cables at $60^\circ$ from horizontal, one aligned with $x$ and two at $60^\circ$ to it in plan, giving $k_x = k_{\text{rope}}\cos^2 60^\circ\,[1 + 2\cos^2 60^\circ]$.

2.7.4Equivalent mass of a distributed member

When the beam or spring itself is not light, its distributed mass is lumped into an effective mass at the tip. For a cantilever of mass $M$ with a tip mass $m$, Inman Eq. (1.75) gives

\begin{equation*} m_{\text{eff}} = \frac{33}{140}M + m, \qquad \wnn = \sqrt{\frac{k}{\frac{33}{140}M+m}}. \end{equation*}(2.14)

The 2020 term-3 paper, Q1, uses exactly this, with $M$ the mass of the steel column shell.

2.8Rotational systems and kinematic constraints

Reference — Kinematic constraints that have appeared

Exam angle

Whenever you use a constraint, differentiate it too: $x=r\theta \Rightarrow \dd x = r\dd\theta \Rightarrow \ddd x = r\ddd\theta$. Kinetic energy needs $\dd x$, and $\frac{d}{dt}(T+U)$ needs $\ddd x$. Writing all three lines takes ten seconds and prevents the most common slip in Slot B.
Explanation and derivation

For rotation about a fixed axis, Newton's law becomes

\begin{equation*} \sum M = I\ddd\theta , \end{equation*}(2.15)

and the direct analogues are: $m\leftrightarrow I$, $x\leftrightarrow\theta$, $F\leftrightarrow M$, $k\leftrightarrow k_t$, so that

\begin{equation*} I\ddd\theta + k_t\theta = 0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \wnn=\sqrt{\frac{k_t}{I}} . \end{equation*}

Lecture 1 also lists the simple pendulum, $\ddd\theta + \frac{g}{l}\theta=0$, so $\wnn=\sqrt{g/l}$ [4].

2.8.1The constraint step

Slot B questions (Table 2.1) always begin by relating a translation to a rotation. Get this wrong and everything after it is wrong, so it is always worth its own marks:

2.8.2Small-angle assumption

For $\theta \ll 1$ rad: $\sin\theta\approx\theta$, $\cos\theta\approx1$, $\tan\theta\approx\theta$. This is what linearises the problem and lets you write a constant-coefficient ODE.

The 2020 term-3 paper, Q3, is explicit about the order of operations: “First write the full geometric equations without any assumptions. Make the small angle assumptions only when the equations are written in matrix form.” Follow that order — writing $\sin\theta$ first and linearising second earns method marks that writing $\theta$ immediately does not.

2.9The energy method

\begin{equation*} T + U = \text{const.} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\frac{d}{dt}\big(T+U\big) = 0\;} \end{equation*}(2.16)
$T$
kinetic energy (translation and rotation)
$U$
potential energy (springs and gravity)
Reference — Energy expressions you need

Energy-method recipe

  1. (a)Kinematics. Relate every coordinate to the one you will solve in ($x=r\theta$, $x_1=2r\theta$, …). Differentiate the relations.
  2. (b)Static deflection. Take moments (or forces) at equilibrium with the dynamic coordinate set to zero, and solve for $\theta_0$ or $\delta_{st}$.
  3. (c)Potential energy $U$. Sum every spring term (using $\delta_{st}+x$ or $\theta_0+\theta$) and every gravity term.
  4. (d)Kinetic energy $T$. Sum every translating and rotating term, all expressed in the single coordinate.
  5. (e)Differentiate and divide. Take $\frac{d}{dt}(T+U)=0$, substitute the static-deflection result to kill the constant terms, and divide through by $\dd\theta$ (or $\dd x$). What is left is the EOM. Read $\wnn=\sqrt{\text{stiffness}/\text{inertia}}$ off it.
Worked example — 2021 Q4 — two masses over a pulley (and the 2022 Q2 variant)
Two masses $m$ are connected through a pulley of inertia $J_0$. The left cable wraps at radius $2r$; its mass slides horizontally against a spring $k$. The right cable wraps at radius $r$; its mass sits on a $30^\circ$ incline against a spring $2k$. Small rotations $\theta$, frictionless.

(a) Kinematics. $x_1 = 2r\theta$, $x_2 = r\theta$.

(b) Static deflection. Only the component of gravity along the incline, $mg\sin30^\circ = \tfrac12 mg$, loads the system. Moments about the pulley centre at equilibrium:

\begin{equation*} \sum M_0 = -(kx_1)(2r) - (2kx_2)(r) + \tfrac12 mg\,r = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; -4kr^2\theta_0 - 2kr^2\theta_0 + \tfrac12 mgr = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \theta_0 = \frac{mg}{12kr} \end{equation*}

(c) Potential energy.

\begin{equation*} U = \underbrace{\tfrac12 k(2r\theta+2r\theta_0)^2}_{\text{spring }k} + \underbrace{\tfrac12 (2k)(r\theta+r\theta_0)^2}_{\text{spring }2k} - \underbrace{\tfrac12 mg(r\theta+r\theta_0)}_{\text{gravity along incline}} \end{equation*}
which expands to $U = 3kr^2\theta^2 + 6kr^2\theta\theta_0 + 3kr^2\theta_0^2 - \tfrac12 mgr(\theta+\theta_0)$.

(d) Kinetic energy.

\begin{equation*} T = \tfrac12 J_0\dd\theta^2 + \tfrac12 m(2r\dd\theta)^2 + \tfrac12 m(r\dd\theta)^2 = \tfrac12 J_0\dd\theta^2 + \tfrac52 mr^2\dd\theta^2 \end{equation*}

(e) Differentiate.

\begin{equation*} 6kr^2\theta\dd\theta + 6kr^2\theta_0\dd\theta - \tfrac12 mgr\dd\theta + J_0\dd\theta\ddd\theta + 5mr^2\dd\theta\ddd\theta = 0 \end{equation*}
Substitute $\theta_0 = mg/12kr$: the term $6kr^2\theta_0 = \tfrac12 mgr$ cancels the gravity term exactly. Divide by $\dd\theta$:
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;(J_0+5mr^2)\,\ddd\theta + 6kr^2\,\theta = 0\;} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \wnn = \sqrt{\frac{6kr^2}{J_0+5mr^2}} \end{equation*}

Checked against the 2021 term-3 memo, Q4 ($\theta_0 = mg/12kr$, $T = \tfrac12J_0\dd\theta^2+\tfrac52mr^2\dd\theta^2$) ✓

The 2022 Q2 variant. Same pulley, springs and radii, but the mass on the $2r$ cable is $2m$ and the other mass hangs vertically, so the full $mg$ acts. Then $\theta_0 = mg/(6kr)$, the gravity term is $-mg(r\theta+r\theta_0)$, and $T = \tfrac12J_0\dd\theta^2 + \tfrac12(2m)(2r\dd\theta)^2 + \tfrac12 m(r\dd\theta)^2 = \tfrac12J_0\dd\theta^2+\tfrac92mr^2\dd\theta^2$, giving $(J_0+9mr^2)\ddd\theta+6kr^2\theta=0$ (2022 memo, Q2 ✓). The stiffness term is the same in both papers, because gravity always cancels against the static deflection; only $\theta_0$ and $T$ change. That is the point — learn the recipe, not the answer.

Worked example — 2023 Q2 — nose-wheel steering (disc rolling on a mass)
A steering rod is a spring–mass system $(m,k_2)$ moving in $x$. A shaft gear is a disc of inertia $J$ with torsional stiffness $k_1$, rolling on the mass without slipping at radius $r$.

(a) $x = r\theta$, i.e. $\theta = x/r$ and $\dd\theta = \dd x/r$.

(b) $\displaystyle U = \tfrac12 k_1\theta^2 + \tfrac12 k_2 x^2 = \tfrac12 k_1\!\left(\frac{x}{r}\right)^{\!2} + \tfrac12 k_2x^2 = \left(\frac{k_1}{2r^2}+\frac{k_2}{2}\right)x^2$

(c) $\displaystyle T = \tfrac12 J\dd\theta^2 + \tfrac12 m\dd x^2 = \left(\frac{J}{2r^2}+\frac{m}{2}\right)\dd x^2$

(d) $\frac{d}{dt}(T+U)=0$ gives $\left(\frac{J}{r^2}+m\right)\ddd x\dd x + \left(\frac{k_1}{r^2}+k_2\right)x\dd x = 0$, so

\begin{equation*} \left(\frac{J}{r^2}+m\right)\ddd x + \left(\frac{k_1}{r^2}+k_2\right)x = 0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\wnn = \sqrt{\frac{k_1+r^2k_2}{J+mr^2}}\;} \end{equation*}
(Multiply numerator and denominator by $r^2$ to get the memo's form.)

(e) The words question. If the disc slipped, with friction coefficient $\mu$, could you still use the energy method?
No, for two reasons: (i) slipping breaks the constraint $x=r\theta$, so $x$ and $\theta$ become independent and the system has two degrees of freedom; and (ii) friction dissipates energy, so the system is no longer conservative and $T+U\neq$ constant. Lagrange's method with a virtual-work term for the non-conservative force would be required — but that is beyond VN354.

Explanation and derivation — every paper has an energy-method question

This is Slot B, and it appears every year. It is often much faster than Newton for systems with pulleys, discs and multiple springs, because you never draw the internal reaction forces.

2.9.1Principle

A conservative system is one in which no energy is added or removed by external forces. For such a system the total mechanical energy is constant [6]:

\begin{equation*} T + U = \text{const.} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;\frac{d}{dt}\big(T+U\big) = 0\;} \end{equation*}(2.16)

2.9.2The five-step recipe

Every energy-method question in every past paper follows the same five steps. The memos award marks step by step, so label them.

2.9.3Simplest possible case, to see the machinery

For the plain spring–mass system, measuring from the unstretched spring position [6]:

\begin{equation*} T + U = \tfrac12 m\dd x^2 + \tfrac12 k(\delta_{st}+x)^2 - mg(\delta_{st}+x) = \text{const.} \end{equation*}

Differentiating:

\begin{equation*} m\dd x\ddd x + k(\delta_{st}+x)\dd x - mg\dd x = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad m\ddd x + kx + \underbrace{k\delta_{st} - mg}_{=\,0} = 0 \end{equation*}

so $m\ddd x + kx = 0$, as before. The gravity and static-spring terms cancel at step (e), which is why step (b) exists.

2.10Rolling without slipping: the classic trap

Exam angle

The factor $3/2$ (instead of 1) is the entire content of the question — it is the rolling inertia. If your answer to a rolling problem looks like the equivalent sliding answer, you have forgotten $T_{\text{roll}}$. For a uniform disc, rolling multiplies the effective inertia by $3/2$; for a uniform sphere, by $7/5$; for a thin hoop, by $2$.
Explanation and derivation

Lecture 4 works a uniform disc of radius $r$ rolling inside a circular track of radius $R$ [6]. Two rotations exist — the disc spin $\phi$ and the position angle $\theta$ — and rolling links them. The kinetic energy has both a rolling part $T_{\text{roll}}=\tfrac12 I_C\dd\phi^2 = \tfrac14 mr^2\dd\phi^2$ and a translation part $T_{\text{trans}}=\tfrac12 m(R-r)^2\dd\theta^2$, and the potential is $U = mg(R-r)(1-\cos\theta)$. Summing, differentiating and applying the small-angle approximation ($\sin\theta\approx\theta$):

\begin{equation*} \frac{3}{2}(R-r)\ddd\theta + g\theta = 0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \wnn = \sqrt{\frac{2g}{3(R-r)}} . \end{equation*}(2.17)

Practice questions — Week 2

Q 2.1Term-3 paper 2022, Question 1[10]

(a) The system in Figure 2.2(a) is represented by the equivalent system in (b). Derive $k_{\text{eff}}$ in terms of $k_1$ and $k_2$. When $m$ hangs from the springs, $k_1$ deflects $x_1$ and $k_2$ deflects $x_2$. [4]
(b) Derive the time response of system (b) for initial conditions $x_0$ and $v_0$. [6]

Step 1 — (a) Series springs

Both springs carry the same force: $F=k_1x_1=k_2x_2$. The total deflection adds: $x=x_1+x_2=F/k_1+F/k_2$. With $F=k_{\text{eff}}x$:

\[\frac1{k_{\text{eff}}}=\frac1{k_1}+\frac1{k_2}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad k_{\text{eff}}=\frac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}\]Step 2 — (b) Equation of motion

From static equilibrium ($k\delta_{st}=mg$ cancels gravity): $m\ddot x+k_{\text{eff}}x=0$, $\omega_n=\sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}/m}$.

Step 3 — Solution with initial conditions

$x=A\sin(\omega_nt+\phi)$: $x_0=A\sin\phi$ and $v_0=A\omega_n\cos\phi$, so

\[x(t)=\frac{\sqrt{\omega_n^2x_0^2+v_0^2}}{\omega_n}\sin\!\left(\omega_nt+\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_nx_0}{v_0}\right)\]
Answer. $k_{\text{eff}}=k_1k_2/(k_1+k_2)$; $x(t)$ as above with $\omega_n=\sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}/m}$. Use the quadrant of $(v_0,\ \omega_nx_0)$ when taking the arctangent.

Matches the 2022 memo.

Q 2.2Term-3 paper 2026, Question 2[10]

A thin uniform disc (mass $2m$, radius $R$) rolls without slipping. A spring $k$ connects its centre to the wall; a cable from its centre runs over a pulley (moment of inertia $J$, radius $r$) to a hanging mass $m$, which is held by a spring $k$ to the ground (Figure 2.3). Rotations are small; the cable stays taut; $\theta=0$ is the position in which both springs are unstretched.

(a) Write $x$ and $\alpha$ in terms of the pulley angle $\theta$. [1]
(b) Find the static deflection $\theta_0$. [2]
(c) Use the energy method to find the equation of motion and natural frequency in terms of $\theta$. [7]

The disc both translates and rotates: two kinetic-energy terms.
Step 1 — (a) Kinematics

Cable over the pulley: $x=r\theta$. The disc centre moves with the cable, $R\alpha=r\theta$, so $\alpha=r\theta/R$.

Step 2 — (b) Static deflection

Disc: cable tension $T_1=kR\alpha_0=kr\theta_0$. Mass: $T_2=mg-kx_0=mg-kr\theta_0$. Pulley moments: $rT_1=rT_2$, so $2kr\theta_0=mg$ and $\theta_0=mg/(2kr)$.

Step 3 — (c) Energies\[T=\tfrac12m(r\dot\theta)^2+\tfrac12(2m)(r\dot\theta)^2+\tfrac12\left(\tfrac12\,2mR^2\right)\dot\alpha^2+\tfrac12J\dot\theta^2\] \[T=\left(\tfrac12J+2mr^2\right)\dot\theta^2,\qquad U=-mgr\theta+kr^2(\theta_0+\theta)^2\]Step 4 — Differentiate

$\frac{d}{dt}(T+U)=0$, divide by $\dot\theta$: $(J+4mr^2)\ddot\theta+2kr^2\theta+(2kr^2\theta_0-mgr)=0$. The bracket is zero by (b).

\[(J+4mr^2)\ddot\theta+2kr^2\theta=0,\qquad\omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{2kr^2}{J+4mr^2}}\]
Answer. (a) $x=r\theta$, $\alpha=r\theta/R$. (b) $\theta_0=mg/(2kr)$. (c) $(J+4mr^2)\ddot\theta+2kr^2\theta=0$, $\omega_n=\sqrt{2kr^2/(J+4mr^2)}$. The disc’s rotation supplies $mr^2$ of the $4mr^2$: forgetting it gives $J+3mr^2$.

Matches the 2026 memo.

Q 2.3Term-3 paper 2020, Question 1[10]

A steel distillation column is modelled as a cantilever (height $h=80$ m, internal diameter 3.6 m, wall thickness 10 mm, $E=200$ GPa) with a lumped mass at the top: 30 000 kg of liquid plus 5 000 kg of equipment. Neglect the column's own inertia. To avoid wind excitation the natural frequency must move by at least 10 %.

(a) Find the current natural frequency. [2] (b) By what percentage does it change if the equipment is removed? [1] (c) Keeping the equipment, what volume of concrete ($\rho=2400$ kg/m³) added to the top lowers it by 10 %? [2]

Alternatively, three pre-tensioned stay cables (area 0.0004 m², $E=100$ GPa, at 60° to the horizontal, 120° apart in plan) are attached to the top (Figure 2.4). Treat them as massless linear springs.

(d) Find the axial stiffness of one cable. [1] (e) Find the effective stiffness of the three cables in the $X$-direction. [2] (f) With liquid and equipment, find the new natural frequency and its percentage change from (a). [2]

A spring at an angle contributes $k\cos^2\theta$ — apply it twice: once in elevation, once in plan.
Step 1 — (a) Column stiffness

$d_o=3.62$ m, $I=\frac{\pi}{64}(d_o^4-d_i^4)=0.1848$ m⁴, $k=3EI/h^3=2.165\times10^5$ N/m. $\omega_n=\sqrt{2.165\times10^5/35\,000}=2.487$ rad/s $=0.396$ Hz.

Step 2 — (b) Remove equipment

$\omega=\sqrt{2.165\times10^5/30\,000}=2.686$ rad/s: +8.0 %. Not enough.

Step 3 — (c) Add concrete

Target $0.9\times2.487=2.238$ rad/s, so $m=k/\omega^2=43\,210$ kg: add 8 210 kg, $V=3.42$ m³.

Step 4 — (d)–(e) Cables

Length $l=h/\sin60^\circ=92.4$ m, $k_c=EA/l=433$ kN/m. Its horizontal component in its own plane: $k_c\cos^2 60^\circ=108.3$ kN/m. In plan, the cables at $\pm120^\circ$ from $X$ contribute $\cos^2120^\circ=0.25$ each:

\[k_X=108.3\,(1+0.25+0.25)=162.4\ \text{kN/m}\]Step 5 — (f) New frequency

Springs in parallel: $k=216.5+162.4=378.9$ kN/m, $\omega_n=\sqrt{378\,900/35\,000}=3.290$ rad/s (0.524 Hz): +32.3 %.

Answer. (a) 2.487 rad/s (0.396 Hz). (b) +8.0 %. (c) 3.42 m³. (d) 433 kN/m. (e) 162 kN/m. (f) 3.29 rad/s, +32.3 %.

Printed: 0.4 Hz ✓, 8 % ✓, 3.4 m³ ✓, 433 kN/m ✓, 162 kN/m ✓, 32.3 % ✓. Recomputed in verify.py.

Q 2.4New question (Lecture 3 content)[8]

A 2 kg block slides on a horizontal surface ($\mu=0.05$) and is attached to a wall by a spring $k=200$ N/m. It is pulled 100 mm to the right and released from rest. Use $g=9.81$ m/s².

(a) Find the natural frequency and the half-width of the dead zone. [2]
(b) By how much does the amplitude drop per cycle? [1]
(c) After how many half-cycles does the block stop, where, and when? [4]
(d) Sketch $x(t)$ and state how it differs from a viscously damped decay. [1]

Motion stops at the first extreme that lies inside the dead zone.
Step 1 — (a)

$\omega_n=\sqrt{200/2}=10$ rad/s. Dead zone: $|x|\le\mu mg/k=0.05(2)(9.81)/200=4.905$ mm.

Step 2 — (b)

Each half-cycle loses $2\mu mg/k=9.81$ mm, so $4\mu mg/k=19.6$ mm per cycle.

Step 3 — (c) Count the half-cycles

Extremes: 100, −90.2, 80.4, −70.6, 60.8, −51.0, 41.1, −31.3, 21.5, −11.7, +1.9 mm. After the tenth half-cycle the block is at +1.9 mm, inside the dead zone ($|x|<4.905$ mm): the spring force $kx=0.38$ N is less than the friction limit $\mu mg=0.98$ N, so it stays there (taking the static friction coefficient equal to the kinetic one, as the course does).

Each half-cycle takes $\pi/\omega_n=0.314$ s, so it stops at $t=10\times0.314=3.14$ s.

Step 4 — (d)

Straight-line (linear) envelope, the frequency stays $\omega_n$, and the block stops at a finite time, generally not at $x=0$. Viscous damping gives an exponential envelope, $\omega_d<\omega_n$, and never quite stops.

Answer. (a) 10 rad/s, ±4.9 mm. (b) 19.6 mm per cycle. (c) 10 half-cycles; stops at +1.9 mm after 3.14 s. (d) Linear decay, ends off-centre.

New question. Checked in verify.py by stepping the half-cycles.
