Week 3

Harmonic excitation

Lectures 5–6

This week in brief

  • $m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=F_0\cos\omega t$. The response is a transient (it decays) plus a steady state at the forcing frequency $\omega$.
  • Everything is a function of the frequency ratio $r=\omega/\omega_n$. Below resonance the response is in phase, at $r=1$ it lags by $90^\circ$, and above resonance it lags by up to $180^\circ$.
  • Undamped: $X=f_0/(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)$. Near $r=1$ you get beating (a slow envelope at $(\omega_n-\omega)/2$). At $r=1$ you get resonance, with the amplitude growing linearly in time.
  • Damped: $X=\dfrac{f_0}{\sqrt{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2}}$ and $\theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2\zeta\omega_n\omega}{\omega_n^2-\omega^2}$. The peak is $\approx 1/(2\zeta)$ times the static deflection.
  • Sketches earn marks for labelled axes, the $r=1$ line, the static value at $r=0$ and the trend with $\zeta$.

3.1The setup

Two frequencies, one ratio

  • $\wnn = \sqrt{k/m}$ — the natural frequency. A property of the system alone.
  • $\omega$ — the driving (excitation) frequency. A property of the input alone.
  • $r = \omega/\wnn$ — the frequency ratio. Dimensionless. Everything about the steady-state response depends on $r$ and $\zeta$, and on nothing else.
Explanation and derivation

Now the system is driven continuously by a harmonic force:

\begin{equation*} m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx = F(t) = F_0\cos\omega t \end{equation*}(3.1)

Two frequencies now exist and must never be confused:

The complete solution has two parts:

\begin{equation*} x(t) = \underbrace{x_h(t)}_{\text{homogeneous}} + \underbrace{x_p(t)}_{\text{particular}} \end{equation*}

$x_h$ is the free response of Week 2–1. With any damping at all it decays to zero, so it is called the transient. $x_p$ oscillates at the driving frequency $\omega$ forever, and is called the steady-state response.

3.2Undamped harmonic excitation

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;f_0 = \frac{F_0}{m}\;}\qquad\text{[N$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$ $\equiv$ m$\cdot$s$^{-2}$]} \end{equation*}(3.2)
$F_0$
amplitude of the applied harmonic force
$f_0$
force amplitude per unit mass
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;X = \frac{f_0}{\wnn^2-\omega^2}\;} \end{equation*}(3.3)

Exam angle

Eq. (3.3) changes sign as $\omega$ passes $\wnn$. Below resonance the mass moves in phase with the force; above resonance it moves $180^\circ$ out of phase. That sign flip is the undamped limit of the phase plot in Figure 3.2.
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;x(t) = \frac{2f_0}{\wnn^2-\omega^2} \sin\!\left(\frac{\wnn-\omega}{2}t\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{\wnn+\omega}{2}t\right)\;} \end{equation*}(3.4)
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\omega_{\text{beat}} = |\wnn - \omega|\;} \end{equation*}(3.5)
$\omega_{\text{beat}}$
beat frequency: the rate at which the envelope repeats

Exam angle

The beat frequency is $|\wnn-\omega|$ (rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$), not $|\wnn-\omega|/2$. The factor of 2 is because the envelope $|\sin|$ has twice the frequency of $\sin$: the envelope reaches a maximum twice per cycle of the modulating sine. Both 2021 Q1(b) and 2023 Q4(b) ask you to name and sketch this.
\begin{equation*} x_p(t) = \frac{f_0}{2\omega}\,t\sin\omega t \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;x(t) = \frac{v_0}{\omega}\sin\omega t + x_0\cos\omega t + \frac{f_0}{2\omega}t\sin\omega t\;} \end{equation*}(3.6)

How to tell beating from resonance in a sketch

Beating: the envelope is itself a sinusoid — the amplitude grows, then shrinks back to zero, then grows again, periodically. Frequency of the envelope $=|\wnn-\omega|$.
Resonance: the envelope is a straight line through the origin. The amplitude never comes back down.
Explanation and derivation

Set $c=0$ in Eq. (3.1):

\begin{equation*} m\ddd x + kx = F_0\cos\omega t \end{equation*}(3.7)

Assume the particular solution has the form of the forcing, $x_p(t) = X\cos\omega t$, and substitute:

\begin{equation*} -\omega^2 mX\cos\omega t + kX\cos\omega t = F_0\cos\omega t \end{equation*}

Divide by $m$ and introduce the mass-normalised force amplitude

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;f_0 = \frac{F_0}{m}\;}\qquad\text{[N$\cdot$kg$^{-1}$ $\equiv$ m$\cdot$s$^{-2}$]} \end{equation*}(3.2)

giving $\big(-\omega^2 X + \wnn^2 X - f_0\big)\cos\omega t = 0$, which holds for all $t$ only if

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;X = \frac{f_0}{\wnn^2-\omega^2}\;} \end{equation*}(3.3)

Adding the homogeneous solution and applying $x(0)=x_0$, $\dd x(0)=v_0$ [7]:

\begin{equation*} x(t) = \frac{v_0}{\wnn}\sin\wnn t + \left(x_0 - \frac{f_0}{\wnn^2-\omega^2}\right)\cos\wnn t + \frac{f_0}{\wnn^2-\omega^2}\cos\omega t \end{equation*}(3.8)

The response is the sum of two sinusoids, one at $\wnn$ and one at $\omega$.

3.2.1Beating

Something visually striking happens when $\omega$ is close to but not equal to $\wnn$. With zero initial conditions Eq. (3.8) reduces to

\begin{equation*} x(t) = \frac{f_0}{\wnn^2-\omega^2}\big(\cos\omega t - \cos\wnn t\big) \end{equation*}

Applying the identity $\cos u - \cos v = 2\sin\!\big(\frac{v-u}{2}\big)\sin\!\big(\frac{v+u}{2}\big)$ [7]:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;x(t) = \frac{2f_0}{\wnn^2-\omega^2} \sin\!\left(\frac{\wnn-\omega}{2}t\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{\wnn+\omega}{2}t\right)\;} \end{equation*}(3.4)

Read this as a fast oscillation at the average frequency $(\wnn+\omega)/2$, whose amplitude is slowly modulated by the slow envelope $\sin\!\big(\frac{\wnn-\omega}{2}t\big)$. That slow swelling and dying is a beat, and

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\omega_{\text{beat}} = |\wnn - \omega|\;} \end{equation*}(3.5)

The maximum amplitude reached is $\left|2f_0/(\wnn^2-\omega^2)\right|$ — twice the steady-state amplitude of Eq. (3.3).

3.2.2Resonance

When $\omega$ is exactly $\wnn$, Eq. (3.3) divides by zero: the assumed particular solution is no longer independent of the homogeneous solution, and must be multiplied by $t$ [7]:

\begin{equation*} x_p(t) = \frac{f_0}{2\omega}\,t\sin\omega t \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;x(t) = \frac{v_0}{\omega}\sin\omega t + x_0\cos\omega t + \frac{f_0}{2\omega}t\sin\omega t\;} \end{equation*}(3.6)

The amplitude grows linearly and without bound. In reality the spring yields or the structure fails. This is resonance.

3.3Damped harmonic excitation

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\; x_p(t) = \underbrace{\frac{f_0}{\sqrt{(\wnn^2-\omega^2)^2+(2\zeta\wnn\omega)^2}}}_{X} \cos\Big(\omega t - \underbrace{\tan^{-1}\frac{2\zeta\wnn\omega}{\wnn^2-\omega^2}}_{\theta}\Big)\;} \end{equation*}(3.9)

Transient versus steady state

For large $t$ the exponential kills the homogeneous part and $x(t)\to X\cos(\omega t-\theta)$. So:
  • If a question says “steady state”, “eventually”, or “after the transient has died out”, use only $X$ and $\theta$ — you never need the initial conditions.
  • If it asks for the response “immediately after” something, or gives you $x_0$ and $v_0$ and asks for $x(t)$, you need both parts.
  • How long is “eventually”? The transient falls to $2\%$ in about $4/(\zeta\wnn)$ seconds.
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\frac{X\wnn^2}{f_0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\;} \qquad\qquad \boxed{\;\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{2\zeta r}{1-r^2}\;} \end{equation*}(3.10)
$r$
frequency ratio $\omega/\omega_n$
$X$
steady-state amplitude
$\theta$
phase lag of the response behind the force

Three numbers worth memorising

\begin{align*} r\to0:&\quad X\to \frac{f_0}{\wnn^2}=\frac{F_0}{k} \quad\text{(the static deflection)}\\ r=1:&\quad X = \frac{f_0}{2\zeta\wnn^2}=\frac{F_0}{c\wnn}, \quad \theta = 90^\circ\\ r\to\infty:&\quad X\to0, \quad \theta\to180^\circ \end{align*}
At $r=1$ the phase is always exactly $90^\circ$, for every value of $\zeta$. All the phase curves cross there. That is a free sanity check on any sketch.

Why bother with complex numbers

Because it turns differentiation into multiplication: $\frac{d}{dt}\to j\omega$, $\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\to -\omega^2$. Every frequency-domain result in the rest of the module (base excitation, transmissibility, FRFs, and MDOF) follows from this one substitution. Take the magnitude last, after clearing the complex denominator by multiplying by its conjugate.
Worked example — Lecture 5 example — two perpendicular rods, forced
Two slender rods of mass per unit length $\rho$, joined perpendicularly and pivoting about their common centre $O$; the horizontal rod (length $4L$) is driven by $F=F_0\cos\omega t$ at a distance $2L$; springs $k_1$ at $2L$ horizontally and $k_2$ at $L$ vertically. Given $\rho=1$ kg$\cdot$m$^{-1}$, $L=1$ m, $k_1=100$, $k_2=50$ N$\cdot$m$^{-1}$, $F_0=6$ N, $\omega=8$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$, zero ICs.

Moments about $O$, counter-clockwise positive:

\begin{equation*} -k_1(2L)^2\cos\theta\sin\theta - k_2L^2\cos\theta\sin\theta + 2FL\cos\theta = I_O\ddd\theta \end{equation*}

Inertia of the cross (each rod about its own centre, $\frac1{12}mL_{\text{rod}}^2$):

\begin{equation*} I_O = \tfrac1{12}(4\rho L)(4L)^2 + \tfrac1{12}(2\rho L)(2L)^2 = 6\rho L^3 \end{equation*}

Small angles ($\sin\theta\to\theta$, $\cos\theta\to1$):

\begin{equation*} 6\rho L^2\ddd\theta + (4k_1L + k_2L)\theta = 2F_0\cos\omega t \end{equation*}

Frequencies: $\wnn = \sqrt{\dfrac{4k_1+k_2}{6\rho L}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{450}{6}} = 8.66$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$, $\quad f_0 = \dfrac{2F_0}{6\rho L^2} = 2$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-2}$.

Response with zero ICs (undamped, so Eq. (3.8) collapses):

\begin{equation*} \theta(t) = \frac{f_0}{\wnn^2-\omega^2}(\cos\omega t - \cos\wnn t) = \frac{2}{75-64}(\cos 8t - \cos 8.66t) = 0.182\,(\cos 8t - \cos 8.66t) \end{equation*}
Since $\omega = 8$ and $\wnn = 8.66$ are close, this beats, at $\omega_{\text{beat}}=0.66$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$ (period 9.5 s).

Note the units: $f_0$ here is a mass-normalised moment over inertia, so it carries rad$\cdot$s$^{-2}$, and $\theta$ comes out dimensionless (rad). Always divide by the generalised inertia, not by $m$, in a rotational problem.

Explanation and derivation

Now keep $c$. Assume the particular solution lags the force by a phase angle $\theta$:

\begin{equation*} x_p(t) = X\cos(\omega t-\theta) \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad x_p(t) = A_s\cos\omega t + B_s\sin\omega t \end{equation*}(3.11)

with $X = \sqrt{A_s^2+B_s^2}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}(B_s/A_s)$ [8]. Substituting and requiring the result to hold at $t=0$ and $t=\pi/2\omega$ gives two equations for $A_s$ and $B_s$, and hence

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\; x_p(t) = \underbrace{\frac{f_0}{\sqrt{(\wnn^2-\omega^2)^2+(2\zeta\wnn\omega)^2}}}_{X} \cos\Big(\omega t - \underbrace{\tan^{-1}\frac{2\zeta\wnn\omega}{\wnn^2-\omega^2}}_{\theta}\Big)\;} \end{equation*}(3.9)

The total solution is

\begin{equation*} x(t) = \underbrace{Ae^{-\zeta\wnn t}\sin(\wdd t+\phi)}_{\text{transient}} + \underbrace{X\cos(\omega t-\theta)}_{\text{steady state}} \end{equation*}(3.12)

with, from the initial conditions [8],

\begin{equation*} \phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{\wdd(x_0-X\cos\theta)}{v_0+(x_0-X\cos\theta)\zeta\wnn - \omega X\sin\theta}, \qquad A = \frac{x_0-X\cos\theta}{\sin\phi}. \end{equation*}(3.13)

3.3.1The normalised frequency response

Dividing Eq. (3.9) through by $\wnn^2$ and writing $r=\omega/\wnn$ gives the two curves that dominate this half of the module [8]:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\frac{X\wnn^2}{f_0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\;} \qquad\qquad \boxed{\;\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{2\zeta r}{1-r^2}\;} \end{equation*}(3.10)

3.3.2Where the true peak is

The peak of $X\wnn^2/f_0$ is not exactly at $r=1$ when damping is present. Differentiating Eq. (3.10) gives

\begin{equation*} r_{\text{peak}} = \sqrt{1-2\zeta^2}, \qquad \left.\frac{X\wnn^2}{f_0}\right|_{\text{peak}} = \frac{1}{2\zeta\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}} \end{equation*}(3.14)

which is real only for $\zeta < 1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707$. Above $\zeta=0.707$ there is no resonant peak at all — the curve decreases monotonically from 1. That is why $\zeta = 0.707$ is the classical “maximally flat” design choice.

For the small $\zeta$ typical in practice, $r_{\text{peak}}\approx1$ and the peak height is $\approx 1/(2\zeta)$, which is the “quality factor” $Q$.

3.3.3The complex (phasor) method

Lecture 6 also gives the shortcut used in Lecture 7 for base excitation [8]. Replace the forcing with a complex exponential:

\begin{equation*} m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx = F_0e^{j\omega t}, \qquad x_p(t) = Xe^{j\omega t} \end{equation*}

Substituting turns the ODE into algebra:

\begin{equation*} \big(-\omega^2 m + jc\omega + k\big)Xe^{j\omega t} = F_0e^{j\omega t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad X = \frac{f_0}{(\wnn^2-\omega^2) + 2j\zeta\wnn\omega} \end{equation*}(3.15)

The physical response is $\Re\{Xe^{j\omega t}\}$; the magnitude $|X|$ recovers Eq. (3.9) and the argument recovers $-\theta$.

Practice questions — Week 3

Q 3.1New question (Lecture 5 content)[8]

An undamped mass–spring system ($m=10$ kg, $k=4000$ N/m) is at rest when a force $F(t)=50\cos18t$ N is applied.

(a) Find $\omega_n$ and the amplitude $X$ of the particular solution. [2]
(b) Write $x(t)$ for $x_0=v_0=0$ and show that it can be written as a product of two sines. Name the phenomenon and give the maximum displacement and the beat period (the time between successive amplitude maxima). [4]
(c) What happens if the forcing frequency is changed to 20 rad/s? Give the amplitude after 2 s. [2]

$\cos A-\cos B=-2\sin\frac{A+B}2\sin\frac{A-B}2$.
Step 1 — (a)

$\omega_n=\sqrt{4000/10}=20$ rad/s, $f_0=F_0/m=5$ m/s², $X=f_0/(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)=5/(400-324)=65.8$ mm.

Step 2 — (b) Beating

With zero initial conditions, $x=X(\cos\omega t-\cos\omega_nt)=2X\sin\frac{(\omega_n-\omega)t}2\sin\frac{(\omega_n+\omega)t}2$.

A fast oscillation at 19 rad/s inside a slow envelope $2X\sin t$: beating. Maximum displacement $2X=132$ mm. The envelope $|2X\sin t|$ repeats every $2\pi/(\omega_n-\omega)=\pi=3.14$ s.

Step 3 — (c) Resonance

At $\omega=\omega_n$ the particular solution becomes $x=\frac{f_0}{2\omega_n}t\sin\omega_nt$: the amplitude grows linearly. After 2 s: $\frac{5}{40}(2)=0.25$ m — and still growing.

Answer. (a) $\omega_n=20$ rad/s, $X=65.8$ mm. (b) Beating; peak 132 mm; envelope period 3.14 s. (c) Resonance; 0.25 m after 2 s, growing linearly.

New question. Recomputed in verify.py.

Q 3.2New question (Lecture 6 content)[8]

A damped system ($m=5$ kg, $k=2000$ N/m, $c=40$ N·s/m) is driven by $F(t)=100\cos25t$ N.

(a) Find $\omega_n$, $\zeta$ and $r$. [2]
(b) Find the steady-state amplitude and phase lag. [4]
(c) Estimate the largest steady-state amplitude this force could produce at any frequency, and at what $r$. [2]

Check the sign of $\omega_n^2-\omega^2$ before taking the arctangent.
Step 1 — (a)

$\omega_n=20$ rad/s, $\zeta=40/(2\sqrt{2000\cdot5})=0.2$, $r=25/20=1.25$.

Step 2 — (b)

$f_0=20$ m/s².

\[X=\frac{f_0}{\sqrt{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2}}=\frac{20}{\sqrt{(-225)^2+200^2}}=66.4\ \text{mm}\]

$\theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2\zeta\omega_n\omega}{\omega_n^2-\omega^2}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{200}{-225}$. The denominator is negative ($r>1$), so $\theta$ is in the second quadrant: $\theta=138.4^\circ$.

Step 3 — (c) Peak

Static deflection $F_0/k=50$ mm. The peak is near $r=1$ and about $1/(2\zeta)$ times static: $\approx125$ mm. Exactly: $1/(2\zeta\sqrt{1-\zeta^2})=2.55$, so 127.6 mm at $r=\sqrt{1-2\zeta^2}=0.959$.

Answer. (a) 20 rad/s, 0.2, 1.25. (b) $X=66.4$ mm, $\theta=138.4^\circ$ (lagging). (c) About 128 mm at $r\approx0.96$.

Quadrant of the phase

A calculator gives $\tan^{-1}(200/-225)=-41.6^\circ$. Above resonance the lag is between 90° and 180°: add 180°.

New question. Recomputed in verify.py (numerical peak search ✓).

Q 3.3Term-3 paper 2021, Question 1(b); Lectures 5–6[6]

(a) A system with negligible damping is driven by $F\sin\omega t$ with $\omega$ close to $\omega_n$. Name and describe the phenomenon, with a sketch. [2]
(b) Sketch $|X|k/F_0$ and the phase $\theta$ against $r$ for $\zeta=0.05$, 0.2 and 0.7, and label the features an examiner looks for. [4]

Step 1 — (a)

Beating: the response is a fast oscillation at about $(\omega_n+\omega)/2$ whose amplitude rises and falls slowly. The envelope varies at $|\omega_n-\omega|/2$, so the loudness/amplitude peaks repeat at the beat frequency $|\omega_n-\omega|$. Sketch: a sine inside a slowly varying sinusoidal envelope.

Step 2 — (b) Features to label
  • Magnitude starts at 1 at $r=0$ (static deflection) for every $\zeta$.
  • Peak near $r=1$, height about $1/(2\zeta)$; the peak moves slightly below $r=1$ as $\zeta$ grows; for $\zeta\ge0.707$ there is no peak.
  • Above resonance the magnitude falls towards 0 like $1/r^2$; all curves converge.
  • Phase: 0° at $r=0$, exactly 90° at $r=1$ for every $\zeta$, tending to 180°. Low damping gives a sharp step; high damping a gradual one.
Answer. (a) Beating. (b) The labelled features above; the $\zeta=0.7$ curve has no peak.

Part (a) matches the 2021 memo. Part (b) from Lecture 6.

On this page
3.1 The setup3.2 Undamped harmonic excitation3.3 Damped harmonic excitationQ Practice questions
Week 4

Base excitation, rotating unbalance and numerical simulation

Lectures 7–8

This week in brief

  • Base excitation $y=Y\sin\omega t$: the input is $ky+c\dot y$. Displacement transmissibility $X/Y=\sqrt{\dfrac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}$.
  • Every transmissibility curve passes through 1 at $r=\sqrt2$. Below $\sqrt2$ damping helps; above it, damping makes things worse.
  • The force transmitted to the base is $F_T/kY=r^2\,X/Y$. Do not confuse it with $X/Y$.
  • A road input is a frequency $\omega=2\pi v/\lambda$. Convert speed and wavelength first, in rad/s.
  • Rotating unbalance: $F_0=m_0e\omega^2$ grows with speed, so $mX/(m_0e)=r^2/\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}\to1$ as $r\to\infty$.
  • Numerical simulation: rewrite as first-order state form $\dot{\mathbf y}=\mathbf f(t,\mathbf y)$ and integrate with Runge–Kutta (ode45) or Simulink. Know how to match a plot to its parameters.

4.1The physical problem

Explanation and derivation

Instead of a force applied to the mass, the support moves. A car on a corrugated road, a suspension seat on a boat, a building in an earthquake, an instrument on a vibrating bench. The base moves as $y(t)$ and the mass responds as $x(t)$; the spring and damper both respond to the relative motion.

4.2The equation of motion

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x + c(\dd x-\dd y) + k(x-y) = 0\;} \end{equation*}(4.1)
$y(t)$
base displacement, $Y\sin\omega_bt$
$Y$
base amplitude (half the peak-to-trough height)
$\omega_b$
base excitation frequency

The key insight

Base excitation is just harmonic forcing with two forcing terms, one in phase with the base displacement (through the spring, amplitude $kY$) and one in phase with the base velocity (through the damper, amplitude $c\omega_b Y$). Solve each with the standard result of §3.3 and add.
Explanation and derivation

The spring force is $k(x-y)$ and the damper force is $c(\dd x-\dd y)$, both opposing the mass's motion, so [9]

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x + c(\dd x-\dd y) + k(x-y) = 0\;} \end{equation*}(4.1)

Assume harmonic base motion $y(t) = Y\sin\omega_b t$, so $\dd y = Y\omega_b\cos\omega_b t$. Move the known terms to the right:

\begin{equation*} m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx = \underbrace{cY\omega_b\cos\omega_b t + kY\sin\omega_b t}_{\text{effective force}} \end{equation*}(4.2)

or, dividing by $m$,

\begin{equation*} \ddd x + 2\zeta\wnn\dd x + \wnn^2 x = 2\zeta\wnn\omega_b Y\cos\omega_b t + \wnn^2 Y\sin\omega_b t \end{equation*}(4.3)

4.3Displacement transmissibility

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\left|\frac{X}{Y}\right| = \sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\;} \qquad\textbf{displacement transmissibility} \end{equation*}(4.4)
Explanation and derivation

Substituting $f_0 = 2\zeta\wnn\omega_b Y$ and $f_0=\wnn^2 Y$ in turn into the particular solution of Eq. (3.9) gives two particular solutions [9]:

\begin{align*} x_p^{(1)} &= \frac{2\zeta\wnn\omega_b Y}{\sqrt{(\wnn^2-\omega_b^2)^2+(2\zeta\wnn\omega_b)^2}}\cos(\omega_b t-\theta_1)\\ x_p^{(2)} &= \frac{\wnn^2 Y}{\sqrt{(\wnn^2-\omega_b^2)^2+(2\zeta\wnn\omega_b)^2}}\sin(\omega_b t-\theta_1) \end{align*}

with $\theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{2\zeta\wnn\omega_b}{\wnn^2-\omega_b^2}$. Adding them (sine and cosine at the same frequency combine into a single cosine with a further phase shift $\theta_2 = \tan^{-1}\frac{\wnn}{2\zeta\omega_b}$) gives

\begin{equation*} x_p(t) = \wnn Y\sqrt{\frac{\wnn^2+(2\zeta\omega_b)^2}{(\wnn^2-\omega_b^2)^2+(2\zeta\wnn\omega_b)^2}} \cos(\omega_b t - \theta_1 - \theta_2) \end{equation*}

whose amplitude, non-dimensionalised with $r=\omega_b/\wnn$, is the result you must know:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\left|\frac{X}{Y}\right| = \sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\;} \qquad\textbf{displacement transmissibility} \end{equation*}(4.4)

4.3.1The same result by the complex method

Much faster, and the method the 2023 memo uses. Let $y = Ye^{j\omega_b t}$ and $x_p = Xe^{j\omega_b t}$ in Eq. (4.1) [9]:

\begin{equation*} \big(\wnn^2-\omega_b^2+2j\zeta\wnn\omega_b\big)Xe^{j\omega_b t} = \big(2j\zeta\wnn\omega_b + \wnn^2\big)Ye^{j\omega_b t} \end{equation*}

\begin{equation*} \Rightarrow\quad \frac{X}{Y} = \frac{\wnn^2+2j\zeta\wnn\omega_b}{\wnn^2-\omega_b^2+2j\zeta\wnn\omega_b} \end{equation*}(4.5)

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator and take the magnitude: $\left|\frac{a+jb}{c+jd}\right| = \frac{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}{\sqrt{c^2+d^2}}$, which gives Eq. (4.4) directly.

4.3.2And by the transfer function

Take the Laplace transform of Eq. (4.1) [9]:

\begin{equation*} (ms^2+cs+k)X = (cs+k)Y \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \frac{X}{Y} = \frac{cs+k}{ms^2+cs+k} \end{equation*}(4.6)

Substituting $s = j\omega_b$ recovers Eq. (4.5). All three routes are examinable; the complex one is fastest under time pressure.

4.4Force transmissibility

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\left|\frac{F_T}{kY}\right| = r^2\sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\;} \qquad\textbf{force transmissibility} \end{equation*}(4.7)
$F_T$
amplitude of the force transmitted to the mass through spring and damper

The relationship worth remembering

\begin{equation*} \left|\frac{F_T}{kY}\right| = r^2\left|\frac{X}{Y}\right| \end{equation*}
Force transmissibility is displacement transmissibility multiplied by $r^2$. That single factor is what makes the force curve keep rising at high $r$ instead of dying away, and it is the reason a soft mount that isolates displacement does not automatically isolate force at high frequency.
Explanation and derivation

Often the question is not how much the mass moves, but how much force is fed through the mounting. The transmitted force is

\begin{equation*} F(t) = k(x-y) + c(\dd x-\dd y) \end{equation*}(4.8)

and its magnitude, non-dimensionalised by $kY$, works out to [9]

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\left|\frac{F_T}{kY}\right| = r^2\sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\;} \qquad\textbf{force transmissibility} \end{equation*}(4.7)

4.5The three facts every base-excitation question tests

Facts to state and to mark on every sketch

  1. At $r=0$, $|X/Y|=1$. At very low frequency the mass simply rides along with the base. The curve starts at 1, for every $\zeta$.
  2. At $r=\sqrt2$, $|X/Y|=1$ for every $\zeta$. All the curves pass through this one point. Substitute $r^2=2$ into Eq. (4.4): $\frac{1+8\zeta^2}{1+8\zeta^2}=1$, independent of $\zeta$.
  3. Isolation occurs only for $r>\sqrt2$. For $r<\sqrt2$ the mass moves more than the base ($|X/Y|>1$), which is amplification, not isolation. This is why an isolator must be soft (low $\wnn$) relative to the disturbance frequency.
Explanation and derivation

4.5.1The damping trade-off

This is the conceptual point that questions 2021 Q3(d)–(e) and 2022 Q4(c) test:

So there is no “best” damping. High damping protects against resonance during run-up and run-down; low damping gives better isolation at the operating point. Real vehicle suspensions compromise around $\zeta \approx 0.2$–$0.4$.

4.6Turning a physical input into $\omega$

Converting the excitation to rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$

\begin{align*} \text{From frequency in Hz:}\quad & \omega = 2\pi f\\[3pt] \text{From a speed $v$ over a wavelength $\lambda$:}\quad & \omega = \frac{2\pi v}{\lambda} \qquad\text{(SI: $v$ in m$\cdot$s$^{-1}$, $\lambda$ in m)} \end{align*}
Convert km$\cdot$h$^{-1}$ to m$\cdot$s$^{-1}$ by $\times\frac{1000}{3600}$, i.e. $\div3.6$.
Worked example — Term-3 paper 2022, Q4 — Trans-Agulhas suspension seat
$m=40$ kg, $k=6250$ N$\cdot$m$^{-1}$, wave $\lambda = 4\pi$ m, wave height 1 m peak-to-trough (so $Y=0.5$ m). Damper $c=40$ N$\cdot$s$\cdot$m$^{-1}$.

System properties:

\begin{equation*} \wnn = \sqrt{\frac{6250}{40}} = 12.5\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}, \qquad \zeta = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{km}} = \frac{40}{2\sqrt{6250\times40}} = 0.04 \end{equation*}

(a)(i) At $v = 54$ km$\cdot$h$^{-1}$ $= 15$ m$\cdot$s$^{-1}$:

\begin{equation*} \omega = \frac{2\pi(15)}{4\pi} = 7.5\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}, \qquad r = \frac{7.5}{12.5} = 0.6 \end{equation*}
\begin{equation*} \left|\frac{X}{Y}\right| = \sqrt{\frac{1+(2\times0.04\times0.6)^2}{(1-0.36)^2+(2\times0.04\times0.6)^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.00230}{0.40960+0.00230}} = 1.560 \end{equation*}
So $X = 1.560\times0.5 = 0.78$ m. The seat moves 56% more than the wave. Bad.

(a)(ii) At $v = 144$ km$\cdot$h$^{-1}$ $= 40$ m$\cdot$s$^{-1}$: $\omega = 20$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$, $r = 1.6$, and

\begin{equation*} \left|\frac{X}{Y}\right| = \sqrt{\frac{1+(0.128)^2}{(1-2.56)^2+(0.128)^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.01638}{2.4336+0.01638}} = 0.644 \end{equation*}
Now $r>\sqrt2$: the seat moves less than the wave. Isolation achieved.

The memo (2022 term-3 paper, Q4) prints 1.565 and 0.659. Neither can be reproduced from the given data: with $\zeta=0.04$ the values are 1.560 and 0.644, and even with no damping they would be 1.563 and 0.641. Work to 1.56 and 0.64; the sketch and the conclusions do not change.

(c) Replacing the damper with $c = 400$ N$\cdot$s$\cdot$m$^{-1}$ ($\zeta = 0.4$): at $r=0.6$ the transmissibility drops to $1.39$ (better), but at $r=1.6$ it rises to $0.80$ (worse). The two curves cross at $r=\sqrt2$. So the stiffer damper helps at low speed and hurts at high speed — state exactly that.

(d) With $c = 2$ N$\cdot$s$\cdot$m$^{-1}$ ($\zeta = 0.002$) at $v=85$ km$\cdot$h$^{-1}$: $v = 23.6$ m$\cdot$s$^{-1}$, $\omega = 11.8$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$, so $r = 0.944$ — very close to resonance with almost no damping. The response will look like beating growing towards a very large amplitude, $\omega_{\text{beat}} = |12.5-11.8| = 0.7$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$. Sketch a beat envelope, note that the small damping eventually limits the steady amplitude to $|X/Y|\approx7.6$, and note that this is a structural failure risk.

Marks note: the memo's answers of 1.565 and 0.659 differ from mine in the third significant figure because it reads $\zeta$ to fewer digits. Any answer within about 1% is accepted; showing $\omega$, $r$ and the substituted expression is what earns the marks.

Worked example — Term-3 paper 2023, Q4 — bus on a corrugated road
$k=1000$ N$\cdot$m$^{-1}$, $m=3000$ kg, $c=650$ N$\cdot$s$\cdot$m$^{-1}$, excitation $0.1$ Hz.

(a) EOM: $m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx = c\dd y + ky$, i.e. Eq. (4.2). (The 2023 memo prints $-c\dd y$ on the right; that sign is a typo — the damper force is $c(\dd y-\dd x)$.)

(b) With $c=0$ at $f = 0.1$ Hz:

\begin{equation*} \wnn = \sqrt{\frac{1000}{3000}} = 0.5774\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}, \qquad \omega = 2\pi(0.1) = 0.6283\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} \end{equation*}
$r = 1.088$ — close to resonance and undamped, so beating:
\begin{equation*} \omega_{\text{beat}} = |0.5774-0.6283| = 0.0510\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1} \quad\Rightarrow\quad f_{\text{beat}} = 0.0081\ \text{Hz}\ \ (\text{a beat every }123\ \text{s}) \end{equation*}
The displacement itself oscillates at the average, $(\wnn+\omega)/2 = 0.603$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$. With the paper's $Y = 50$ mm, the envelope peaks at $2(k/m)Y/|\wnn^2-\omega^2| = 2(0.3333)(0.05)/0.0614 = 0.54$ m (memo: 0.542 m ✓). Sketch the fast oscillation inside a slow envelope, starting from zero (zero ICs).

(c) Choosing the right expression. The question offers three expressions (Table 4: A, B, C) and you must pick. It is asking for displacement transmissibility, so the answer is Option C, Eq. (4.4), $\sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}$ — not the one with the leading $r^2$, which is force transmissibility. Free marks: check whether the numerator has a $1+$ (base excitation) or not (direct force), and whether there is a leading $r^2$ (force or unbalance).

(d) With $c = 650$: $\zeta = c/(2\sqrt{km}) = 650/(2\sqrt{1000\times3000}) = 0.1876$. Sketch $|X/Y|$ against $r$, mark the current operating point $r=1.088$, and shade $r>\sqrt2$ as the isolation region.

(e) The driver should speed up: increasing $v$ increases $\omega_b$, pushing $r$ past $\sqrt2$ and into isolation. Slowing down moves $r$ towards 1 and makes it worse.

4.7Formula recognition table

Exam angle

Sanity-check any transmissibility answer with the limits: base-excitation $|X/Y|\to1$ as $r\to0$; unbalance $mX/m_0e\to0$ as $r\to0$ and $\to1$ as $r\to\infty$; force transmissibility $\to0$ as $r\to0$. If your number does not obey these, you have picked the wrong formula.
Explanation and derivation

Four formulas on the formula sheet look alike. Getting them mixed up is the most expensive single error available in this paper, so learn to identify them by shape.

4.8The physical problem

Explanation and derivation

Any rotating machine — a fan, a pump, a washing machine drum, a car wheel — has some of its mass off the axis of rotation. That eccentric mass $m_0$ at radius $e$, spinning at $\omega_r$, produces a rotating centrifugal force that shakes the machine. Unlike base excitation, the excitation amplitude itself grows with frequency, and that changes the shape of the answer.

4.9Derivation

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx = m_0e\omega_r^2\sin\omega_r t\;} \end{equation*}(4.9)
$m_0$
unbalanced (eccentric) mass
$e$
distance of $m_0$ from the rotation axis
$\omega_r$
rotor speed [rad/s]
$m$
total machine mass, including $m_0$

The one thing that makes it different

The forcing amplitude $F_0 = m_0e\omega_r^2$ is proportional to $\omega_r^2$, not constant. Substituting this into the standard steady-state amplitude $X = f_0/\big[\wnn^2\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}\big]$ and noting $\omega_r^2/\wnn^2 = r^2$ gives the extra $r^2$:
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;X = \frac{m_0e}{m}\cdot\frac{r^2}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\;} \qquad\text{or}\qquad \frac{mX}{m_0e} = \frac{r^2}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}} \end{equation*}
Explanation and derivation

Let $m$ be the total mass of the machine (including $m_0$), $x$ the vertical displacement of the machine, and $x_r$ the vertical displacement of $m_0$ relative to the machine. With $x_r = e\sin\omega_r t$ [9],

\begin{equation*} \ddd x_r = -e\omega_r^2\sin\omega_r t . \end{equation*}(4.10)

Applying Newton's second law to the eccentric mass, the force it exerts on the machine is $-F_r$ where

\begin{equation*} m_0(\ddd x + \ddd x_r) = -F_r . \end{equation*}

Applying Newton's second law to the rest of the machine (mass $m-m_0$), supported on the spring and damper:

\begin{equation*} (m-m_0)\ddd x = F_r - c\dd x - kx . \end{equation*}

Adding the two eliminates $F_r$ and gives the equation of motion [9]:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx = m_0e\omega_r^2\sin\omega_r t\;} \end{equation*}(4.9)

This is standard harmonic forcing with

\begin{equation*} F_0 = m_0e\omega_r^2 \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad f_0 = \frac{m_0e\omega_r^2}{m}. \end{equation*}

4.10Reading the curve

Exam angle

The $r\to\infty$ limit $X = m_0e/m$ is a useful check and a good short-answer point. It also explains why increasing the mass of a machine base reduces its vibration at high speed, and why balancing (reducing $m_0e$) is the only fix that works at all speeds.

4.11Worked check

Worked example — Typical unbalance calculation
A 50 kg fan runs at 1500 rpm on mounts giving $\wnn = 40$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$ and $\zeta = 0.1$. The rotor carries an unbalance of $m_0e = 0.02$ kg$\cdot$m. Find the steady-state amplitude, and the amplitude if the fan is slowed to 300 rpm.

Convert rpm to rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$: $\omega_r = \dfrac{2\pi N}{60}$, so $1500$ rpm $= 157.1$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$ and $300$ rpm $=31.4$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$.

At 1500 rpm: $r = 157.1/40 = 3.927$.

\begin{equation*} \frac{mX}{m_0e} = \frac{3.927^2}{\sqrt{(1-15.42)^2+(2\times0.1\times3.927)^2}} = \frac{15.42}{\sqrt{207.9+0.617}} = 1.068 \end{equation*}
\begin{equation*} X = 1.068\times\frac{0.02}{50} = 4.27\times10^{-4}\ \text{m} = 0.43\ \text{mm} \end{equation*}
Already close to the high-speed limit $m_0e/m = 0.40$ mm, as expected for $r\approx4$.

At 300 rpm: $r = 0.785$.

\begin{equation*} \frac{mX}{m_0e} = \frac{0.6169}{\sqrt{(1-0.6169)^2+(0.1571)^2}} = \frac{0.6169}{0.4141} = 1.490 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad X = 0.60\ \text{mm} \end{equation*}
Slowing down made it worse, because 300 rpm moves $r$ towards resonance. If the fan must operate near $r=1$ the correct fix is to change the mounts (change $\wnn$), add damping, or balance the rotor — not to change speed slightly.

Exam angle

Rotating unbalance was not the main subject of a recent term-3 question, but it is named in the A2 layout alongside base excitation, it was Question 3 of the 2024 A2, and its formula is on the sheet. The cheapest way it can appear is a one-line “which of these expressions applies” question, or a sketch. Know the shape (starts at 0, peaks at $\approx1/2\zeta$, tends to 1).

4.12Why numerical integration is needed

Definition

“A numerical solution is a discretised approximation of an analytical solution.” — Nickerson, Lecture 8 [10]
Explanation and derivation

Every system solved so far had a closed-form solution. Many do not: Coulomb friction combined with viscous damping (Eq. (2.10)), non-linear springs, arbitrary forcing. For these you integrate the equation of motion numerically.

4.13Converting a second-order ODE to first-order state form

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\; \begin{aligned} \dd x_1(t) &= x_2(t)\\ \dd x_2(t) &= -\frac{c}{m}x_2(t) - \frac{k}{m}x_1(t) \end{aligned}\;} \end{equation*}(4.11)
$x_1,\ x_2$
state variables: $x_1=x$, $x_2=\dot x$
Explanation and derivation

ODE solvers accept only first-order systems. The standard trick is to introduce state variables. For $m\ddd x + c\dd x + kx = 0$, let $x_1 = x$ and $x_2 = \dd x$:

\begin{equation*} \boxed{\; \begin{aligned} \dd x_1(t) &= x_2(t)\\ \dd x_2(t) &= -\frac{c}{m}x_2(t) - \frac{k}{m}x_1(t) \end{aligned}\;} \end{equation*}(4.11)

or in matrix form,

\begin{equation*} \begin{Bmatrix}\dd x_1\\ \dd x_2\end{Bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1\\ -k/m & -c/m\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}x_1\\ x_2\end{Bmatrix} + \begin{Bmatrix}0\\ F(t)/m\end{Bmatrix} \end{equation*}

Notice this is the “two states” idea from Week 1 made concrete: one degree of freedom, two states.

4.14Runge–Kutta and ode45

Reference — Which MATLAB solver, and when
Explanation and derivation

The standard method is fourth-order Runge–Kutta. For $\dd x = f(x,t)$ with $x(0)=x_0$ [10]:

\begin{equation*} x_{n+1} = x_n + \frac{\Delta t}{6}\big(k_{n1} + 2k_{n2} + 2k_{n3} + k_{n4}\big) \end{equation*}(4.12)

where

\begin{align*} k_{n1} &= f(x_n,\ t_n) \\ k_{n2} &= f\!\left(x_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}k_{n1},\ t_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\right)\\ k_{n3} &= f\!\left(x_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}k_{n2},\ t_n + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\right)\\ k_{n4} &= f\!\left(x_n + \Delta t\,k_{n3},\ t_n + \Delta t\right) \end{align*}

The method evaluates the slope four times per step — at the start, twice in the middle, and at the end — and takes a weighted average. The step size $\Delta t$ may be fixed or adapted automatically according to how quickly the solution is changing.

In MATLAB the call is

\begin{equation*} \texttt{[t, x] = ode45(odefun, tspan, x0);} \end{equation*}

with odefun a function returning $\dd{\mathbf x}$, tspan the integration interval, and x0 the initial state vector. Lecture 8's guidance: “Generally, you will start with ode45 and look to others if that does not work” [10].

4.15Simulink

Reference — Simulink practicalities

Simulink practicalities from Lecture 8 [10]

  • Initial conditions are set inside the integrator blocks, not elsewhere.
  • Solver settings live under Simulation $\to$ Model Configuration Parameters. It is sometimes necessary to reduce Max step size — particularly with a Sign block, where the derivative is discontinuous.
  • Coulomb friction is added with a Sign block on the velocity signal, scaled by $\mu N/m$.
Explanation and derivation

The alternative is to build the equation as a block diagram. Write the EOM with acceleration alone on the left [10]:

\begin{equation*} \ddd x = -\frac{c}{m}\dd x - \frac{k}{m}x \end{equation*}(4.13)

then wire it as: a summing junction produces $\ddd x$; an integrator gives $\dd x$; a second integrator gives $x$; feedback gains $-c/m$ and $-k/m$ return those to the summing junction.

4.16MATLAB Assignment 1 — what was in it

Reference — MATLAB Assignment 1 scope and the physical
Reference — Task 1 cross-check values

Exam angle

Questions drawn from the assignment are unlikely to ask for MATLAB syntax. What they can ask: given a set of parameters, compute $\wnn$ and $\zeta$, classify the damping, and match the parameter set to one of several plotted responses. That is exactly the 2022 term-3 paper, Q3(a) — a table of four systems ($m,k,c,\mu,x_0,v_0,F_0,\omega$) to be matched to seven plots (A)–(G). Practise reading a plot for: does it oscillate? does the envelope decay exponentially or linearly? does it grow? is there beating? what is the period?
Reference — Plot-matching decision tree

Plot-matching decision tree

  1. Does it grow without bound? $\Rightarrow$ resonance, $r=1$, $\zeta=0$.
  2. Does the amplitude swell and collapse periodically? $\Rightarrow$ beating, $r$ near but not equal to 1, small $\zeta$.
  3. Does it oscillate with constant amplitude? $\Rightarrow$ $\zeta=0$, free or steady-state forced.
  4. Does it oscillate with a curved decaying envelope? $\Rightarrow$ underdamped viscous. Measure the peak ratio for $\zeta$.
  5. Does it oscillate with a straight-line envelope, stopping off-centre? $\Rightarrow$ Coulomb.
  6. Does it not oscillate at all? $\Rightarrow$ $\zeta\ge1$. If it just decays, critically or overdamped; check whether it crosses zero once ($v_0$ opposing $x_0$).
  7. Read the period off the plot to get $\wdd\approx\wnn$, then check $\wnn=\sqrt{k/m}$ against the candidate parameter sets.

Practice questions — Week 4

Q 4.1Term-3 papers 2026 Q3 and 2021 Q3[12]

A vehicle on a corrugated road is modelled as in Figure 4.3: lumped stiffness $k=1000$ N/m, damping $c=650$ N·s/m, mass $m=3000$ kg, base input $y=Y\sin\omega_bt$ with $Y=80$ mm.

(a) Calculate $\omega_n$ and $\zeta$. [2]
(b) Using Figure 4.4(a), what is $X$ when $\omega_b=\omega_n$? [2]
(c) Safe driving requires $X\le Y$ and $F_T/kY<2$. Using both curves, over what range of $\omega_b$ is this met? [2]
(d) With a sketch, explain the effect of a larger $\zeta$ on $X$. [3]
(e) With a sketch, explain the effect of a larger $\zeta$ on the transmitted force. [3]

The force condition alone also allows small $r$, but there $X>Y$.
Step 1 — (a)

$\omega_n=\sqrt{1000/3000}=0.577$ rad/s; $\zeta=650/(2\sqrt{1000\times3000})=0.188$.

Step 2 — (b)

Read $X/Y\approx2.85$ at $r=1$ (exact $\sqrt{1+(2\zeta)^2}/(2\zeta)=2.85$), so $X\approx228$ mm.

Step 3 — (c) Combine the two conditions

$X/Y\le1$ needs $r\ge\sqrt2$. $F_T/kY<2$ holds for $r<0.88$ and again for $\sqrt2<r<4.3$ (at $r=\sqrt2$, $F_T/kY=r^2\cdot1=2$ exactly). Only the overlap counts:

\[\sqrt2<r<4.3\quad\Rightarrow\quad0.82<\omega_b<2.49\ \text{rad/s}\]Step 4 — (d)–(e) Effect of damping

Displacement: all curves start at 1; a larger $\zeta$ lowers the resonant peak but raises $X/Y$ above $r=\sqrt2$ (less isolation). Force: $F_T/kY$ starts at 0; a larger $\zeta$ lowers the peak but makes the force grow faster above $r=\sqrt2$, because the damper force rises with frequency.

These are the paper’s numbers. They imply a static deflection of 29 m and $f_n=0.09$ Hz, which no vehicle has; the method is what is examined.

Answer. (a) 0.577 rad/s, 0.188. (b) $X\approx228$ mm. (c) $0.82<\omega_b<2.49$ rad/s (the memo writes $\le$ at the lower end; at exactly $\sqrt2$ the force ratio equals 2). (d)–(e) Damping helps only near resonance and hurts above $\sqrt2$.

Printed: $\omega_n=0.5774$ ✓, $\zeta=0.1876$ ✓, $X=224$ mm from reading 2.8 (exact 2.85 → 228 mm), range $0.8166\le\omega_b<2.4828$ ✓. Recomputed in verify.py.

Q 4.2Term-3 paper 2012, Question 2(b)–(c)[6]

For the base-excitation model of Figure 4.3: (a) draw the free-body diagram and derive $|X/Y|$ in terms of $r$ and $\zeta$. [4] (b) Sketch $|X/Y|$ against $r$ for the undamped and an underdamped system. [2]

Step 1 — EOM

The spring and damper act on the relative motion: $m\ddot x=-k(x-y)-c(\dot x-\dot y)$, so $m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=ky+c\dot y$.

Step 2 — Harmonic solution

With $y=Ye^{j\omega t}$, $x=Xe^{j\omega t}$: $X(k-m\omega^2+jc\omega)=Y(k+jc\omega)$. Divide by $k$:

\[\left|\frac XY\right|=\sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\]Step 3 — Sketch

Both start at 1. Undamped: goes to infinity at $r=1$, passes 1 at $r=\sqrt2$, then falls like $1/(r^2-1)$. Underdamped: finite peak near $r=1$; also passes 1 at $r=\sqrt2$; decays more slowly above it.

Answer. $|X/Y|$ as above; every curve passes through 1 at $r=\sqrt2$.

Matches the 2012 memo.

Q 4.3New question (Lecture 8 content)[6]

You must simulate $m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=F_0\cos\omega t$ with MATLAB's ode45.

(a) Write the equation in first-order state form, defining the state vector. [3]
(b) What must ode45 be given, and what does it return? [2]
(c) The simulated response grows without bound although $c>0$. Name one likely cause. [1]

Step 1 — (a) State form

$\mathbf y=[x,\ \dot x]^T$: $\dot y_1=y_2$, $\dot y_2=\frac1m(F_0\cos\omega t-cy_2-ky_1)$, i.e.

\[\dot{\mathbf y}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-k/m&-c/m\end{bmatrix}\mathbf y+\begin{bmatrix}0\\F_0\cos\omega t/m\end{bmatrix}\]Step 2 — (b)

A function handle f(t,y) returning $\dot{\mathbf y}$, the time span and the initial state $[x_0,\ v_0]$. It returns the time vector and the state at each time (columns $x$ and $\dot x$).

Step 3 — (c)

A sign error in the state equation (e.g. $+c y_2$ or $+k y_1$) makes the system unstable; or the damping term uses $y_1$ instead of $y_2$.

Answer. (a) Two first-order equations in $[x,\dot x]$. (b) Handle, time span, initial state. (c) A sign or index error in $f$.

New question, from Lecture 8 and MATLAB Assignment 1.

Q 4.4A2 2024, Question 3 (c)–(d)[6]

An undamped motor on mounts has an unbalance $m_0$ at radius $e$, so $F(t)=F_0\cos\omega t$ with $F_0=m_0e\omega^2$. It runs at 95 % of the natural frequency and starts from rest at equilibrium. (c) Find $x(t)$ symbolically. (d) Sketch it, give the frequency of the oscillation and the maximum amplitude.

(c) With $f_0=F_0/m$ and $x_0=v_0=0$ (Week 3): \[x(t)=\frac{f_0}{\omega_n^2-\omega^2}(\cos\omega t-\cos\omega_nt)=\frac{2f_0}{\omega_n^2-\omega^2}\sin\frac{(\omega_n-\omega)t}{2}\,\sin\frac{(\omega_n+\omega)t}{2}\] With $\omega=0.95\omega_n$: $\omega_n^2-\omega^2=0.0975\omega_n^2$ and $f_0=m_0e(0.95\omega_n)^2/m$, so \[x(t)=18.5\,\frac{m_0e}{m}\,\sin(0.025\,\omega_nt)\,\sin(0.975\,\omega_nt)\] (d) Beating: a fast oscillation at $(\omega_n+\omega)/2=0.975\omega_n$ inside a slow envelope; beat frequency $|\omega_n-\omega|=0.05\omega_n$ (beat period $2\pi/0.05\omega_n=126/\omega_n$). Starts at zero.
Answer. Oscillation at $0.975\omega_n$; maximum amplitude $2f_0/(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)=18.5\,m_0e/m$, with $m$ the total mass including $m_0$ (Inman's convention).

No 2024 memo; derived from the Week 3 undamped solution.

Week 5

Two-degree-of-freedom systems

Lecture 9

This week in brief

  • Two coordinates give two coupled EOMs: $\mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf x}+\mathbf K\mathbf x=\mathbf 0$. Write $\mathbf M$ and $\mathbf K$ by inspection; $\mathbf K$ is symmetric.
  • Assume $\mathbf x=\mathbf u e^{j\omega t}$, so $(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)\mathbf u=\mathbf 0$. A non-trivial $\mathbf u$ needs $\det(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)=0$. Say this in the exam.
  • Each $\omega_i$ has a mode shape $\mathbf u_i$, known only up to a scale factor: report the ratio $u_2/u_1$. In-phase and out-of-phase modes are sketched as arrows on the masses.
  • $\omega=0$ is a rigid-body mode: the system moves without deforming a spring.
  • The free response is a sum of the two modes, with four constants from $\mathbf x_0$ and $\dot{\mathbf x}_0$.

5.1Two new concepts

What changes when you add a second degree of freedom

  • One natural frequency per DOF. A 2DOF system has two; an $n$-DOF system has $n$.
  • Each natural frequency has a mode shape — a vector giving the relative displacements of the degrees of freedom when the system vibrates at that frequency. A mode shape has no absolute scale: only the ratio $u_1:u_2$ is meaningful.
  • The equations are coupled. The motion of $x_1$ affects $x_2$ and vice versa. Coupling through the stiffness matrix is called elastic coupling.

5.2Writing the equations of motion

\begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} m_1 & 0\\ 0 & m_2\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix} \ddd x_1\\ \ddd x_2\end{Bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} k_1+k_2 & -k_2\\ -k_2 & k_2\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\end{Bmatrix} = \mathbf 0 \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \boxed{\;\mathbf M\ddd{\mathbf x} + \mathbf K\mathbf x = \mathbf 0\;} \end{equation*}(5.1)

Rules for writing $\mathbf M$ and $\mathbf K$ by inspection

  • $\mathbf M$ is diagonal whenever each coordinate has its own lumped mass. Off-diagonal mass terms appear only with inertial coupling (e.g. a coordinate measured at a point that is not the centre of mass).
  • $K_{ii}$ = sum of all stiffnesses connected to DOF $i$.
  • $K_{ij}$ ($i\neq j$) = minus the stiffness connecting DOF $i$ and DOF $j$.
  • $\mathbf K$ is always symmetric: $K_{ij}=K_{ji}$. If yours is not, you have made a sign error. This is a free check worth taking.
Explanation and derivation

Take the standard two-cart system: $m_1$ attached to ground by $k_1$ and to $m_2$ by $k_2$ [11].

5.2.1By free-body diagram

Draw each mass separately, in a displaced position, and be careful with the coupling spring: its extension is the relative displacement $x_1-x_2$.

\begin{align*} m_1\ddd x_1 + (k_1+k_2)x_1 - k_2x_2 &= 0\\ m_2\ddd x_2 - k_2x_1 + k_2x_2 &= 0 \end{align*}

5.2.2In matrix form

\begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} m_1 & 0\\ 0 & m_2\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix} \ddd x_1\\ \ddd x_2\end{Bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} k_1+k_2 & -k_2\\ -k_2 & k_2\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\end{Bmatrix} = \mathbf 0 \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \boxed{\;\mathbf M\ddd{\mathbf x} + \mathbf K\mathbf x = \mathbf 0\;} \end{equation*}(5.1)

5.3Solving: the eigenvalue problem

\begin{equation*} \mathbf x(t) = \mathbf u e^{j\omega t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \ddd{\mathbf x}(t) = -\omega^2\mathbf u e^{j\omega t} \end{equation*}(5.2)
$\mathbf u$
mode-shape vector: the relative amplitudes of the DOFs
$\omega$
natural frequency to be found

Why the determinant must be zero (state this in the exam)

If $(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)$ had an inverse, we could pre-multiply Eq. (5.4) by it and obtain $\mathbf u e^{j\omega t}=\mathbf 0$, i.e. $\mathbf u = \mathbf 0$ — the trivial solution, meaning no motion at all. For an oscillating solution to exist, $(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)$ must therefore have no inverse, i.e. be singular. A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant vanishes:
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\det\!\big(\mathbf K - \omega^2\mathbf M\big) = 0\;} \end{equation*}
\begin{equation*} \Rightarrow\quad m_1m_2\,\omega^4 - (m_1k_2+m_2k_1+m_2k_2)\,\omega^2 + k_1k_2 = 0 \end{equation*}(5.3)

Exam angle

Do not try to solve Eq. (5.3) as a quartic in $\omega$. Substitute $\lambda = \omega^2$, solve the quadratic, then $\omega_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$. If your $\lambda$ comes out negative or complex, you have a sign error in $\mathbf K$ — for a physical system both roots are real and non-negative.
Explanation and derivation — asked in most papers

Assume that every DOF oscillates at the same frequency with a fixed relative amplitude [11]:

\begin{equation*} \mathbf x(t) = \mathbf u e^{j\omega t} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \ddd{\mathbf x}(t) = -\omega^2\mathbf u e^{j\omega t} \end{equation*}(5.2)

Substituting into Eq. (5.1):

\begin{equation*} \big(-\omega^2\mathbf M + \mathbf K\big)\mathbf u e^{j\omega t} = \mathbf 0 \end{equation*}(5.4)

Now the crucial argument, which carries marks:

For the two-cart system this gives

\begin{equation*} \det\begin{bmatrix} k_1+k_2-m_1\omega^2 & -k_2\\ -k_2 & k_2-m_2\omega^2\end{bmatrix}=0 \end{equation*}

\begin{equation*} \Rightarrow\quad m_1m_2\,\omega^4 - (m_1k_2+m_2k_1+m_2k_2)\,\omega^2 + k_1k_2 = 0 \end{equation*}(5.3)

This is the characteristic equation. It is a quadratic in $\omega^2$ — solve it with the quadratic formula in the variable $\lambda=\omega^2$, then take positive square roots.

5.4Mode shapes

Worked example — Lecture 9 example — worked in full [11]
$m_1 = 9$ kg, $m_2 = 1$ kg, $k_1 = 24$ N$\cdot$m$^{-1}$, $k_2 = 3$ N$\cdot$m$^{-1}$.

Matrices:

\begin{equation*} \mathbf M = \begin{bmatrix}9&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf K = \begin{bmatrix}27&-3\\-3&3\end{bmatrix} \end{equation*}

Characteristic equation:

\begin{equation*} \det\begin{bmatrix}27-9\omega^2 & -3\\ -3 & 3-\omega^2\end{bmatrix} = (27-9\omega^2)(3-\omega^2) - 9 = 0 \end{equation*}
\begin{equation*} \Rightarrow\; 9\omega^4 - 54\omega^2 + 72 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \omega^4 - 6\omega^2 + 8 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (\omega^2-2)(\omega^2-4)=0 \end{equation*}
\begin{equation*} \boxed{\;\omega_1 = \sqrt2 = 1.414\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}, \qquad \omega_2 = 2\ \text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\;} \end{equation*}

Mode 1 ($\omega^2 = 2$):

\begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix}27-18 & -3\\ -3 & 3-2\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}u_{11}\\u_{12}\end{Bmatrix} = \mathbf 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 9u_{11}-3u_{12}=0 \;\Rightarrow\; u_{12}=3u_{11} \end{equation*}
Setting $u_{11}=1$: $\mathbf u_1 = \{1,\ 3\}^T$. The masses move in phase, with mass 2's amplitude three times mass 1's.

Mode 2 ($\omega^2 = 4$):

\begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix}27-36 & -3\\ -3 & 3-4\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}u_{21}\\u_{22}\end{Bmatrix} = \mathbf 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad -9u_{21}-3u_{22}=0 \;\Rightarrow\; u_{22}=-3u_{21} \end{equation*}
Setting $u_{21}=1$: $\mathbf u_2 = \{1,\ -3\}^T$. The masses move out of phase.

Check the second row: for mode 1, $-3(1)+1(3)=0$ ✓. Always check — if the second row does not also give zero, you have an arithmetic error in $\omega_i$.

Sketching mode shapes — what earns the marks

Draw the physical system twice, once per mode, and on each drawing:
  1. An arrow at each DOF showing the direction (sign of $u_i$).
  2. Arrow lengths in proportion to $|u_i|$ — if $u_2 = 3u_1$, draw it three times longer.
  3. A label stating in words: “masses move in phase, mass 2 amplitude is 3$\times$ mass 1”.
  4. The associated $\omega_i$ written next to the sketch.
Explanation and derivation

Substitute each $\omega_i$ back into Eq. (5.4). The matrix is now singular, so both rows give the same information — you cannot determine $u_1$ and $u_2$ absolutely, only their ratio. Set one component to 1 (arbitrarily) and read off the other.

5.5Rigid-body modes

What $\omega=0$ means (2020 term-3 paper, Q3(b))

A zero natural frequency means the system can move without storing any strain energy: all the degrees of freedom translate (or rotate) together, with the same amplitude, and none of the elastic elements is deformed. The corresponding mode shape is $\mathbf u = \{1,\ 1\}^T$ (or whatever ratio leaves the connecting springs unstretched). It is not a vibration — it is a free-body drift.
Explanation and derivation

If $\omega_1 = 0$, the system has a rigid-body mode. This happens when the system is unrestrained — no spring connects it to ground.

The 2020 term-3 paper, Q3, does this with two pinned discs coupled by a spring, with the system $\begin{bmatrix}2.25&0\\0&6.75\end{bmatrix}\ddd{\bm\theta} + \begin{bmatrix}225&-225\\-225&225\end{bmatrix}\bm\theta = \mathbf 0$. Notice $\mathbf K$ is singular — its rows sum to zero — which is the algebraic signature of a rigid-body mode. Solving: $\omega_1 = 0$ and $\omega_2 = \sqrt{225/2.25 + 225/6.75} = 11.55$ rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$.

5.6The free response of a 2DOF system

\begin{equation*} \mathbf x(t) = A_1\sin(\omega_1t+\varphi_1)\,\mathbf u_1 + A_2\sin(\omega_2t+\varphi_2)\,\mathbf u_2 \end{equation*}(5.5)
$\omega_i,\ \mathbf u_i$
$i$-th natural frequency and mode shape
$A_i,\ \varphi_i$
amplitude and phase set by the initial conditions

Exam angle

The 2021–2023 papers stop at natural frequencies and mode shapes; none asked for the full time response with four ICs. Budget your revision accordingly — get parts (a) and (b) perfect before worrying about the free response.
Explanation and derivation

The general solution is a linear combination of the two modes [11]:

\begin{equation*} \mathbf x(t) = A_1\sin(\omega_1t+\varphi_1)\,\mathbf u_1 + A_2\sin(\omega_2t+\varphi_2)\,\mathbf u_2 \end{equation*}(5.5)

Written out for the Lecture 9 example:

\begin{equation*} \begin{Bmatrix}x_1(t)\\ x_2(t)\end{Bmatrix} = \begin{Bmatrix} A_1\sin(\sqrt2\,t+\varphi_1) + A_2\sin(2t+\varphi_2)\\ 3A_1\sin(\sqrt2\,t+\varphi_1) - 3A_2\sin(2t+\varphi_2) \end{Bmatrix} \end{equation*}

There are now four unknowns ($A_1,A_2,\varphi_1,\varphi_2$), determined by four initial conditions ($x_{10},x_{20},\dd x_{10},\dd x_{20}$). With $x_{10}=1$ mm, $x_{20}=0$, and both initial velocities zero, Lecture 9 obtains $\varphi_1=\varphi_2=\pi/2$ and $A_1=A_2=\tfrac12$, so

\begin{equation*} \begin{Bmatrix}x_1(t)\\x_2(t)\end{Bmatrix} = \begin{Bmatrix} \tfrac12\cos(\sqrt2\,t) + \tfrac12\cos(2t)\\ \tfrac32\cos(\sqrt2\,t) - \tfrac32\cos(2t) \end{Bmatrix}\ \text{mm} \end{equation*}

Practice questions — Week 5

Q 5.1Term-3 paper 2026, Question 5[10]

Two trolleys, each of mass $m=15$ kg, move through $x_1$ and $x_2$ (Figure 5.2). $k_1=15$ N/m, $k_2=30$ N/m.

(a) Derive the equations of motion and write them symbolically in matrix form. [4]
(b) Find the natural frequencies and mode shapes, and sketch each mode. [6]

Series springs halve; then the result is in parallel with the lower $k_1$.
Step 1 — (a) Coupling stiffness

The two $k_2$ springs in series: $k_2/2$. Between the trolleys this acts in parallel with $k_1$: coupling $k_1+k_2/2$.

\[m\ddot x_1=-k_1x_1-(k_1+\tfrac12k_2)(x_1-x_2),\qquad m\ddot x_2=-(k_1+\tfrac12k_2)(x_2-x_1)-k_1x_2\] \[\begin{bmatrix}m&0\\0&m\end{bmatrix}\ddot{\mathbf x}+\begin{bmatrix}2k_1+\frac12k_2&-k_1-\frac12k_2\\-k_1-\frac12k_2&2k_1+\frac12k_2\end{bmatrix}\mathbf x=\mathbf 0\]Step 2 — (b) Numbers

$\mathbf M=15\mathbf I$, $\mathbf K=\begin{bmatrix}45&-30\\-30&45\end{bmatrix}$. $\det(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)=0$ gives $(3-\omega^2)^2=4$, so $\omega^2=1$ or 5.

$\omega_1=1$ rad/s, $\mathbf u_1=[1,\ 1]^T$: in phase, the coupling springs are not stretched. $\omega_2=\sqrt5=2.24$ rad/s, $\mathbf u_2=[1,\ -1]^T$: out of phase, the centre of the coupling stands still.

Answer. $\omega_1=1$ rad/s, $[1,1]$; $\omega_2=2.24$ rad/s, $[1,-1]$.

Printed: $\omega_1=1$, $\omega_2=\sqrt5=2.24$ rad/s ✓ (the memo text says "$\omega_2=\sqrt8$" in one line — a typo). Recomputed in verify.py.

Q 5.2Term-3 paper 2020, Question 3(d)–(f)[5]

Two discs coupled by a spring have the equation of motion (SI units)

\[\begin{bmatrix}2.25&0\\0&6.75\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}\ddot\theta_1\\\ddot\theta_2\end{Bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}225&-225\\-225&225\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}\theta_1\\\theta_2\end{Bmatrix}=\mathbf 0\]

(a) Calculate the natural frequencies in rad/s. [2]
(b) One natural frequency is zero. What does this mean? [1]
(c) Determine and sketch the mode shapes. [2]

Step 1 — (a)\[(225-2.25\omega^2)(225-6.75\omega^2)-225^2=0\ \Rightarrow\ \omega^2(15.19\,\omega^2-2025)=0\]

so $\omega_1=0$ and $\omega_2=\sqrt{133.3}=11.55$ rad/s.

Step 2 — (b)

A rigid-body mode: both discs rotate together without twisting the spring. Nothing restores them — the system is not attached to ground.

Step 3 — (c)

$\omega_1=0$: $\mathbf u_1=[1,\ 1]^T$. $\omega_2$: row 1, $(225-2.25\times133.3)\theta_1=225\theta_2$, so $\theta_2=-\theta_1/3$: $\mathbf u_2=[1,\ -1/3]^T$, i.e. $[3,\ -1]^T$. The heavier disc 2 moves a third as far, in the opposite direction; the momentum balance $2.25(3)+6.75(-1)=0$ confirms it.

Answer. $\omega_1=0$ (rigid-body), $\omega_2=11.55$ rad/s; $\mathbf u_1=[1,1]$, $\mathbf u_2=[3,-1]$.

Printed: $\omega_2=11.54$ ✓. The memo gives $\mathbf u_2=[-1,\ 3]^T$; row 1 gives $\theta_2=-\theta_1/3$, i.e. $[3,\ -1]^T$ (equivalently $[-3,\ 1]$). Recomputed in verify.py.

Week 6

Modal analysis of MDOF systems

Lecture 10 · Additional 2DOF problem

This week in brief

  • Any 2DOF system (bars on springs, vehicles in bounce and pitch, pendulums) follows the same recipe: choose coordinates, write $T$ and $U$ or the FBDs, build $\mathbf M$, $\mathbf K$, then solve the determinant.
  • Modal analysis decouples the equations: $\mathbf M^{-1/2}$, $\tilde{\mathbf K}=\mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf K\mathbf M^{-1/2}$, eigenvectors $\mathbf P$, $\mathbf S=\mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf P$.
  • In modal coordinates each equation is an independent SDOF: $\ddot r_i+\omega_i^2r_i=0$, with $\mathbf r(0)=\mathbf S^{-1}\mathbf x_0$. Then transform back with $\mathbf x=\mathbf S\mathbf r$.
  • None of the eight steps is on the formula sheet. Learn the order.

6.1Systems that are not two carts

The universal 2DOF recipe

  1. Choose one coordinate per DOF; state the positive direction.
  2. Free-body diagram for each body, in a displaced position. Coupling elements respond to the relative coordinate.
  3. Write $\sum F = m\ddd x$ or $\sum M = I\ddd\theta$ for each. Keep $\sin$ and $\cos$ until the matrix stage if the question says so.
  4. Assemble $\mathbf M\ddd{\mathbf x}+\mathbf K\mathbf x = \mathbf 0$; check $\mathbf K$ is symmetric.
  5. $\det(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)=0$; substitute $\lambda=\omega^2$; solve the quadratic; take positive roots.
  6. Back-substitute each $\omega_i$; use one row to get the ratio $u_{i2}/u_{i1}$; set $u_{i1}=1$; verify with the other row.
  7. Sketch both modes with proportional arrows and one sentence each.
Explanation and derivation

The examiners disguise the same problem. Three past disguises:

6.1.1Coupled pendulums (2022 Q5)

Two pendulums of mass $m_i$ on rods of length $L$, coupled by a spring $k_2$ at the bob, with springs $k_1$ and $k_3$ to ground. Taking moments about each pivot, before the small-angle assumption:

\begin{equation*} m_1L^2\ddot\theta_1 = -k_1L\sin\theta_1\,L\cos\theta_1 - k_2(L\sin\theta_1-L\sin\theta_2)L\cos\theta_1 \end{equation*}

and similarly for $\theta_2$. Then linearise ($\sin\theta\to\theta$, $\cos\theta\to1$) and include the gravity restoring moment $-m_igL\theta_i$:

\begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} m_1L^2 & 0\\ 0 & m_2L^2\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}\ddot\theta_1\\ \ddot\theta_2\end{Bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} (k_1+k_2)L^2+m_1gL & -k_2L^2\\ -k_2L^2 & (k_2+k_3)L^2+m_2gL\end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}\theta_1\\ \theta_2\end{Bmatrix} = \mathbf 0 \end{equation*}

Gravity contributes a $mgL$ term to the stiffness matrix — a pendulum's restoring "spring" is gravity. Forget it and both natural frequencies are wrong.

6.1.2Rotating discs (2020 Q3)

Two discs pinned at their centres, coupled by a spring attached at radius $r$ on one and $R$ on the other. Take moments about each centre; the mass matrix entries are $\tfrac12 m_ir_i^2$ (thin disc) and the stiffness entries are $kr^2$, $krR$, $kR^2$. Same machinery, rotational coordinates.

6.1.3Vertically coupled masses (2021 Q5)

Two masses hanging in a vertical chain of springs. Provided you measure each $x_i$ from its own static equilibrium, gravity cancels exactly as in the SDOF case (Week 1), and the matrices are identical to the horizontal cart problem.

6.2Extension to MDOF

Exam angle

That last transformation is Lecture 10 material: Week 6 works through all eight steps and uses it to find the free response.
Explanation and derivation

Nothing changes structurally for $n$ degrees of freedom [12]. The matrices become $n\times n$; $\det(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)=0$ becomes a polynomial of degree $n$ in $\omega^2$; there are $n$ natural frequencies and $n$ mode shapes. Beyond $n=2$ this is done numerically (MATLAB eig).

The formula sheet also lists the mass-normalised form used in Lecture 10:

\begin{equation*} \mathbf I\ddd{\mathbf q}(t) + \tilde{\mathbf K}\mathbf q(t) = \mathbf Q(t), \qquad \tilde{\mathbf K} = \mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf K\mathbf M^{-1/2}, \qquad \mathbf Q = \mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf F \end{equation*}

Introduction to this topic

Week 5 found natural frequencies and mode shapes from $\det(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)=0$. A2 also asks for the free response of a 2DOF system: what each mass does after given initial conditions. Lecture 10 does this by changing coordinates until the two coupled equations become two independent SDOF equations. Each of those is solved exactly as in Week 2, and the answer is transformed back.

6.3Why change coordinates

Explanation and derivation

In physical coordinates the equations are coupled: the stiffness matrix of the chain in Figure 6.1 has off-diagonal terms, so $x_1$ appears in the equation for $m_2$ and vice versa. The idea of modal analysis is to find coordinates in which both $\mathbf M$ and $\mathbf K$ are diagonal. Then each equation contains one coordinate only.

For the chain, Newton's second law on each mass gives

\[\begin{bmatrix}m_1&0\\0&m_2\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}\ddot x_1\\\ddot x_2\end{Bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}k_1+k_2&-k_2\\-k_2&k_2+k_3\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{Bmatrix}=\begin{Bmatrix}F_1(t)\\0\end{Bmatrix}\]

6.4The eight steps of Lecture 10

  1. Mass-normalise. $\mathbf M^{-1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt{m_1},\,1/\sqrt{m_2})$ for a diagonal mass matrix.
  2. Symmetric stiffness. $\tilde{\mathbf K}=\mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf K\mathbf M^{-1/2}$. For a diagonal $\mathbf M$: $\tilde K_{ij}=K_{ij}/\sqrt{m_im_j}$.
  3. Symmetric eigenvalue problem. $\det(\tilde{\mathbf K}-\omega^2\mathbf I)=0$ gives $\omega_1,\omega_2$ (the same values as $\det(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)=0$). Each eigenvector $\mathbf v_i$ follows from $(\tilde{\mathbf K}-\omega_i^2\mathbf I)\mathbf v_i=\mathbf 0$.
  4. Normalise and assemble. $\hat{\mathbf v}_i=\mathbf v_i/\sqrt{\mathbf v_i^T\mathbf v_i}$, then $\mathbf P=[\hat{\mathbf v}_1\;\hat{\mathbf v}_2]$. $\mathbf P$ is orthonormal: $\mathbf P^T\mathbf P=\mathbf I$.
  5. Transformation matrix. $\mathbf S=\mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf P$, $\;\mathbf S^{-1}=\mathbf P^T\mathbf M^{1/2}$.
  6. Modal initial conditions. $\mathbf r(0)=\mathbf S^{-1}\mathbf x_0,\;\dot{\mathbf r}(0)=\mathbf S^{-1}\dot{\mathbf x}_0$.
  7. Solve each modal equation $\ddot r_i+\omega_i^2r_i=0$ exactly as an SDOF system: $r_i(t)=r_{i0}\cos\omega_it+(\dot r_{i0}/\omega_i)\sin\omega_it$.
  8. Back to physical coordinates: $\mathbf x(t)=\mathbf S\,\mathbf r(t)$.
$\tilde{\mathbf K}$
mass-normalised stiffness matrix, $\mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf K\mathbf M^{-1/2}$
$\mathbf P$
matrix whose columns are the normalised eigenvectors of $\tilde{\mathbf K}$
$\mathbf S$
transformation from modal to physical coordinates
$\mathbf r(t)$
modal coordinates: one independent SDOF oscillator per mode

What to remember

The columns of $\mathbf S$ are the mode shapes (scaled). So the physical response is always \[\mathbf x(t)=\sum_i \mathbf u_i\,\big(a_i\cos\omega_it+b_i\sin\omega_it\big)\] — a weighted sum of the mode shapes, each oscillating at its own natural frequency. If the initial displacement looks like one mode shape, only that mode is excited. The same idea returns for strings and beams in Week 9.

Signs in $\mathbf K$

The off-diagonal terms are minus the stiffness that connects the two masses, and $\mathbf K$ must be symmetric. A spring from $m_2$ to the wall ($k_3$) adds to $K_{22}$ only. If your $\tilde{\mathbf K}$ is not symmetric, the error is in $\mathbf K$.

6.5Worked: the Lecture 9 system, all eight steps

$m_1=9$, $m_2=1$ kg, $k_1=24$, $k_2=3$ N/m, $k_3=0$; released from $\mathbf x_0=[1,\,0]^T$ m at rest (MATLAB Assignment 2, Task 2a).

$\mathbf M^{-1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(1/3,\,1)$ and $\tilde{\mathbf K}=\begin{bmatrix}27/9&-3/3\\-3/3&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-1&3\end{bmatrix}$. Then $\det(\tilde{\mathbf K}-\lambda\mathbf I)=(3-\lambda)^2-1=0$, so $\lambda=2,4$ and $\omega_1=\sqrt2=1.414$, $\omega_2=2$ rad/s.

$\hat{\mathbf v}_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}[1,\,1]^T$, $\hat{\mathbf v}_2=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}[-1,\,1]^T$, so $\mathbf S=\mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf P=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1/3&-1/3\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf S^{-1}=\mathbf P^T\mathbf M^{1/2}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\-3&1\end{bmatrix}$.

$\mathbf r(0)=\mathbf S^{-1}[1,0]^T=[2.121,\,-2.121]^T$, $\dot{\mathbf r}(0)=\mathbf 0$, so $r_1=2.121\cos\sqrt2t$, $r_2=-2.121\cos2t$. Transforming back:

\[x_1(t)=0.5\cos\sqrt2\,t+0.5\cos2t,\qquad x_2(t)=1.5\cos\sqrt2\,t-1.5\cos2t\]

Check: $\mathbf x(0)=[1,\,0]^T$ ✓. The mode-1 shape $[1,3]$ and mode-2 shape $[1,-3]$ match Week 5 ✓. Recomputed with numpy.linalg.eigh ✓.

Practice questions — Week 6

Q 6.1New question (Lecture 10), on the 2026 Q5 trolleys[8]

For the trolleys of Figure 5.2 ($\mathbf M=15\mathbf I$, $\mathbf K=\begin{bmatrix}45&-30\\-30&45\end{bmatrix}$), trolley 1 is displaced 0.1 m and both are released from rest.

(a) Use modal analysis ($\mathbf M^{-1/2}$, $\tilde{\mathbf K}$, $\mathbf P$, $\mathbf S$) to find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$. [6]
(b) Describe the motion in words. [2]

$[0.1,0]$ is half of $[1,1]$ plus half of $[1,-1]$, times 0.1.
Step 1 — Mass-normalise

$\mathbf M^{-1/2}=\mathbf I/\sqrt{15}$, $\tilde{\mathbf K}=\mathbf K/15=\begin{bmatrix}3&-2\\-2&3\end{bmatrix}$: eigenvalues 1 and 5, $\mathbf P=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf S=\mathbf M^{-1/2}\mathbf P$.

Step 2 — Modal initial conditions\[\mathbf r(0)=\mathbf S^{-1}\mathbf x_0=\mathbf P^T\mathbf M^{1/2}\mathbf x_0=\sqrt{15/2}\,[0.1,\ 0.1]^T=[0.274,\ 0.274]^T\]

and $\dot{\mathbf r}(0)=\mathbf 0$, so $r_i=r_i(0)\cos\omega_it$.

Step 3 — Back to physical

$\mathbf x=\mathbf S\mathbf r$:

\[x_1=0.05(\cos t+\cos\sqrt5\,t),\qquad x_2=0.05(\cos t-\cos\sqrt5\,t)\ \ \text{m}\]Step 4 — (b)

Equal parts of both modes. $x_1$ starts at 0.1 m and $x_2$ at zero; energy moves between the trolleys because the two cosines drift in and out of phase. The motion is not periodic, since $\sqrt5$ is irrational.

Answer. $x_1=0.05(\cos t+\cos2.236t)$, $x_2=0.05(\cos t-\cos2.236t)$ m.

New question. Checked against numerical integration (solve_ivp) at $t=1$ and 2.5 s in verify.py ✓.

Q 6.2Tutorial 2, Additional problem 1[—]

For the chain of Figure 6.1 (wall–$k_1$–$m_1$–$k_2$–$m_2$–$k_3$–wall) with $m_1=8$ kg, $m_2=2$ kg, $k_1=24$ N/m, $k_2=3$ N/m, $k_3=3$ N/m and no damping or forcing:

(a) Write the equations of motion in matrix form. (b) Find the natural frequencies and mode shapes, and describe each mode in words. (c) Find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ for $\mathbf x_0=[1,\,0]^T$ m, $\dot{\mathbf x}_0=\mathbf 0$.

Write $\mathbf x_0$ as a combination of the two mode shapes: $a\mathbf u_1+b\mathbf u_2=[1,0]^T$. That gives the cosine amplitudes directly.
Step 1 — Matrices $\mathbf M=\begin{bmatrix}8&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf K=\begin{bmatrix}27&-3\\-3&6\end{bmatrix}$. Step 2 — Frequencies $\det(\mathbf K-\omega^2\mathbf M)=(27-8\omega^2)(6-2\omega^2)-9=16\omega^4-102\omega^2+153=0$, so $\omega^2=2.414$ and $3.961$: \[\omega_1=1.554\ \text{rad/s}\ (0.247\ \text{Hz}),\qquad \omega_2=1.990\ \text{rad/s}\ (0.317\ \text{Hz})\] Step 3 — Mode shapes Row 1: $u_2/u_1=(27-8\omega^2)/3$. Mode 1: $\mathbf u_1=[1,\;2.562]^T$ — both masses move in the same direction, $m_2$ about 2.6 times as far. Mode 2: $\mathbf u_2=[1,\;-1.562]^T$ — the masses move in opposite directions. Step 4 — Free response With $\mathbf x(t)=\mathbf S\mathbf r(t)$ and starting from rest, only cosines appear: \[x_1(t)=0.379\cos1.554t+0.621\cos1.990t,\qquad x_2(t)=0.970\,(\cos1.554t-\cos1.990t)\]
Answer. $\omega_1=1.554$, $\omega_2=1.990$ rad/s; $\mathbf u_1=[1,\,2.56]$, $\mathbf u_2=[1,\,-1.56]$. Because $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are close, $x_2$ beats: energy passes back and forth between the masses with beat period $2\pi/(\omega_2-\omega_1)=14.4$ s.

No printed answer. Recomputed in verify.py (modes()) and checked: $\mathbf x(0)=[1,0]^T$ ✓; the FRF peaks of Figure 7.2 fall at 0.247 and 0.317 Hz ✓.

Q 6.3A2 2024, Question 6(b)[4]

A vehicle is modelled with bounce $x$ [m] and pitch $\theta$ [rad] about the centre of gravity (SI units: mass terms in kg and kg·m², stiffness terms in N/m, N/rad and N·m/rad):

\[\begin{bmatrix}4000&0\\0&2560\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}\ddot x\\\ddot\theta\end{Bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}40\,000&10\,000\\10\,000&55\,400\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}x\\\theta\end{Bmatrix}=\mathbf 0\]

Calculate the natural frequencies and mode shapes.

Step 1 — Characteristic equation $(40\,000-4000\omega^2)(55\,400-2560\omega^2)-10\,000^2=0$. Divide by $10^6$: $10.24\,\omega^4-324.0\,\omega^2+2116=0$. Step 2 — Roots $\omega^2=9.214$ or $22.43$, so $\omega_1=3.04$ rad/s (0.483 Hz) and $\omega_2=4.74$ rad/s (0.754 Hz). Step 3 — Mode shapes from row 1 $\theta/x=-(40\,000-4000\omega^2)/10\,000$. Mode 1: $\theta/x=-0.314$ rad/m. Mode 2: $\theta/x=+4.97$ rad/m.
Answer. $\omega_1=3.04$ rad/s, $\mathbf u_1=[1,\;-0.314]^T$ (mostly bounce, a little pitch). $\omega_2=4.74$ rad/s, $\mathbf u_2=[1,\;4.97]^T$ (mostly pitch). Here $\mathbf K$ is coupled through a positive off-diagonal term, so the sign of $\theta/x$ depends on the sign convention for $\theta$ — state it on your sketch.

No memo available for 2024. Recomputed (verify.py, modes()); row 2 gives the same ratios ✓.

Q 6.4Tutorial 2, Additional problem 2[—]

An overhead crane: the girder ($EI=17\times10^9$ N·m², span $L=10$ m) carries the trolley ($m_1=2000$ kg) at midspan; a steel rope ($l=7$ m, area 710 mm²) carries the load ($m_2=50$ kg). Model it as a 2DOF chain: the girder (simply supported, trolley at midspan) as a spring $k_1$ to ground, the rope as a spring $k_2$ between trolley and load. Neglect the masses of the girder and rope.

(a) Find $k_1$ and $k_2$. (b) Find the natural frequencies and mode shapes.

Use the midspan stiffness of a pinned–pinned beam from Table 2.3 and $k=EA/l$ for the rope.
Step 1 — Stiffnesses Girder, simply supported, load at midspan: $k_1=48EI/L^3=48(17\times10^9)/10^3=816\times10^6$ N/m. Rope in tension: $k_2=EA/l=(200\times10^9)(710\times10^{-6})/7=20.3\times10^6$ N/m, using $E=200$ GPa for steel (Inman Table 1.2). Step 2 — Matrices $\mathbf M=\operatorname{diag}(2000,\,50)$, $\mathbf K=\begin{bmatrix}k_1+k_2&-k_2\\-k_2&k_2\end{bmatrix}$. Step 3 — Solve $\omega_1=589$ rad/s (93.8 Hz), $\mathbf u_1=[1,\;6.97]^T$: trolley and load in phase, the load moving 7 times as far. $\omega_2=690$ rad/s (110 Hz), $\mathbf u_2=[1,\;-5.74]^T$: in antiphase.
Answer. $k_1=816$ MN/m, $k_2=20.3$ MN/m; $\omega_{1,2}=589,\ 690$ rad/s. The uncoupled frequencies $\sqrt{k_1/m_1}=639$ and $\sqrt{k_2/m_2}=637$ rad/s are almost equal, so the coupling is strong and both modes involve large load motion.

Note: a stranded wire rope has an effective modulus well below that of solid steel (often around 100 GPa). That would halve $k_2$ and lower $\omega_1$; state the value you assume.

No printed answer. $E=200$ GPa is assumed for the rope (the tutorial does not state it). Recomputed ✓.
