Week 7

Signal processing and experimental modal analysis

Signal processing · EMA

This week in brief

  • Sampling: $f_s=1/\Delta t$, resolution $\Delta f=f_s/N=1/T$, and Nyquist requires $f_s>2f_{max}$. Under-sampling aliases high frequencies onto low ones.
  • The DFT of a record that does not hold a whole number of periods leaks. A window reduces leakage at the cost of resolution and needs an amplitude correction.
  • PSD: the power per Hz. The area under it is the mean square. Averaging reduces noise.
  • FRF $H(\omega)=X/F=1/(k-m\omega^2+jc\omega)$. At $\omega_n$ the magnitude peaks, the phase is $-90^\circ$ and the imaginary part peaks.
  • Half power: $\zeta=(f_b-f_a)/2f_d$. A driving-point FRF has anti-resonances between every pair of peaks. Use $H_1$ when noise is on the output and $H_2$ when it is on the input; coherence near 1 means the measurement can be trusted.
Introduction to this topic

Measured vibration arrives as a list of numbers in time. Most of what we want — natural frequencies, the frequency content of a fault, a frequency response — is easier to see in the frequency domain. The signal processing lecture is mainly conceptual: its own "what you need to know" slide says you must understand the derivations and be able to read DFT and PSD plots, not grind through transforms.

7.1Sampling

Sample every $\Delta t$ seconds for $N$ samples:

  • sample rate $f_s=1/\Delta t$; record length $T=N\Delta t$
  • frequency resolution $\Delta f=1/T=f_s/N$ — longer records give finer resolution
  • highest frequency represented: the Nyquist frequency $f_s/2$. To capture a frequency $f_{max}$ you need $f_s>2f_{max}$.

Aliasing: a component above $f_s/2$ is not lost — it reappears at a false, lower frequency. It cannot be removed after sampling, so an analogue anti-aliasing (low-pass) filter is applied before sampling.

7.2The discrete Fourier transform

\[X(k)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x(n)\,e^{-j2\pi kn/N},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,N-1,\qquad f_k=k\,\Delta f\]
$x(n)$
$n$-th sample, taken at $t=n\Delta t$
$X(k)$
$k$-th frequency bin
$N$
number of samples
$\Delta f$
bin spacing $f_s/N$

Each bin compares the signal with a cosine and a sine that complete exactly $k$ cycles in the record. Properties to know:

  • Periodicity: $X(k+N)=X(k)$. The DFT treats the record as one period of a signal that repeats forever.
  • Symmetry for a real signal: $|X(N-k)|=|X(k)|$. Bins above $N/2$ mirror the ones below — they are the negative frequencies. A cosine of amplitude $A$ appears as two peaks of $NA/2$; scaling by $1/N$ gives $A/2$ each.
  • FFT: an efficient algorithm for the DFT — about $N\log_2N$ operations instead of $N^2$. "FFT" is often used loosely for the DFT itself.

7.3Leakage and windowing

If the record does not contain a whole number of cycles, the assumed periodic repeat has a jump at the join. That jump spreads energy into neighbouring bins: leakage. It is a bias error in amplitude (the true peak value is underestimated) and it smears peaks. It happens whenever a frequency in the signal does not fall exactly on a bin $f_k=k\Delta f$.

Windowing multiplies the record by a function that goes smoothly to zero at both ends (Hann/Hanning is the default), forcing approximate periodicity. Because the window removes energy, the amplitude is corrected by $A_w=N/\sum w(n)$ (2 for Hann). Impact (hammer) tests use force/exponential windows instead.

7.4Power spectral density and averaging

Which tool, when

  • Clean periodic signal, want amplitudes at specific frequencies → scaled DFT (with a window if the frequency is not on a bin).
  • Random or noisy signal, want where the energy is → averaged PSD.
  • Relationship between input and output → cross-spectra and FRF.
Explanation and derivation

For random signals, or to see small components through noise, use the power spectral density, $G_{xx}(f)=X(f)X^*(f)=|X(f)|^2$ suitably scaled. Its key property: the area under the PSD between $f_1$ and $f_2$ is the mean-square value (rms²) of the signal in that band. The cross-spectrum $G_{xy}=X\,Y^*$ keeps the phase between two signals and is the building block of measured FRFs (Week 7).

Averaging: split a long record into segments (often 50 % overlap), window each, and average the spectra (Welch's method; MATLAB pwelch). Random error falls as more averages are used; resolution is set by the segment length.

Introduction to this topic

Experimental modal analysis (EMA) finds natural frequencies, damping ratios and mode shapes from measurements: excite the structure with a known force (shaker or hammer), measure the response, and form frequency response functions. The Week 7 lectures and Practical 2 are EMA in miniature.

7.5The SDOF FRF

Laplace-transform $m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx=f(t)$ with zero initial conditions and set $s=j\omega$:

\[H(\omega)=\frac{X(\omega)}{F(\omega)}=\frac{1}{k-m\omega^2+jc\omega}=\frac{1/m}{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)+2j\zeta\omega_n\omega}\]
$H(\omega)$
frequency response function (receptance)
$X,\ F$
Fourier transforms of response and force
  • At low frequency $H\approx1/k$: only the spring resists (Tutorial 3, Additional problem 4).
  • The phase is $0^\circ$ well below resonance, $-90^\circ$ at $\omega=\omega_n$, and $-180^\circ$ well above it: above resonance the mass moves opposite to the force because the inertia force dominates.
  • The magnitude peak sits at (approximately) the damped natural frequency.
  • Displacement/force is receptance; velocity/force is mobility ($j\omega H$); acceleration/force is accelerance ($-\omega^2H$). An accelerance tends to $1/m$ at high frequency instead of falling away — that is how you tell which quantity a plotted FRF shows.

7.6Reading modal parameters off an FRF

  1. Natural frequency: the peak frequency, or where the phase crosses $-90^\circ$ (also: the zero of the real part, the peak of the imaginary part of the receptance).
  2. Damping: half-power bandwidth, $\zeta=(\omega_b-\omega_a)/2\omega_d$, where $|H(\omega_a)|=|H(\omega_b)|=|H|_{max}/\sqrt2$. This one is on the formula sheet, in Hz.
  3. Mode shape: the peak magnitudes of the FRFs at each measured point give relative amplitudes (quadrature picking); the phases ($-90^\circ$ or $+90^\circ$) give the relative signs — in phase or out of phase.

7.7FRFs of an MDOF system

An $N$-DOF system has an $N\times N$ matrix of FRFs, $H_{pq}=X_p/F_q$ (response at $p$, force at $q$). Each is a sum of SDOF-like terms, one per mode:

\[H_{pq}(\omega)=\sum_{r=1}^{N}\frac{u_{pr}u_{qr}/m_r}{\omega_r^2-\omega^2+2j\zeta_r\omega_r\omega}\]
$H_{pq}$
response at point $p$ per unit force at point $q$
$u_{pr}$
mode $r$ amplitude at point $p$
$m_r,\ \omega_r,\ \zeta_r$
modal mass, natural frequency and damping ratio of mode $r$
  • Driving-point FRF ($p=q$, e.g. $H_{11}$): force and response at the same point. It has an anti-resonance between every pair of resonances, and its phase stays between $0^\circ$ and $-180^\circ$. It is needed to scale the mode shapes.
  • Transfer FRF ($p\ne q$): no guaranteed anti-resonances. If $p$ sits at a node of mode $r$, that peak is missing.
  • Reciprocity: $H_{pq}=H_{qp}$. So one row or one column of the matrix (one excitation point, several response points — or the reverse with a roving hammer) is enough to get every mode shape.

7.8Measuring FRFs: estimators and coherence

With the spectra of Week 7: $\hat H_1=G_{fx}/G_{ff}$ (best when noise is on the output), $\hat H_2=G_{xx}/G_{xf}$ (best when noise is on the input), and the coherence $\gamma^2=\hat H_1/\hat H_2$, between 0 and 1. $\gamma^2\approx1$ means the output is explained by the measured input; dips usually appear at anti-resonances (little response, so noise dominates) and indicate a poor measurement elsewhere.

Peak frequency is $\omega_d$, not $\omega_n$

The Tutorial 3 solutions point this out: the peak gives $\omega_d$. Convert with $\omega_n=\omega_d/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$ — not $\omega_d\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$, which is what the solutions print in Additional problem 5(d). For $\zeta$ of a few percent the difference is negligible.

Practice questions — Week 7

Q 7.1A2 2020, Question 6[5]

Match each description to one term from: piezo-electric phenomenon, PSD, DFT, FFT, aliasing, windowing, leakage (each term at most once; two are not used).

  1. The mean-square value of a signal equals the area bounded by this spectrum.
  2. An efficient algorithm that transforms a sampled time signal to the frequency domain.
  3. Causes spurious frequency components when appropriate filtering is not applied.
  4. A method of reducing amplitude errors when calculating a spectrum estimate.
  5. A bias error that causes uncertainty in the true amplitude of a periodic component.
Answer. 1 PSD; 2 FFT; 3 aliasing; 4 windowing; 5 leakage.

Note 3 vs 5: aliasing comes from sampling too slowly (fixed by a filter before sampling); leakage comes from a non-periodic record (reduced by a window).

2020 A2 student memo: PSD, FFT, aliasing, windowing, leakage ✓.

Q 7.2A2 2020, Question 5 (5)–(7)[3]

(5) What minimum sample rate is needed for experimental FRFs covering 0–25 Hz? (6) With $f_s=60$ Hz and $N=600$ samples (and 600 frequency lines), what is the frequency resolution? (7) Independently of (6): true or false — if the natural frequencies are 3.5 Hz and 16.3 Hz and the resolution is 0.5 Hz, there is no leakage error.

(5) Nyquist: $f_s>2f_{max}=50$ Hz. (In practice analysers use about $2.56f_{max}$.) (6) $\Delta f=f_s/N=60/600=0.1$ Hz. (7) Bins are at multiples of 0.5 Hz. 3.5 Hz is on a bin; 16.3 Hz is not (16.0 and 16.5 Hz are), so that peak leaks.
Answer. 50 Hz; 0.1 Hz; false.

2020 A2 student memo: $f_s=2\times25=50$ Hz; 0.1 Hz; false ✓ (memo reason "resolution too low"). The paper's "600 samples and 600 frequency lines" is loose: 600 samples give 300 lines up to Nyquist; $\Delta f=f_s/N$ is unaffected.

Q 7.3Signal processing lecture example[—]

$x(n)=\cos(2\pi\cdot2n/20)$ for $n=0,\dots,19$. At which bins does the unscaled DFT have peaks, and how high are they? What is the frequency of bin $k=2$ if $f_s=20$ Hz?

Two whole cycles fit in the record, so the energy lands exactly on bin $k=2$ and its mirror $k=N-2=18$. Each has height $N/2=10$ (scaled by $1/N$: 0.5, half the amplitude). With $f_s=20$ Hz, $\Delta f=f_s/N=1$ Hz, so bin 2 is 2 Hz and bin 18 is the negative frequency $-2$ Hz.
Answer. $|X(2)|=|X(18)|=10$, every other bin 0; bin 2 is 2 Hz.

Lecture slide: $X(k)=10$ at $k=2$ and $k=18$ ✓; recomputed with numpy (Figure 7.1).

Q 7.4A2 2024, Question 7(b)[1]

A 3DOF system has natural frequencies of 45, 152 and 242 Hz. What is the minimum sampling rate to measure all of them?

Answer. $f_s>2\times242=484$ Hz.

(The paper prints "$\omega_1=45$ Hz²" — read it as 45 Hz.)

Q 7.5Tutorial 3, Additional problem 5 (values read off the close-up plots)[—]

Four FRFs ($H_{11},H_{12},H_{21},H_{22}$) of a lightly damped system each show two peaks. The close-ups give:

Peak$f_d$ [Hz]half-power points $f_a$, $f_b$ [Hz]
17.957.74, 8.15
213.713.3, 14.45

(a) How many DOFs? (b) Estimate the damping ratios and natural frequencies. (c) $H_{11}$ and $H_{22}$ show an anti-resonance between the peaks; $H_{12}$ does not. Which are driving-point FRFs and why do they matter? (d) In mode 1 the phases of $H_{11}$ and $H_{21}$ are both $-90^\circ$; in mode 2 they are $-90^\circ$ and $+90^\circ$. Describe the mode shapes.

(a) Two peaks in every FRF: 2 DOF. (b) $\zeta_1=(8.15-7.74)/(2\times7.95)=0.0258$, $\zeta_2=(14.45-13.3)/(2\times13.7)=0.0420$. Then $f_{n}=f_d/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$: 7.95 Hz and 13.71 Hz — the damping barely matters. (c) $H_{11}$ and $H_{22}$ (force and response at the same point). Their anti-resonance between resonances is the signature. They are needed to scale the measured mode shapes. (d) Mode 1: same phase → masses move together. Mode 2: opposite phase → masses move against each other.
Answer. 2 DOF; $\zeta_1\approx0.026$, $\zeta_2\approx0.042$; $f_1\approx7.95$, $f_2\approx13.7$ Hz; driving points $H_{11}$, $H_{22}$; mode 1 in phase, mode 2 out of phase.

Tutorial 3 solutions: 0.0258 and 0.0420 (true values 0.0250 and 0.0433); 7.95 and 13.7 Hz ✓. The second peak's half-power points (−0.40/+0.75 Hz about 13.7) are lopsided, which suggests a reading error from the plot; that is why $\zeta_2$ is off by 3 %. The solutions write $\omega_n=\omega_d\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$; it should be $\omega_d/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$.

Q 7.6Tutorial 3, Additional problem 3[—]

For the chain of Figure 6.1 (wall–$k_1$–$m_1$–$k_2$–$m_2$–$k_3$–wall, force on $m_1$) with $m_1=8$, $m_2=2$ kg, $k_1=24$, $k_2=3$, $k_3=3$ N/m, $c_1=0.1$, $c_2=0.05$, $c_3=0.01$ N·s/m (each damper in parallel with the spring of the same number), forced at $m_1$: (a) derive $H_{11}$ using Laplace transforms; [(b) is a MATLAB plot — see Figure 7.2]; (c) at what frequency does $m_2$ act as an absorber for $m_1$? Comment on the motion there.

(a) Transform both equations with $s=j\omega$: \[\begin{bmatrix}m_1s^2+(c_1+c_2)s+k_1+k_2&-(c_2s+k_2)\\-(c_2s+k_2)&m_2s^2+(c_2+c_3)s+k_2+k_3\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}X_1\\X_2\end{Bmatrix}=\begin{Bmatrix}F_1\\0\end{Bmatrix}\] so \[H_{11}=\frac{m_2s^2+(c_2+c_3)s+k_2+k_3}{\big[m_1s^2+(c_1+c_2)s+k_1+k_2\big]\big[m_2s^2+(c_2+c_3)s+k_2+k_3\big]-(c_2s+k_2)^2}\] (c) The numerator of $H_{11}$ is (almost) zero when $k_2+k_3=m_2\omega^2$: $\omega=\sqrt{6/2}=1.732$ rad/s $=0.276$ Hz. There $m_1$ barely moves (anti-resonance) while $m_2$ moves and its spring force cancels the applied force.
Answer. 0.276 Hz (Figure 7.2).

Tutorial 3 solutions: anti-resonance at about 0.276 Hz ✓. The printed $H_{11}$ omits $k_3$ and $c_3$ (it is the expression for $k_3=0$); with $k_3=0$ the anti-resonance would be at 0.195 Hz, so the 0.276 Hz the solutions read off their plot confirms $k_3$ belongs in it.

Q 7.7A2 2024, Question 7(a), (c)[6]

[Part (b) is Q 7.4. Part (d) — sketch the three mode shapes from the paper’s FRF plots — is left out: the plots are not in the folder. For the method, see Q 7.5(d).] (a) In a set of measured FRFs, how do you recognise the driving-point FRF? (c) List four ways to obtain a natural frequency from an FRF.

Answer. (a) The FRF with force and response at the same point; it shows an anti-resonance between every pair of adjacent resonances (and its phase stays between 0° and −180°). (c) (1) the frequency of the magnitude peak; (2) where the phase passes −90°; (3) where the real part of the receptance crosses zero; (4) the peak of the imaginary part (or the Nyquist circle's point of fastest change).

Week 8

Vibration suppression: isolation and absorbers

Lecture 11

This week in brief

  • Isolation works only for $r>\sqrt2$, so make the mount soft: $\omega_n$ well below the operating speed. Then $R=1-\text{TR}$ is the reduction.
  • Undamped design: $\text{TR}=1/(r^2-1)$, so pick $r$ from the TR target, then $k=m\omega^2/r^2$. The static deflection is $\Delta=g/\omega_n^2$.
  • Damping in an isolator lowers the resonance peak (the machine passes through it while starting up) but raises TR at the operating speed.
  • A vibration absorber adds $m_a$, $k_a$ tuned so that $\omega_a=\sqrt{k_a/m_a}=\omega$. The main mass then stands still, and $X_a=-F_0/k_a$.
  • The absorber splits one resonance into two, one on each side of $\omega$. The usable band is narrow (Figure 8.2); $\mu=m_a/m$ sets how far apart the new peaks are.
Introduction to this topic

Lecture 11 starts the design part of the module: change $k$, $c$ and $m$ so that the vibration is acceptable. There are two routes. Isolation (this chapter) changes the mounts so that less force or motion gets through. Absorption (Week 8) adds a second mass–spring that cancels the motion at one frequency.

8.1Two isolation problems, one curve

Lecture 11 separates two problems:

  • Problem 1 — protect the system from its surroundings (vehicle suspension, instrument on a vibrating floor). This is base excitation: the quantity is the displacement transmissibility $X/Y$ (Week 4).
  • Problem 2 — protect the surroundings from the machine (pump, fan, compressor on mounts). The machine force $F_0\cos\omega t$ is transmitted through the spring and damper, $F_T=kx+c\dot x$. The quantity is the force transmissibility ratio.

The two ratios are the same expression, and it is on the formula sheet:

\[\text{TR}=\frac{F_T}{F_0}=\frac{X}{Y}=\sqrt{\frac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}\]
$\text{TR}$
transmissibility ratio
$F_T$
amplitude of the force transmitted to the floor
$F_0$
amplitude of the machine force
$r$
$\omega/\omega_n$, with $\omega$ the running speed

8.2Reading the curve for design

  • Isolation requires $r>\sqrt2$, i.e. $\omega_n<\omega/\sqrt2$: soft mounts. Every curve passes through $\text{TR}=1$ at $r=\sqrt2$.
  • Below $r=\sqrt2$, damping helps (it limits the resonant peak). Above it, damping hurts. A machine that runs up through resonance needs some damping; one that sits far above it wants very little.
  • Lecture 11 and Inman: when damping is not given, design with it neglected: $\text{TR}=1/(r^2-1)$ for $r>\sqrt2$. Inman calls $R=1-\text{TR}$ the percentage reduction; solving gives $r^2=(2-R)/(1-R)$.
  • Springs are often specified by their static deflection: $\Delta=mg/k=g/\omega_n^2$. A target $\omega_n$ therefore fixes $\Delta$ — the reason soft isolation needs space.

Other design checks Lecture 11 lists

Maximum allowable transmitted force; static deflection; rattle space (static deflection plus the dynamic amplitude must fit); and the difference between vibration (long disturbance — low damping preferred) and shock (short disturbance — high damping preferred).

Which ratio, which $r$

For a machine on mounts, $r=\omega/\omega_n$ uses the running speed $\omega$ converted to rad/s ($\omega=2\pi N/60$). Do not use $|F_T/kY|$ (that is the force passed to a body by a moving base, Week 4). If a question gives the unbalance $m_0e$, the force amplitude is $F_0=m_0e\omega^2$.

Introduction to this topic

An absorber (tuned mass damper) adds a second mass $m_a$ on a spring $k_a$ to the machine $m$. The 1DOF problem becomes 2DOF, and at one frequency the primary mass stands still.

8.3Equations and the tuning condition

\[X=\frac{(k_a-m_a\omega^2)F_0}{(k+k_a-m\omega^2)(k_a-m_a\omega^2)-k_a^2},\qquad X_a=\frac{k_aF_0}{(k+k_a-m\omega^2)(k_a-m_a\omega^2)-k_a^2}\]
$m_a,\ k_a$
absorber mass and spring
$X_a$
absorber amplitude
\[\frac{Xk}{F_0}=\frac{1-(\omega/\omega_a)^2}{\big[1+\mu\beta^2-(\omega/\omega_p)^2\big]\big[1-(\omega/\omega_a)^2\big]-\mu\beta^2}\]
$\mu$
mass ratio $m_a/m$
$\omega_a$
absorber natural frequency $\sqrt{k_a/m_a}$
$\omega_p$
primary natural frequency $\sqrt{k/m}$
$\beta$
frequency ratio $\omega_a/\omega_p$
$X$
primary-mass amplitude

Design rules from Lecture 11

  • Size the absorber spring from the allowed absorber stroke: $k_a=F_0/|X_a|$; then $m_a=k_a/\omega^2$.
  • Check the mass ratio: $\mu$ is typically 0.05–0.25 (Tutorial 3 solutions).
  • Works only if the driving frequency is known and steady; the absorber spring must carry the full force $F_0$; damping makes $X\ne0$ but widens the useful band and stops the two new resonances from being unbounded.
  • A larger $\mu$ pushes the two new peaks further apart and widens the useful band.

Pendulum absorber

A pendulum of length $L_a$ has $\omega_a=\sqrt{g/L_a}$, so tuning to $\omega$ means $L_a=g/\omega^2$. Its mass sets $\mu$ but not the frequency.

Explanation and derivation

With the machine on $k$ and forced by $F_0\sin\omega t$:

\[\begin{bmatrix}m&0\\0&m_a\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}\ddot x\\\ddot x_a\end{Bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}k+k_a&-k_a\\-k_a&k_a\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}x\\x_a\end{Bmatrix}=\begin{Bmatrix}F_0\\0\end{Bmatrix}\sin\omega t\]

Solving for the steady-state amplitudes (Lecture 11, Eqs 6–7):

\[X=\frac{(k_a-m_a\omega^2)F_0}{(k+k_a-m\omega^2)(k_a-m_a\omega^2)-k_a^2},\qquad X_a=\frac{k_aF_0}{(k+k_a-m\omega^2)(k_a-m_a\omega^2)-k_a^2}\]

$X=0$ when $k_a-m_a\omega^2=0$, i.e. the absorber is tuned: $\omega_a=\sqrt{k_a/m_a}=\omega$. At that frequency the denominator is $-k_a^2$, so $X_a=-F_0/k_a$: the absorber moves in antiphase with the force, and its spring force $k_aX_a=-F_0$ cancels the excitation exactly.

In normalised form, with $\mu=m_a/m$, $\beta=\omega_a/\omega_p$, $\omega_p=\sqrt{k/m}$, $k_a/k=\mu\beta^2$ (Inman Eq. 5.24, the corrected form of Example 5.3.2):

\[\frac{Xk}{F_0}=\frac{1-(\omega/\omega_a)^2}{\big[1+\mu\beta^2-(\omega/\omega_p)^2\big]\big[1-(\omega/\omega_a)^2\big]-\mu\beta^2}\]

Practice questions — Week 8

Q 8.1Inman 5.11 (data as in the 2023 Tutorial 3 solutions)[—]

A 70 kg machine is mounted on an isolator with $k=30\,000$ N/m and $\zeta=0.2$. It is driven by $F_0\cos\omega t$ with $F_0=450$ N at $\omega=13$ rad/s. Find the steady-state amplitude, the phase of the displacement relative to the force, the transmissibility ratio, the transmitted force amplitude and the velocity amplitude.

Step 1 — System $\omega_n=\sqrt{30\,000/70}=20.70$ rad/s, $r=13/20.70=0.628$, $f_0=F_0/m=6.43$ m/s². Step 2 — Amplitude and phase \[X=\frac{f_0}{\sqrt{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2}}=0.0229\ \text{m},\qquad \theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{2\zeta\omega_n\omega}{\omega_n^2-\omega^2}=0.393\ \text{rad}\] Step 3 — Transmission $\text{TR}=1.57$, so $F_T=1.57\times450=708$ N, and $\dot X=\omega X=0.297$ m/s.
Answer. $X=22.9$ mm, $\theta=0.393$ rad, TR $=1.57$, $F_T=708$ N, $\dot X=0.297$ m/s. With $r=0.63<\sqrt2$ the mount amplifies the force — this is not an isolator at this speed.

Tutorial 3 solutions: 0.0229 m, 0.393 rad, 1.57, 708 N, 0.297 m/s ✓ (all recomputed).

Q 8.2Inman 5.10 (data as in the 2023 Tutorial 3 solutions)[—]

A 25 kg machine runs at 180 rpm with an unbalance force amplitude of 25 N. Design an isolator (choose $k$ and $c$) so that only 10 % of the force is transmitted.

TR $<1$ needs $r>\sqrt2$. Square the TR expression and treat $r^2$ as the unknown.
Step 1 — Choose a damping ratio None is given, so pick one — say $\zeta=0.1$ — and check it is reasonable. Step 2 — Solve TR $=0.1$ for $r$ Square and rearrange into a quadratic in $r^2$: $r^4+r^2\big[4\zeta^2(1-1/\text{TR}^2)-2\big]+(1-1/\text{TR}^2)=0$, giving $r=3.66$. Step 3 — Stiffness and damping $\omega=180(2\pi/60)=18.85$ rad/s, so $\omega_n=\omega/r=5.16$ rad/s, $k=m\omega_n^2=665$ N/m and $c=2\zeta m\omega_n=25.8$ N·s/m.
Answer. For $\zeta=0.1$: $k=665$ N/m, $c=25.8$ N·s/m. Other valid designs: $\zeta=0.01$ → $k=806$, $c=2.84$; $\zeta=0.05$ → $k=769$, $c=13.9$; $\zeta=0.2$ → $k=399$, $c=39.9$. More damping forces a softer spring.

Tutorial 3 solutions table: $r=3.66$, $k=665$, $c=25.8$ ✓. For $\zeta=0.2$ the table prints $k=402$, $c=40.1$; recomputing $r=4.72$ gives $k=399$, $c=39.9$ (the table rounds $r$ to 4.70).

Q 8.3Inman 5.16 (data as in the 2023 Tutorial 3 solutions)[—]

A 350 kg machine runs at 800 rpm. Design an undamped isolator that makes the transmitted force 25 % smaller than the applied force, and give the static deflection of the mount.

Step 1 — Required ratio $R=0.25$, so TR $=0.75=1/(r^2-1)$ and $r^2=(2-R)/(1-R)=2.333$, $r=1.528$. Step 2 — Stiffness $\omega=800(2\pi/60)=83.78$ rad/s, $\omega_n=\omega/r=54.84$ rad/s, $k=m\omega_n^2=1.053\times10^6$ N/m. Step 3 — Static deflection $\Delta=mg/k=g/\omega_n^2=3.26$ mm.
Answer. $k\approx1.05$ MN/m, static deflection 3.26 mm.

If you read the requirement as reducing the force to 25 % (TR $=0.25$): $r^2=1+1/0.25=5$, $k=491$ kN/m, $\Delta=6.99$ mm.

Tutorial 3 solutions: $\Delta_{st}=3.26$ mm ✓.

Q 8.4Inman 5.13 (data as in the 2023 Tutorial 3 solutions)[—]

A 500 kg machine runs at 1500 rpm and should be isolated with a frequency ratio of about 3 (the usual rule of thumb for compressors). Find the required stiffness. Two isolators are available: R-3 ($\omega_n=44.7$ rad/s on this machine) and R-4 ($\omega_n=60.0$ rad/s). Which would you choose?

Step 1 — Target $\omega=1500(2\pi/60)=157.1$ rad/s, so $\omega_n=157.1/3=52.4$ rad/s and $k=m\omega_n^2=1.37$ MN/m. Step 2 — Compare the options R-3: $r=157.1/44.7=3.51$ (better isolation, softer, larger static deflection). R-4: $r=157.1/60.0=2.62$ (stiffer, less isolation).
Answer. $k_{req}=1371$ kN/m. R-3 meets "$r\ge3$"; R-4 does not. There is no unique answer: justify the choice.

Tutorial 3 solutions: $\omega_n=52.3$ rad/s, $k=1371$ kN/m, $r_{R-3}=3.51$, $r_{R-4}=2.62$ ✓.

Q 8.5A2 2024, Question 3 (a)–(b)[4]

A motor of mass $m$ on mounts ($k$, $c$) has an unbalance $m_0$ at radius $e$ and runs at $\omega$. (a) What is the amplitude $F_0$ of the harmonic excitation force? (b) Sketch the force transmissibility ratio $|F_T/F_0|$ against $r$ for the undamped system and mark the static response, the response at resonance and the isolation range.

(a) The unbalance mass moves on a circle of radius $e$, so $F_0=m_0e\omega^2$. (b) Undamped: $|F_T/F_0|=1/|1-r^2|$. It equals 1 at $r=0$ (static: the full force goes through), is unbounded at $r=1$ (resonance), falls to 1 again at $r=\sqrt2$, and is below 1 for $r>\sqrt2$ — the isolation range. See Figure 8.1 with $\zeta\to0$.
Answer. $F_0=m_0e\omega^2$; TR $=1$ at $r=0$, $\to\infty$ at $r=1$, $<1$ for $r>\sqrt2$.

No memo for 2024; follows directly from the formula sheet.

Q 8.6Tutorial 3, Additional problem 1[—]

A 200 kg machine on mounts of 400 kN/m is driven by a 500 N harmonic force at 50 rad/s. Design an undamped absorber by choosing a spring from the table so that the machine amplitude is zero and the absorber amplitude is below 4.5 mm. Comment on the phase of the absorber motion relative to the applied force.

SLH403404405406407408409410411
kg/mm1.52.12.73.75.46.79.012.117.0
At tuning, $X_a=-F_0/k_a$. The amplitude limit therefore sets a minimum $k_a$.
Step 1 — Minimum spring rate $k_a\ge F_0/|X_a|=500/0.0045=111$ kN/m. Step 2 — Pick a spring Convert the table: 1 kg/mm $=9.81$ kN/m. SLH 409 gives 88.3 kN/m (too soft); SLH 410 gives $12.1\times9.81=118.7$ kN/m ✓. Then $|X_a|=500/118\,700=4.2$ mm. Step 3 — Absorber mass and check $m_a=k_a/\omega^2=118\,700/50^2=47.5$ kg, $\mu=47.5/200=0.24$ — inside the usual 0.05–0.25.

Q 8.7Tutorial 3, Additional problem 2 = A2 2020, Question 4[7]

A building ($M=3000$ t, height $H=30$ m) stands on 9 concrete columns ($E=30$ GPa, section 1 m × 1 m), each modelled as a cantilever. Damping is negligible. The critical wind load is harmonic at the building's fundamental frequency.

(a) Find the effective bending stiffness. (b) With $m_{eff}=\tfrac{33}{140}M$, find the fundamental frequency. (c) Design a pendulum absorber with $\mu=m_a/m_{eff}=0.1$ and $\beta=1$.

(a) Stiffness $I=bh^3/12=1/12=0.0833$ m⁴. One cantilever: $3EI/H^3$. Nine in parallel: $k_{eff}=9\times3(30\times10^9)(0.0833)/30^3=2.50\times10^6$ N/m. (b) Frequency $m_{eff}=\tfrac{33}{140}(3\times10^6)=7.07\times10^5$ kg, $\omega_p=\sqrt{k_{eff}/m_{eff}}=1.88$ rad/s (0.299 Hz). (c) Absorber $m_a=\mu m_{eff}=7.07\times10^4$ kg; $\omega_a=\beta\omega_p=1.88$ rad/s; pendulum length $L_a=g/\omega_a^2=2.77$ m.
Answer. $k_{eff}=2.5$ MN/m, $\omega_p=1.88$ rad/s, $m_a=70.7$ t, $L_a=2.77$ m.

The paper says to model each column as a cantilever (free top). If a rigid floor slab is taken to stop the column tops rotating, each column is fixed–guided, $12EI/H^3$: $k_{eff}$ is 4 times larger, $\omega_p=3.76$ rad/s and $L_a=0.69$ m. Use the paper's model unless told otherwise.

Tutorial 3 solutions: 2500 kN/m, 1.88 rad/s, $7.1\times10^4$ kg, 2.8 m ✓. The solutions write "$k_{eq}=\tfrac{33}{140}M$" — that is the equivalent mass.

Q 8.8Inman 5.31 (Tutorial 3)[—]

A 3000 kg machine tool has a large resonance at 120 Hz. The plant manager attaches a 600 kg absorber tuned to 120 Hz ($\mu=0.2$, $\beta=1$). Over what range of frequencies is the machine amplitude smaller with the absorber than without it?

Plot or compare $|Xk/F_0|$ with and without the absorber; the question is about the ratio of the two, not about the static deflection.
Step 1 — The two responses With $q=\omega/\omega_a$ and $\beta=1$: without absorber $Xk/F_0=1/(1-q^2)$; with absorber $Xk/F_0=(1-q^2)/\big[(1.2-q^2)(1-q^2)-0.2\big]$. Step 2 — Compare magnitudes Solving $|X_{with}|=|X_{without}|$ (numerically, or by squaring) gives $q=0.854$ and $q=1.171$. Between them the absorber helps; outside them it makes things worse, because the two new resonances (at $q=0.80$ and $1.25$) sit just outside this band.
Answer. $0.854\,\omega_a<\omega<1.171\,\omega_a$, i.e. about 102.5 Hz to 140.5 Hz (Figure 8.2).

The Tutorial 3 solutions answer a different question: where $|Xk/F_0|\le1$ (amplitude no larger than under a static load), giving $0.923\le\omega/\omega_a\le1.10$ and $\omega\ge1.53\,\omega_a$. Those values are correct for that question (recomputed), but above $1.17\,\omega_a$ the machine moves more with the absorber than without it (e.g. at $q=2$: 0.37 vs 0.33). The solutions’ own MATLAB "approach 2" compares the two curves, which is what Inman asks.

Q 8.9Inman 5.29 (data as in the 2023 Tutorial 3 solutions)[—]

An internal combustion engine, modelled as a mass on a spring, has a measured resonance at 100 rad/s and is excited there by a harmonic force of 100 N. Design an absorber so that the absorber amplitude is 10 mm.

Step 1 — Tuning The engine is excited at its resonance, $\omega=100$ rad/s, so the absorber must be tuned there: $\omega_a=\sqrt{k_a/m_a}=100$ rad/s ($\beta=1$). Step 2 — Spring from the stroke At tuning $|X_a|=F_0/k_a$, so $k_a=100/0.01=10$ kN/m. Step 3 — Mass $m_a=k_a/\omega^2=10\,000/100^2=1$ kg.
Answer. $k_a=10$ kN/m, $m_a=1$ kg. (With the textbook's own data, 120 N and 20 mm: $k_a=6$ kN/m, $m_a=0.6$ kg.)

Tutorial 3 solutions: $k_a=10$ kN/m ✓. They then choose $\beta=2$ and $m_a=0.25$ kg, i.e. an absorber tuned to 200 rad/s, which does not stop the engine at its 100 rad/s resonance. Note: the textbook problem uses 120 N and 0.02 m; the solutions use 100 N and 0.01 m.

Week 9

Distributed systems: the string

Lecture 12

This week in brief

  • A taut string obeys the wave equation $w_{tt}=c^2w_{xx}$ with $c=\sqrt{\tau/\rho}$.
  • Separation of variables $w=X(x)T(t)$ gives $X=a\sin\sigma x+b\cos\sigma x$. The boundary conditions fix $\sigma_n$, and $\omega_n=\sigma_nc$.
  • Fixed–fixed: $\sigma_n=n\pi/l$. Fixed–free: $\cos\sigma l=0$, so $\sigma_n=(2n-1)\pi/2l$. A free end means zero slope, $w_x=0$.
  • The initial conditions fix $c_n$ and $d_n$ through orthogonality integrals.
Introduction to this topic

Every system so far has had a finite number of masses. Real structures are continuous: mass and stiffness are spread along them, so there are infinitely many degrees of freedom and infinitely many natural frequencies. Lectures 12 and 13 show that strings, rods and shafts all obey the same equation — only the wave speed $c$ changes.

9.1The string: deriving the wave equation

Linear or volume density?

Lecture 12 uses $\rho$ in kg/m for the string, so $c=\sqrt{\tau/\rho}$ (as on the formula sheet). Inman Eq. 6.1 uses a volume density, so it writes $\sqrt{\tau/\rho A}$. For rods and beams $\rho$ is the volume density in kg/m³. Check the units before you substitute.

Explanation and derivation — 2024 Q8 builds on it

Take an element $\Delta x$ of a string with tension $\tau$ and linear density $\rho$ [kg/m]. For small slopes the tension is the same at both ends and $\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta=\partial w/\partial x$. Vertical force balance on the element:

\[\tau\left[\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\Big|_{x+\Delta x}-\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\Big|_{x}\right]=\rho\,\Delta x\,\frac{\partial^2w}{\partial t^2}\]

Divide by $\Delta x$ and let $\Delta x\to0$:

\[\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x^2}=\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial t^2},\qquad c=\sqrt{\tau/\rho}\]
$w(x,t)$
transverse displacement at position $x$, time $t$
$\tau$
string tension [N]
$\rho$
mass per unit length [kg/m]
$c$
wave speed [m/s]

The lecture's recipe (worth marks on its own): draw the FBD, sum forces, take the limit, rearrange.

9.2Separation of variables

EndsCharacteristic equation$\sigma_n$Mode shape $X_n$
pinned–pinned (fixed–fixed)$\sin\sigma l=0$$n\pi/l$$\sin(n\pi x/l)$
pinned–free (fixed–free)$\cos\sigma l=0$$(2n-1)\pi/2l$$\sin\big((2n-1)\pi x/2l\big)$
free–free$\sin\sigma l=0$$n\pi/l$, $n=0,1,\dots$$\cos(n\pi x/l)$; $n=0$ is rigid-body motion
Explanation and derivation

Assume $w(x,t)=X(x)T(t)$. Substituting gives $X''/X=\ddot T/(c^2T)=-\sigma^2$, a constant. So

\[X''+\sigma^2X=0\ \Rightarrow\ X=a_1\sin\sigma x+a_2\cos\sigma x,\qquad \ddot T+\sigma^2c^2T=0\ \Rightarrow\ \omega=\sigma c\]
$X(x),\ T(t)$
spatial and temporal parts of $w=X(x)T(t)$
$\sigma$
separation constant, fixed by the boundary conditions

The boundary conditions fix $\sigma$. A pinned (fixed) end has $X=0$. A free end (a string end on a frictionless vertical slide, or the free end of a rod) has zero slope, $X'=0$.

and in every case $\omega_n=\sigma_nc$.

9.3Initial conditions

The free response is a sum of all the modes, $w=\sum_n\big(c_n\sin\omega_nt+d_n\cos\omega_nt\big)X_n(x)$. Orthogonality of the mode shapes gives the coefficients. For the pinned–pinned string:

\[d_n=\frac{2}{l}\int_0^l w(x,0)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l}\,dx,\qquad c_n=\frac{2}{n\pi c}\int_0^l \dot w(x,0)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l}\,dx\]
$c_n,\ d_n$
weights of mode $n$ in $w=\sum(c_n\sin\omega_nt+d_n\cos\omega_nt)X_n$
$w(x,0),\ \dot w(x,0)$
initial shape and velocity

If the initial shape is exactly one mode shape, only that mode is excited — the same idea as Week 6.

Practice questions — Week 9

Q 9.1A2 2024, Question 8 (also Tutorial 4, Additional problem 1)[10]

A string of tension $\tau$ and linear density $\rho$ is pinned at $x=0$; the end $x=l$ is free to move vertically. (a) Find the natural frequencies and mode shapes. (b) Sketch the first three mode shapes.

A free end of a string cannot carry a vertical force, and the vertical tension component is $\tau\,\partial w/\partial x$.
Step 1 — Separate $w=X(x)T(t)$ gives $X''+\sigma^2X=0$, $X=A\sin\sigma x+B\cos\sigma x$. Step 2 — Boundary conditions Pinned at 0: $X(0)=0\Rightarrow B=0$. Free end (no vertical force, so zero slope): $X'(l)=A\sigma\cos\sigma l=0\Rightarrow\sigma_n l=\pi/2,\,3\pi/2,\dots$, so $\sigma_n=(2n-1)\pi/2l$. Step 3 — Frequencies $\ddot T+\sigma^2c^2T=0$, so \[\omega_n=\frac{(2n-1)\pi}{2l}\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{\rho}},\qquad X_n=\sin\frac{(2n-1)\pi x}{2l}\] Step 4 — Sketch Figure 9.1 (right): mode 1 is a quarter sine wave with zero slope at the free end; mode 2 has one node at $x=2l/3$; mode 3 has nodes at $2l/5$ and $4l/5$. Every mode has its maximum at the free end.
Answer. $\omega_n=(2n-1)\pi c/2l$, $c=\sqrt{\tau/\rho}$; $X_n=\sin\big((2n-1)\pi x/2l\big)$.

Tutorial 4 solutions (Additional problem 1): $\sigma_n=(2n-1)\pi/2l$, $\omega_n=(2n-1)\pi/2l\sqrt{\tau/\rho}$ ✓.

Q 9.2Inman 6.6 (Tutorial 4)[—]

Write the response as $w=\sum_n\big(c_n\sin\omega_nt+d_n\cos\omega_nt\big)\sin(n\pi x/l)$. A pinned–pinned string is released from rest from the triangular shape $w(x,0)=2x/l$ for $0\le x\le l/2$ and $2(l-x)/l$ for $l/2<x\le l$. Find $c_n$ and $d_n$ and comment on which modes appear.

Use $\int x\sin kx\,dx=-\tfrac{x}{k}\cos kx+\tfrac{1}{k^2}\sin kx$ (given on the tutorial).
Step 1 Released from rest, so $c_n=0$. Step 2 Split the integral at $l/2$ and integrate by parts: \[d_n=\frac{2}{l}\int_0^l w(x,0)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l}dx=\frac{8}{(n\pi)^2}\sin\frac{n\pi}{2}\]
Answer. $c_n=0$; $d_n=8/(n\pi)^2\sin(n\pi/2)$: $d_1=0.811$, $d_2=0$, $d_3=-0.090$, $d_5=0.032$. Only odd modes appear, because the initial shape is symmetric about the midpoint and the even modes are antisymmetric. Mode 1 dominates (9× mode 3), because it looks most like the initial shape.

Tutorial 4 solutions: $d_n=8/(n\pi)^2\sin(n\pi/2)$, even $d_n=0$ ✓.

Q 9.3Tutorial 4, Additional problem 1(c)[—]

The pinned–free string of Q 9.1, with $l=1$ m, is released from rest from $w(x,0)=\sin(\pi x/2)$. Find $c_n$ and $d_n$ and describe the motion.

With $l=1$ the first mode shape is $\sin(\pi x/2)$ — the initial shape is mode 1. Orthogonality gives $d_1=1$, $d_n=0$ for $n\ge2$, and $c_n=0$ (released from rest).
Answer. $w(x,t)=\sin(\pi x/2)\cos\omega_1t$, with $\omega_1=(\pi/2)\sqrt{\tau/\rho}$: the string vibrates in mode 1 only, keeping its shape.

Not worked in the Tutorial 4 solutions. Assumes $l=1$ m, which is what makes $\sin(\pi x/2)$ the first mode shape; for another length the shape is not a mode shape and several $d_n$ are non-zero.

Week 10

Rods, shafts, beams and condition monitoring

Lecture 13 · Vibration condition monitoring

This week in brief

  • Rods (axial) and shafts (torsion) use the same wave equation, with $c=\sqrt{E/\rho}$ and $c=\sqrt{G\gamma/\rho J}$. The boundary conditions: fixed means $w=0$; free means $w_x=0$.
  • Beams are fourth order: $\omega_n=\beta_n^2\sqrt{EI/\rho A}$, with $\beta_nL$ from the boundary conditions (table). There are two conditions at each end: pinned is $w=w_{xx}=0$, clamped is $w=w_x=0$, free is $w_{xx}=w_{xxx}=0$.
  • To design against resonance, keep the operating frequency away from every $\omega_n$ and add a margin.
  • Condition monitoring: know the maintenance philosophies, how monitoring is done, and the fault table. Unbalance: $1\times$, radial. Angular misalignment: $1\times$, high axial. Parallel misalignment: $2\times$, high radial. Bent shaft: high axial. Gears: GMF $=$ teeth $\times$ shaft speed, with sidebands. Bearings: defect frequencies, in four stages.

10.1Rods and shafts

Explanation and derivation

A force balance on a rod element with $F=EA\,\partial w/\partial x$ gives the same wave equation with $c=\sqrt{E/\rho}$. A moment balance on a shaft element with torque $GJ\,\partial\theta/\partial x$ gives it for the twist angle $\theta$, with $c=\sqrt{G\gamma/\rho J}$ ($\gamma$ is the torsional constant from Inman Table 6.3; $\gamma=J$ for a circular shaft). Both speeds are on the formula sheet. A clamped end has $w=0$ (or $\theta=0$); a free end has zero strain $\partial w/\partial x=0$. So a clamped–free rod has the same $\sigma_n$ as the pinned–free string. Only the meaning changes: rod modes are axial displacements, shaft modes are angles of twist.

Bending gives a fourth-order equation (Euler–Bernoulli, Lecture 13):

\[\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial t^2}+c^2\frac{\partial^4 w}{\partial x^4}=0,\qquad c=\sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho A}}\]
$I$
second moment of area about the bending axis
$A$
cross-sectional area
$\rho$
density [kg/m³]
$\beta_n$
from $\beta_nL$ in Table 6.6; $\omega_n=\beta_n^2\sqrt{EI/\rho A}$

It assumes a slender beam: length at least ten times the depth. Otherwise shear and rotary inertia matter (Timoshenko theory, not in this module).

10.2Four boundary conditions

A fourth-order equation needs two conditions at each end:

EndZero quantities
clamped (fixed)deflection $w$ and slope $\partial w/\partial x$
pinned (simply supported)deflection and bending moment $EI\,\partial^2w/\partial x^2$
freebending moment and shear force $\partial/\partial x\,(EI\,\partial^2w/\partial x^2)$
slidingslope and shear force

10.3The recipe (Lecture 13)

  1. Identify the boundary conditions and find $\beta_nL$ in Inman Table 6.6.
  2. $\beta_n=(\beta_nL)/L$; then $\omega_n=\beta_n^2\sqrt{EI/\rho A}$ (on the formula sheet).
  3. Look up the mode-shape expression and $\sigma_n$ in the same table.
  4. Sketch the mode shapes; mark the nodes.
Ends (Inman Table 6.6)$\beta_1L$$\beta_2L$$\beta_3L$large $n$
clamped–free (cantilever)1.8754.6947.855$(2n-1)\pi/2$
pinned–pinned$\pi$$2\pi$$3\pi$$n\pi$
clamped–clamped, free–free4.7307.85310.996$(2n+1)\pi/2$
clamped–pinned3.9277.06910.210$(4n+1)\pi/4$
clamped–sliding2.3655.4988.639$(4n-1)\pi/4$

Mode shapes for the clamped cases have the form $X_n=\cosh\beta_nx-\cos\beta_nx-\sigma_n(\sinh\beta_nx-\sin\beta_nx)$ with $\sigma_n$ from the table; pinned–pinned is simply $\sin(n\pi x/L)$. Free–free beams also have two rigid-body modes at $\omega=0$.

Where to put a machine on a beam

A harmonic force at a node of a mode cannot excite that mode. So if the running frequency is close to a natural frequency, mount the machine at a node of that mode. A force at an antinode excites it most. The same logic tells you where an accelerometer sees a mode and where it misses it (Q 10.4).

Introduction to this topic

This lecture is descriptive. The lecture's own "important for assessments" slide lists exactly what is examinable: what predictive maintenance and condition monitoring are; how predictive maintenance compares to other philosophies; how vibration monitoring fits into a predictive maintenance plan; time- versus frequency-domain monitoring; and how to diagnose unbalance, misalignment, gear defects and bearing defects.

10.4Maintenance philosophies

PhilosophyWhen work is doneSuits
Breakdown (reactive, run-to-failure)after failuregeneral-purpose machines: low risk, low repair cost
Preventive (time-based)at fixed intervals, whatever the conditionessential machines
Predictive (condition-based)when monitored "symptoms" show a developing faultcritical and essential machines
Proactiveremove root causes (alignment, balance, lubrication) before faults startcritical machines

Predictive maintenance works like medical diagnosis: symptoms are monitored, the fault is diagnosed, a remedy is prescribed. Advantages: no unnecessary disassembly (and the poor reassembly that follows it), less unscheduled downtime, fewer wrecks, lower insurance cost, longer machine life. Disadvantages: needs highly skilled staff or contractors, special equipment and training.

10.5How vibration monitoring is done

  • Types: continuous (permanent sensors, costly), periodic (route-based, cost-effective), trending against a baseline.
  • When: daily for machines with a history of problems, monthly for most, quarterly for proven machines; always under the same conditions — full load, same speed (about 10 % speed variation is tolerable on fans and pumps).
  • Where: axial and radial at each bearing housing, marked so readings are repeatable, sensor perpendicular to the surface.
  • Mounting, best first: stud, adhesive, magnetic base, hand-held probe. Stiffer mounting gives a higher mounted-sensor resonance and so a wider usable frequency range.
  • Time domain: single numbers (rms, peak) trended over time — simple, but they mix all frequencies. Frequency domain: FFT/PSD or octave bands — shows which frequency grew, which is what identifies the fault. Waterfall plots show spectra over time or speed.
  • Acceptability: ISO 2372 machine classes, API, AGMA, IRD severity charts.

10.6Diagnosing the common faults

FaultDominant frequencyDirection and phase
Unbalance1× rpm, amplitude grows with speed²radial; clean sinusoidal waveform
Bent shaft1× (bend near the centre), 2× (bend near the ends)high axial; axial phase 180° between ends
Angular misalignment1× (with 2×, 3×)high axial; axial phase 180° across the coupling
Parallel misalignment2× rpm (two "hits" per revolution)high radial; radial phase 180° across the coupling
Gear wear / defectsgear mesh frequency GMF $=N_{teeth}\times$ shaft speed, with sidebands at the shaft speed of the bad gearuniform wear: GMF peak grows; local fault (cracked tooth): wide sidebands
Rolling bearingsdefect frequencies BPFO, BPFI, BSF, FTF and their sidebandsfour stages: ultrasonic (>20 kHz) → bearing resonances (30–120 kHz) → defect frequencies with harmonics → broadband noise, rising 1×, heat

Preventive is not predictive

2024 Q5(b) asks for advantages of preventative maintenance. Preventive (time-based) work prevents unexpected failures and can be planned, but it replaces parts that may still be good. The advantage list on the lecture slide is for predictive maintenance. If a question says "preventative", answer for time-based maintenance, or say which one you mean.

Practice questions — Week 10

Q 10.1Inman 6.30 (Tutorial 4)[—]

A uniform bar of length $l$ moving along its axis with constant velocity $v$ is suddenly stopped at the end $x=0$, so that $w(x,0)=0$ and $\dot w(x,0)=v$. Calculate the vibration response.

Step 1 — Boundary conditions The stopped end is held: $w(0,t)=0$. The other end is free: zero strain, $\partial w/\partial x(l,t)=0$. So this is a clamped–free rod: $X_n=\sin\sigma_nx$, $\sigma_n=(2n-1)\pi/2l$, $\omega_n=\sigma_nc$, $c=\sqrt{E/\rho}$. Step 2 — Coefficients $w(x,0)=0$ gives $d_n=0$. From the velocity, $\sum c_n\omega_n\sin\sigma_nx=v$; multiply by $\sin\sigma_mx$ and integrate over $0..l$: \[c_m\omega_m\frac{l}{2}=v\int_0^l\sin\sigma_mx\,dx=\frac{v}{\sigma_m}\quad\Rightarrow\quad c_n=\frac{2v}{l\,\omega_n\sigma_n}=\frac{8vl}{(2n-1)^2\pi^2c}\]
Answer. \[w(x,t)=\frac{8vl}{\pi^2c}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2n-1)^2}\sin\frac{(2n-1)\pi x}{2l}\,\sin\frac{(2n-1)\pi c\,t}{2l}\] Mode 1 dominates; the free end oscillates about the stopped position.

The Tutorial 4 solutions treat the bar as free–free and conclude $c_n=0$ — a bar that does not move after being given a velocity. Inman states the bar is stopped at $x=0$, which makes that end fixed. Series checked numerically: $\sum c_n\omega_n\sin\sigma_nx$ reproduces $v$ along the bar (verify.py).

Q 10.2Inman 6.40 (Tutorial 4)[—]

Compare the natural frequencies and mode shapes of a clamped–free rod in longitudinal vibration with those of a clamped–free shaft in torsion.

Both obey the wave equation with clamped–free conditions, so \[\omega_n=\frac{(2n-1)\pi c}{2l},\qquad X_n=\sin\frac{(2n-1)\pi x}{2l}\] with $c=\sqrt{E/\rho}$ for the rod and $c=\sqrt{G\gamma/\rho J}$ for the shaft.
Answer. Same form; only the wave speed (material and section) differs. The rod mode shape is an axial displacement; the shaft mode shape is an angle of twist.

Tutorial 4 solutions ✓.

Q 10.3A2 2020, Question 3 (also Tutorial 4, Additional problem 3)[10]

A slightly unbalanced fan (negligible mass) running at 900 rpm in the YZ-plane is to be mounted on a steel I-beam: $L=10$ m, $A=85.5$ cm², $I_{yy}=25\,000$ cm⁴, $I_{zz}=200$ cm⁴, $E=200$ GPa, $\rho=7850$ kg/m³.

Use the $\beta_nL$ values in the Table 6.6 extract. (a) Clamped–clamped: first three natural frequencies for bending about yy. (b) The same about zz. (c) The fan must sit between 1.5 m and 8.5 m: choose the position. (d) What changes if both ends become pinned? (e) Pinned–pinned: the natural frequencies closest to the fan frequency, about yy and zz.

Convert 900 rpm to Hz first, then look for the natural frequency it sits next to.
(a) yy $\sqrt{EI_{yy}/\rho A}=863.1$ m²/s. With $\beta_nL=4.730,\ 7.853,\ 10.996$: $f=\beta_n^2\sqrt{EI/\rho A}/2\pi=$ 30.7, 84.7, 166.1 Hz. (b) zz $\sqrt{EI_{zz}/\rho A}=77.2$ m²/s: 2.75, 7.58, 14.85 Hz. (c) Position 900 rpm $=15$ Hz, right next to the third zz mode (14.85 Hz). Mount the fan at a node of that mode: $x\approx3.6$ m or $6.4$ m (Figure 10.1). (d) Pinned ends Less rotational restraint, so lower stiffness: every natural frequency drops ($\beta_nL$ falls from 4.730 to $\pi$ for mode 1) and the mode shapes change, so the nodes move. (e) Pinned–pinned $f_n=(n\pi/L)^2\sqrt{EI/\rho A}/2\pi$. yy: 13.6, 54.2 Hz — mode 1 at 13.6 Hz is closest. zz: 1.21, 4.85, 10.9, 19.4 Hz — 10.9 Hz (mode 3) is closest.

Note: $I_{zz}=200$ cm⁴ is as given in the paper; it is low for a real I-section of this area, but use it.

Answer. yy: 30.7/84.7/166.1 Hz; zz: 2.75/7.58/14.85 Hz; mount at 3.6 m or 6.4 m. With pinned ends the yy fundamental (13.6 Hz) moves close to 15 Hz — a worse design.

Tutorial 4 solutions: 30.7, 84.7, 166.1 Hz; 2.7, 7.6, 14.9 Hz; $x\approx3.6$ m and 6.4 m ✓. Part (e) is not in the tutorial; the 2020 student memo is illegible there, so (e) is recomputed only.

Q 10.4Tutorial 4, Additional problem 2[—]

A clamped–sliding aluminium pipe ($E=80$ GPa, $\rho=2100$ kg/m³) has span 10 m, outside diameter 120 mm and wall thickness 6 mm. (a) Find the first four natural frequencies (using the Table 6.6 extract) and give the mode-shape equation. (b) Sketch the expected FRF magnitude between a hammer force at $x=L/10$ and an accelerometer at $x=L/3$.

(a) Section $A=\pi(0.06^2-0.054^2)=2.149\times10^{-3}$ m², $I=\pi(0.06^4-0.054^4)/4=3.50\times10^{-6}$ m⁴, $\sqrt{EI/\rho A}=249.1$ m²/s. Frequencies $\beta_nL=2.365,\ 5.498,\ 8.639,\ 11.781$ give $\omega_n=13.93,\ 75.30,\ 185.9,\ 345.8$ rad/s (2.22, 11.98, 29.59, 55.03 Hz). Mode shape: $X_n=\cosh\beta_nx-\cos\beta_nx-\sigma_n(\sinh\beta_nx-\sin\beta_nx)$, $\sigma_1=0.9825$, $\sigma_{n\ge2}\approx1$. (b) FRF Force and response at different points, so it is a transfer FRF: no guaranteed anti-resonance between peaks. Each peak of an accelerance FRF is roughly proportional to $X_n(\text{force point})\,X_n(\text{response point})/\zeta_n$ — the product of the mode shape at both points. With the mass-normalised shapes of Figure 10.2: mode 1 gives $0.024$ (the hammer at $L/10$ is close to the clamp, where mode 1 hardly moves), mode 2 $0.34$, mode 3 $0.68$, mode 4 $0.017$ (the accelerometer at $L/3$ sits almost on its node at 3.35 m).
Answer. 13.9, 75.3, 185.9, 345.8 rad/s. Sketch: a transfer FRF with a tall peak at mode 3, about half that height at mode 2, and only small bumps at modes 1 and 4 (similar damping assumed).

ρ = 2100 kg/m³ and E = 80 GPa are as given in the tutorial (aluminium is usually about 2700 kg/m³ and 70 GPa). Tutorial 4 solutions: 13.93, 75.29, 185.93 ✓. For (b) the solutions consider only the accelerometer position and say modes 2 and 3 give "approximately equal" peaks; including the hammer position (mode-shape product, verify.py) makes mode 3 about twice mode 2 and mode 1 almost absent. For mode 4 the solutions print $\beta_4L=11.79097$ and 346.32 rad/s; $(4n-1)\pi/4$ for $n=4$ is 11.78097, which gives 345.75 rad/s. The printed value has a digit slip.

Q 10.5Practical 3 worksheet[—]

An aluminium cantilever ($E=70$ GPa, $\rho=2700$ kg/m³, $l=450$ mm, $b=42$ mm, $h=3$ mm). (a) Calculate the first three natural frequencies (using the Table 6.6 extract). (b) A small motor (negligible mass) running at 6000 rpm is to be attached. Where should it go so that it excites the beam as little as possible, and why?

(a) $I/A=h^2/12$, so $\sqrt{EI/\rho A}=\sqrt{(70\times10^9)(0.003^2/12)/2700}=4.410$ m²/s. With $\beta_nl=1.875,\ 4.694,\ 7.855$: $\omega_n=(\beta_nl/l)^2(4.410)=$ 76.6, 479.8, 1343.5 rad/s. (b) 6000 rpm $=628$ rad/s, between modes 2 and 3 and closest to mode 2 ($r=1.31$). Put the motor at the node of mode 2, $x\approx0.78l=0.35$ m from the clamp (Figure 10.3), so it does not drive the nearest mode. Close to the clamp all modes move little, which also keeps the response small.
Answer. 76.6, 479.8, 1343.5 rad/s; mount near $x=0.35$ m.

Prac 3 worksheet listing: 76.6, 479.8, 1343.5 rad/s ✓. The worksheet prints these values in the "Experimental" column; they are the analytical values.

Q 10.6A2 2024, Question 5[10]

(a) Give two machinery faults (other than misalignment) that can be identified from vibration measurements. (b) Give two advantages of preventative maintenance. (c) Explain the difference between angular and parallel misalignment and how vibration measurement diagnoses each.

Answer. (a) Any two of: unbalance, bent shaft, looseness, gear defects, bearing defects, resonance, rubs, oil whirl, cavitation, belt problems. (b) Failures are prevented before they occur; maintenance can be planned, so there is less unscheduled downtime and safer operation. (For predictive maintenance: no unnecessary disassembly, longer machine life, lower insurance cost.) (c) Angular: shaft centrelines meet at an angle → mainly axial vibration at 1× (with 2×), 180° axial phase across the coupling. Parallel: centrelines parallel but offset → mainly radial vibration at 2×, 180° radial phase across the coupling. Measure axial and radial at the bearings on both sides of the coupling and compare the amplitudes, the dominant order and the phase.

No memo for 2024; answers taken from the condition-monitoring lecture slides.

Q 10.7New question (lecture content)[—]

A motor running at 1480 rpm drives a pump through a gearbox; the motor shaft carries a 25-tooth pinion. Radial spectra show peaks at (i) 24.7 Hz, growing month by month, with a clean sinusoidal waveform; (ii) 49.3 Hz, with 180° radial phase across the coupling; (iii) 617 Hz with sidebands at ±24.7 Hz. Diagnose each.

Shaft speed $=1480/60=24.7$ Hz.
Answer. (i) 1× with a clean waveform: unbalance. (ii) 2× radial with 180° radial phase across the coupling: parallel misalignment. (iii) $25\times24.7=617$ Hz is the gear mesh frequency; sidebands at the pinion speed point to a fault on the pinion (wear if the GMF peak is growing; a local defect if the sidebands spread widely).

Newly written; checked against the lecture fault table.

Week 11

Sound, decibels, noise rating and noise control

Noise lectures 1–4 · SANS 10083, SANS 10103, WC regulations

This week in brief

  • $c=20.05\sqrt T$ in m/s; $\lambda=c/f$. SPL $L_P=20\log(p/20\,\mu\text{Pa})$.
  • Decibels add as energies: $L=10\log\sum10^{L_i/10}$. Two equal sources add 3 dB, doubling the pressure adds 6 dB, and a perceived doubling is about +10 dB.
  • A-weighting follows the 40-phon curve and C-weighting the 60-phon curve. Both are 0 at 1 kHz. Apply the corrections band by band before adding.
  • SANS 10083 covers occupational exposure: $L_{Req,8h}$ and the 85 dB(A) limit. SANS 10103 covers environmental noise: $L_{Req}=L_{Aeq}+C_i+C_t+k_n$, and $L_{R,dn}$ with the 10 dB night penalty.
  • Prediction: for a point source $L_P=L_W-20\log r-8$, so doubling the distance gives $-6$ dB. For a line source $L_P=L_W-10\log r-5$, so doubling gives $-3$ dB. Control at the source, along the path, or at the receiver.
Introduction to this topic

Sound is a pressure disturbance travelling through an elastic medium (infrasonic, audible and ultrasonic). Noise is sound a person finds objectionable. The sound pressure $p$ is the variation above and below atmospheric pressure, in pascals.

11.1Speed and wavelength

In air at absolute temperature $T$ [K]: $c=20.05\sqrt{T}$ m/s — 343 m/s at 20 °C. Wavelength $\lambda=c/f$ (on the sheet only as $c=\lambda f$): 34 m at 10 Hz, 343 mm at 1 kHz. Sound is slowest in gases, faster in liquids, fastest in solids (about 4400 m/s in rock).

11.2Decibels

The ear spans pressures from 20 µPa to over 100 Pa, so levels are logarithmic. Sound pressure level, with $p_{ref}=20\ \mu$Pa (on the sheet):

\[L_p=10\log\frac{p_{rms}^2}{p_{ref}^2}=20\log\frac{p_{rms}}{p_{ref}}\ \text{dB}\]
$L_p$
sound pressure level [dB]
$p_{rms}$
rms sound pressure [Pa]
$p_{ref}$
reference pressure, $20\ \mu$Pa

Levels add as energies, never arithmetically (sheet): $L_{tot}=10\log\sum10^{L_i/10}$. Subtract background the same way (sheet): $L_{machine}=10\log(10^{L_{tot}/10}-10^{L_{bg}/10})$.

ChangeEffect on $L_p$
sound pressure doubles+6 dB ($20\log2$)
second identical source added (energy doubles)+3 dB ($10\log2$)
perceived loudness doublesabout +10 dB
just noticeable changeabout 1 dB
distance from a point source doubles (free field)−6 dB
distance from a line source doubles−3 dB

11.3Hearing and weighting

Pressure moves the eardrum; the cochlea converts it to nerve impulses. Damage to the cochlea is irreversible. The ear is most sensitive between 2 and 5 kHz. Equal-loudness (phon) contours come from listening tests that match a tone's loudness to a 1 kHz reference. Weighting networks imitate them: A-weighting follows the 40-phon contour; C-weighting the 60-phon contour. A is the default; C is used for very loud noise or noise with strong low-frequency content. Low-frequency noise means energy predominantly below 100 Hz.

11.4Octave-band arithmetic

Add the weighting correction to each band level, then add the corrected bands as energies. This is the 10-mark "fill in the table" question of 2020 and 2024.

Introduction to this topic

Two South African standards and one regulation are examinable. Know what each is for before any formula: Tutorial 5 Q9 and 2024 Q10 ask exactly that.

DocumentScopeKey number
SANS 10083measurement and assessment of occupational noise for hearing conservation$L_{Req,8h}\ge85$ dB(A) → noise zone
SANS 10103measurement and rating of environmental noise with respect to annoyance and speech communicationdistrict rating levels (table below)
Western Cape Noise Control Regulations (2013)legal definitions: nuisance, disturbing noise7 dBA / 3 dBA rules

11.5SANS 10083: occupational exposure

The equivalent continuous A-weighted level $L_{Aeq,T}$ is the steady level with the same energy as the fluctuating one. For a shift made of intervals:

\[L_{Aeq,T}=10\log\sum_i f_i\,10^{L_{Aeq,T_i}/10},\qquad f_i=T_i/T\]
$L_{Aeq,T}$
equivalent continuous A-weighted level over time $T$
$f_i$
fraction of $T$ spent in interval $i$
$L_{Aeq,T_i}$
level measured in interval $i$

Add the impulse correction, $L_{Req,T}=L_{Aeq,T}+C_i$, with $C_i=5$ dB for regular impulsive sound and $12$ dB for highly impulsive sound (small-arms fire, hammering, pile driving, drop forging…). Normalise to an 8-hour day (on the sheet): $L_{Req,8h}=L_{Req,T}+10\log(T/8)$.

  • $L_{Req,8h}\ge85$ dB(A): the area is a noise zone — hearing conservation measures: first the best practicable engineering controls (enclose the machine, process or operator; reduce at source; block the path), then hearing protection and exposure limits as interim measures, plus audiometry.
  • $L_{Req,8h}\ge130$ dB(A): ordinary hearing conservation is not adequate — get expert advice.

11.6SANS 10103: environmental noise

The rating level for a period adds corrections for impulsiveness, tonality and night (on the sheet): $L_{Req,T}=L_{Aeq,T}+C_i+C_t+k_n$, with $C_t=5$ dB for an audible tone (whine, hum), $k_n=10$ dB for night-time 22:00–06:00. Daytime is 06:00–22:00, so $d=16$ h. The day/night rating level:

\[L_{R,dn}=10\log\left[\frac{d}{24}10^{L_{Req,d}/10}+\frac{24-d}{24}10^{(L_{Req,n}+k_n)/10}\right]\]
$L_{R,dn}$
day/night rating level
$d$
daytime hours, 16 (06:00–22:00)
$L_{Req,d},\ L_{Req,n}$
day and night rating levels
$k_n$
night adjustment, 10 dB

Lecture 2 and SANS 10103 clause 3.7 put $k_n$ inside the night rating level; the night limits in SANS 10103 Table 2 exclude it (it is added only when forming $L_{R,dn}$). Both give the same $L_{R,dn}$ — just never add the 10 dB twice.

District (SANS 10103 Table 2, outdoors)$L_{R,dn}$day $L_{Req,d}$night $L_{Req,n}$
rural454535
suburban, little road traffic505040
urban555545
urban with workshops, business premises, main roads606050
central business district656555
industrial707060

Indoors with open windows the values are 10 dB lower (natural ventilation gives about 10 dBA insulation).

11.7Western Cape Noise Control Regulations

  • Ambient noise: the all-encompassing sound, measured with an integrating impulse sound level meter over at least 10 minutes.
  • Residual noise: the same, but excluding the noise complained about.
  • Noise nuisance: any sound that impairs or may impair the convenience or peace of a reasonable person.
  • Disturbing noise (not unamplified voice) — it (a) exceeds the rating level by 7 dBA; (b) exceeds the residual level where the residual is above the rating level; (c) exceeds the residual level by 3 dBA where the residual is below the rating level; or (d) for low-frequency noise, exceeds the SANS 10103 Annex B level.

11.8Predicting levels with distance

From the source sound power level $L_W$ (both on the sheet): point source (spherical spreading, −6 dB per doubling of distance) $L_p=L_W-20\log r-8$; line source such as a road or railway (cylindrical, −3 dB per doubling) $L_p=L_W-10\log r-5$.

11.9Noise control

  • At the source: change the process or the machine; buy quieter; acoustic enclosure.
  • In the path: barriers; absorption (porous lining turns sound energy into heat at reflections — reduces reverberant build-up); isolation (a barrier or wall between source and receiver — the ratio of incident to transmitted sound); vibration isolators so structure-borne sound does not reach the floor.
  • At the receiver: hearing protection, soundproof booths/refuges, job rotation.
  • Materials: rock wool and glass wool (absorption and thermal insulation), dry-wall with a filled cavity (isolation), porous ceiling tiles (absorption).

Q 11.1Tutorial 5, Questions 1–6[—]

(1) Speed of sound in dry air at 20 °C? (2) Sensors in air, water or the ground for an earthquake warning system? (3) Wavelength of 300 Hz at 20 °C? (4) Threshold of pain (100 Pa rms) in dB? (5) Add 75, 70 and 90 dB. (6) Low-frequency noise has its energy mainly below ___ Hz.

Answer. (1) $c=20.05\sqrt{293.15}=343$ m/s. (2) The ground: sound travels fastest in solids (~4400 m/s in rock), so the warning arrives first. (3) $\lambda=343/300=1.14$ m. (4) $20\log(100/20\times10^{-6})=134$ dB. (5) $10\log(10^{7.5}+10^{7.0}+10^{9.0})=90.2$ dB. (6) 100 Hz.

Week 12

Sound measurement

Sound measurement 2025

This week in brief

  • Sound level meters come in types 0, 1 and 2. Time weighting is Fast (125 ms) or Slow (1 s). Calibrate at 94 dB at 1 kHz before and after measuring.
  • Place the microphone 1.2–1.5 m above the ground, away from reflecting surfaces, with wind below 5 m/s. Use a windshield.
  • Background correction: if the machine raises the level by less than 3 dB, the measurement is not valid. Otherwise subtract energetically.
  • A reportable measurement states the instrument, calibration, position, conditions, duration and the result.

12.1Sound level meters

A sound level meter (SLM) combines a microphone (usually a condenser microphone, chosen for its flat frequency response), preamplifier and processing.

  • Type 0: laboratory reference, used to calibrate others. Type 1: precision, required by most standards. Type 2: general surveys, not for reportable measurements.
  • Weighting: A or C, applied by digital filtering or analogue circuits.
  • Time weighting: Fast follows changes quickly (time constant 125 ms); Slow averages over about 1 s, so a fluctuating level can be read; Peak holds the maximum; Impulse uses a special network for impulsive sound.
  • Frequency analysis: narrow band (FFT/PSD in dB) to find specific tones; 1/1, 1/3 or 1/8 octave bands when broad content matters.

"125 µs" in the notes

The 2020 notes and 2025 slides print the Fast time constant as 125 µs. The sound level meter standard (IEC 61672) uses 125 ms. If asked, write 125 ms and give the reason: Fast tracks changes, Slow smooths them for reading.

12.2Where and how to measure

  • Away from façades, walls and other reflecting surfaces and obstacles; microphone 1.2–1.5 m above the ground.
  • Downwind of the source, dry conditions, wind below 5 m/s (use a windscreen).
  • Calibration: annually by a SANAS-accredited laboratory, and a field check before and after every measurement with a calibrator at 94 dB (or 114 dB) at 1 kHz.
  • Background: the Brüel & Kjær Measuring Sound booklet (in Weeks Content/Week 11/Booklets and Regulations/) says the total must be at least 3 dB above the background; with less than 3 dB the background is too high for an accurate measurement.

Practice questions — Week 12

Q 12.1A2 2020, Question 7 (1)–(2)[3]

(1) Background is 83 dB(A); with a machine on it rises to 85 dB(A). What does the machine produce? (2) A technician submits this measurement for approval. Do you sign it off: (a) yes; (b) yes, under specific circumstances; (c) no, the measurement is not accurate?

(1) $10\log(10^{8.5}-10^{8.3})=80.7$ dB(A). (2) The machine raises the level by only 2 dB — below the 3 dB minimum in Measuring Sound. With such a small difference the subtracted value is very sensitive to the ±1 dB uncertainty of each reading (85 vs 84 would give 78.1; 86 vs 83 gives 83.0).
Answer. 80.7 dB(A); (c) — the source cannot be reliably separated from the background with a 2 dB difference.

Part (1): Lecture 2 problem 5 and the 2020 student memo give 80.7 dB ✓. Part (2) is not answered in the student memo; the 3 dB rule is from the Measuring Sound booklet.

Q 12.2New question (lecture content)[—]

List the steps for a reportable environmental noise measurement, from choosing the instrument to reporting.

Answer. Type 1 SLM with valid annual SANAS calibration; field-calibrate at 94 dB / 1 kHz before; microphone 1.2–1.5 m high, away from reflecting surfaces and obstacles, downwind, wind below 5 m/s, dry, with windscreen; A-weighting (C if loud or low-frequency), suitable time weighting; record over a representative period (≥10 min for ambient/residual under the WC regulations); note tonal and impulsive character; field-calibrate again after.

Newly written from the Lecture 3 notes and 2025 slides.

Exam

Exam technique and final checks

All weeks

E.1The method, stated once

Reference — Writing an assessment is an optimisation problem

Writing an assessment is an optimisation problem

Maximise marks subject to a time constraint. The method:
  1. Look at total time and total marks; determine minutes per mark.
  2. Determine how many minutes for each question.
  3. Decide on question order — easiest for you first, hardest last.
  4. Answer each question, but do not spend more than the allocated minutes on it. This stops you being stuck on one question while marks sit unclaimed in another.
  5. Any time saved by finishing a question early goes back into finishing incomplete ones.
Explanation and derivation

From the lecturers' revision lecture [2]:

For A2: 180 minutes, 80 marks, 2.25 min/mark — about 20 minutes per 10-mark block, with about 20 minutes to read the paper first and check at the end (§2.8).

E.2Question-by-question tactics

Reference — What to do in the first 60 seconds

E.3Habits that protect marks

Every question, every time

  1. Draw the free-body diagram, even when not asked. It is the “first-principle physical law” evidence the GA 2 rubric criterion B is looking for.
  2. Name the principle you are applying in words: “Newton's second law”, “conservation of mechanical energy”, “the system is singular at a natural frequency”. Criterion B and C marks attach to this.
  3. Carry symbols to the last line, then substitute numbers once. Errors are easier to find and partial credit is easier to award.
  4. Write units on every numerical answer, and state whether a frequency is rad$\cdot$s$^{-1}$ or Hz.
  5. Sanity check the magnitude. Is $\zeta$ between 0 and 1? Is $\wnn$ of the right order? Does $|X/Y|$ start at 1?
  6. Never leave a “words” part blank. They are one mark each and cost thirty seconds.
  7. If stuck, write the method anyway. “I would now apply the log decrement $\delta=\frac1n\ln(x_1/x_{1+n})$ to find $\zeta$, then $c=2\zeta\sqrt{km}$” can earn most of the marks for that part.

E.4The ten most common errors in the past memos

E.5Self-test checklist

E.6A final word on the GA 2 question

Reference — Answering a GA 2 question

Answering a GA 2 question

  • Criterion A (mathematics): show the mathematical steps — the substitution, the differentiation, the algebra — not just the result.
  • Criterion B (first-principle physical laws): draw the FBD and name the law: “Applying Newton's second law in the $x$-direction …” or “The system is conservative, so $\frac{d}{dt}(T+U)=0$ …”
  • Criterion C (engineering technique / empirical information): identify the standard engineering relation you are invoking — “the displacement transmissibility for a base-excited SDOF system is …”, “the logarithmic decrement relates the measured peak ratio to $\zeta$ by …” — and state where the empirical numbers came from.
A correct final number with none of this visible can still score Fail on all three criteria. Conversely, all three shown correctly with a slipped decimal still scores Pass, because a non-fundamental error that leads to a wrong answer is explicitly allowed.
Explanation and derivation

One question on the paper will carry the rubric of Table 2.3 printed alongside it. Treat that as an instruction, not decoration. It is telling you what to write:

Good luck.
