Mock paper

Mock A2 paper

10 questions · 80 marks · 3 hours

How to use this paper

Ten questions, 80 marks, 3 hours, closed book except for the formula sheet. The blocks follow the lecturers' A2 layout: SDOF (Q 1–3), 2DOF (Q 4), suppression (Q 5–6), continuous systems (Q 7), additional lectures (Q 8–9) and sound (Q 10). Budget about 2.25 minutes per mark.

Every question is new, written for this document. The numbers are computed in qcalc_mock.py and checked in verify.py. Sit it under time with the memos hidden, then mark it question by question.

Use $g=9.81$ m/s².

Practice questions — Mock A2 paper

Q M.1Mock paper — SDOF, energy method[8]

A uniform rod ($m=3$ kg, $L=0.9$ m) hangs from a frictionless pivot O. A horizontal spring $k=400$ N/m is attached $a=0.6$ m below O and is unstretched when the rod hangs vertically (Figure M.1). Small angles.

(a) Use the energy method to derive the equation of motion in $\theta$. [4]
(b) Calculate $\omega_n$ in rad/s and Hz. What fraction of the restoring stiffness comes from gravity? [2]
(c) What spring stiffness would double $\omega_n$? [2]

Gravity helps here: the rod hangs below the pivot.
Step 1 — (a) Energies

$T=\tfrac12J_O\dot\theta^2$ with $J_O=\tfrac13mL^2=0.81$ kg·m². The spring stretches $a\sin\theta\approx a\theta$; the centre of mass rises $\tfrac L2(1-\cos\theta)\approx\tfrac L4\theta^2$:

\[U=\tfrac12ka^2\theta^2+mg\tfrac L2(1-\cos\theta)\approx\tfrac12\left(ka^2+mg\tfrac L2\right)\theta^2\]

$\frac{d}{dt}(T+U)=0$ and divide by $\dot\theta$:

\[\tfrac13mL^2\,\ddot\theta+\left(ka^2+\tfrac12mgL\right)\theta=0\]Step 2 — (b)

$k_t=400(0.36)+3(9.81)(0.45)=144+13.24=157.2$ N·m/rad. $\omega_n=\sqrt{157.2/0.81}=13.93$ rad/s $=2.22$ Hz. Gravity supplies $13.24/157.2=8.4$ % of the stiffness.

Step 3 — (c)

Doubling $\omega_n$ needs $4k_t=629.0$ N·m/rad, so $ka^2=629.0-13.24$ and $k=1710$ N/m (not $4\times400$, because the gravity term does not scale).

Answer. (a) $\tfrac13mL^2\ddot\theta+(ka^2+\tfrac12mgL)\theta=0$. (b) 13.93 rad/s, 2.22 Hz; gravity 8.4 %. (c) $k=1710$ N/m.

Computed in qcalc_mock.py; verify.py.

Q M.2Mock paper — SDOF, rotating unbalance[8]

A washing machine (total mass $M=40$ kg) spins a drum with an unbalance $m_0e=0.02$ kg·m at 1000 rpm. It stands on mounts with total stiffness $k=60$ kN/m and $\zeta=0.1$.

(a) Find the natural frequency (in rpm) and the frequency ratio at 1000 rpm. [2]
(b) Find the steady-state amplitude of the machine at 1000 rpm. [3]
(c) Find the force transmitted to the floor at 1000 rpm. [2]
(d) Estimate the amplitude as the drum passes through resonance while speeding up. [1]

Step 1 — (a)

$\omega_n=\sqrt{60\,000/40}=38.73$ rad/s $=370$ rpm. $\omega=1000(2\pi/60)=104.7$ rad/s, so $r=2.70$.

Step 2 — (b)

$F_0=m_0e\,\omega^2=0.02(104.7)^2=219.3$ N.

\[X=\frac{F_0/k}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}=\frac{3.655\ \text{mm}}{\sqrt{(1-7.31)^2+0.541^2}}=0.58\ \text{mm}\]

(Check: for large $r$, $X\to m_0e/M=0.5$ mm.)

Step 3 — (c)

$\text{TR}=\sqrt{\dfrac{1+(2\zeta r)^2}{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}}=0.180$, so $F_T=0.180\times219.3=39.4$ N.

Step 4 — (d)

At $r=1$: $X=\dfrac{m_0e}{M}\dfrac{1}{2\zeta}=\dfrac{0.5\ \text{mm}}{0.2}=2.5$ mm — about four times the running amplitude.

Answer. (a) 370 rpm, $r=2.70$. (b) 0.58 mm. (c) 39.4 N. (d) About 2.5 mm at resonance.

The force grows with speed

$F_0=m_0e\omega^2$ is not a constant: compute it at the speed asked, and use the unbalance curve $MX/m_0e$ (not $Xk/F_0$) when the speed changes.

Computed in qcalc_mock.py; verify.py.

Q M.3Mock paper — SDOF, damping identification[8]

A 4 kg mass on a spring slides on a horizontal surface. It is pulled 20.0 mm from the unstretched-spring position and released from rest. Measured from that position, the release point and the following positive peaks are 20.0, 16.4, 12.8 and 9.2 mm, one every 0.50 s.

(a) Is the damping viscous or Coulomb? Justify from the data. [2]
(b) Find the spring stiffness and the friction coefficient. [3]
(c) Where and when does the mass come to rest? [3]

Compare differences and ratios of successive peaks.
Step 1 — (a)

The peaks drop by a constant amount (3.6 mm per cycle); the ratios 1.22, 1.28, 1.39 are not constant. Linear decay: Coulomb friction.

Step 2 — (b)

Coulomb damping does not change the period: $\omega_n=2\pi/0.5=12.57$ rad/s, $k=m\omega_n^2=631.7$ N/m.

Loss per cycle $4\mu mg/k=3.6$ mm, so $\mu=0.0036(631.7)/(4\times4\times9.81)=0.0145$.

Step 3 — (c)

Dead zone $\mu mg/k=0.9$ mm (static and kinetic $\mu$ taken equal); each half-cycle loses 1.8 mm. Extremes: 20.0, −18.2, 16.4, …; after $n$ half-cycles $|x|=20-1.8n$. The first value inside the dead zone is at $n=11$: $|x|=0.2$ mm, on the negative side.

It stops 0.2 mm on the opposite side of the release point from equilibrium, after $11\times0.25=2.75$ s.

Answer. (a) Coulomb. (b) $k=632$ N/m, $\mu=0.0145$. (c) Stops at $x=-0.2$ mm after 2.75 s.

Computed in qcalc_mock.py; verify.py.

Q M.4Mock paper — 2DOF[8]

The building of Figure M.2 has rigid floors $m_1=m_2=1000$ kg. The columns give storey stiffnesses $k_1=400$ kN/m (ground to floor 1) and $k_2=200$ kN/m (floor 1 to floor 2).

(a) Write the equations of motion in matrix form. [3]
(b) Find the natural frequencies in Hz and the mode shapes, and sketch the modes. [5]

Step 1 — (a)\[\begin{bmatrix}m_1&0\\0&m_2\end{bmatrix}\ddot{\mathbf x}+\begin{bmatrix}k_1+k_2&-k_2\\-k_2&k_2\end{bmatrix}\mathbf x=\mathbf 0,\qquad\mathbf K=\begin{bmatrix}600&-200\\-200&200\end{bmatrix}\ \text{kN/m}\]Step 2 — (b) Frequencies

With $\lambda=\omega^2$ in units of $10^3$ (rad/s)²: $(600-\lambda)(200-\lambda)-200^2=0$, i.e. $\lambda^2-800\lambda+80\,000=0$, so $\lambda=117.2$ or $682.8$.

$\omega_1=10.82$ rad/s (1.72 Hz), $\omega_2=26.13$ rad/s (4.16 Hz).

Step 3 — Mode shapes (row 1)

$x_2/x_1=(600-\lambda)/200$. Mode 1: $[1,\ 2.41]^T$ — both floors sway the same way, the top floor more. Mode 2: $[1,\ -0.41]^T$ — the floors move in opposite directions.

Answer. $f_1=1.72$ Hz, $\mathbf u_1=[1,\ 2.41]$; $f_2=4.16$ Hz, $\mathbf u_2=[1,\ -0.41]$.

Computed with numpy eig in qcalc_mock.py; verify.py.

Q M.5Mock paper — isolation design[8]

A 150 kg compressor runs at 1200 rpm. The force transmitted to the floor must be reduced by 85 %.

(a) Ignoring damping, find the required mount stiffness and the static deflection. [4]
(b) The chosen rubber mounts have $\zeta=0.1$. With the stiffness from (a), is the 85 % target met? If not, what stiffness is needed? [3]
(c) Why might you still want some damping? [1]

Damping raises TR above $r=\sqrt2$.
Step 1 — (a)

$\text{TR}=0.15=1/(r^2-1)$, so $r^2=7.667$ and $r=2.769$. $\omega=125.7$ rad/s, $\omega_n=\omega/r=45.38$ rad/s.

$k=m\omega_n^2=150(45.38)^2=309$ kN/m; $\Delta_{st}=g/\omega_n^2=4.8$ mm.

Step 2 — (b)

With $\zeta=0.1$ at $r=2.769$: $\text{TR}=0.171$, only 82.9 % reduction — not met. Solving $\text{TR}(r,0.1)=0.15$ gives $r=2.953$, so $k=m(\omega/2.953)^2=272$ kN/m (softer).

Step 3 — (c)

The compressor passes through resonance at start-up and shut-down. With $\zeta=0.1$ the transmissibility at $r=1$ is about 5.1; with almost no damping it would be very large.

Answer. (a) $k=309$ kN/m, $\Delta_{st}=4.8$ mm. (b) TR = 0.171, not met; use $k\approx272$ kN/m. (c) To limit the resonance at start-up.

Computed in qcalc_mock.py (brentq for $r$); verify.py.

Q M.6Mock paper — vibration absorber[8]

An 80 kg machine runs at 1500 rpm, which happens to equal the natural frequency of its mounting. The unbalance force amplitude is 200 N. An undamped absorber with mass ratio $\mu=0.1$ is to be added.

(a) Find the absorber mass and stiffness. [2]
(b) What is the machine amplitude and the absorber amplitude at 1500 rpm? [2]
(c) Find the two new natural frequencies in rpm, and say what this means at start-up. [4]

Step 1 — (a)

$m_a=0.1(80)=8$ kg. Tune $\omega_a=\omega=157.1$ rad/s: $k_a=m_a\omega^2=197.4$ kN/m.

Step 2 — (b)

Machine: $X=0$ at the tuned speed. Absorber: $X_a=F_0/k_a=200/197\,400=1.01$ mm (in anti-phase with the force).

Step 3 — (c)

With $\beta=\omega_a/\omega_p=1$, $\left(\omega/\omega_a\right)^2=1+\tfrac\mu2\pm\sqrt{\mu+\tfrac{\mu^2}4}=0.730$ or $1.370$.

$\omega=134.2$ and $183.9$ rad/s: 1281 rpm and 1756 rpm. The machine now passes through a resonance at 1281 rpm while running up to 1500 rpm.

Answer. (a) 8 kg, 197 kN/m. (b) Machine 0, absorber 1.01 mm. (c) 1281 and 1756 rpm.

Computed in qcalc_mock.py; verify.py.

Q M.7Mock paper — continuous systems[8]

(a) A steel shaft ($L=1.2$ m, $d=40$ mm, $G=80$ GPa, $\rho=7800$ kg/m³) is fixed at one end and free at the other. Apply the boundary conditions to find the first two torsional natural frequencies in Hz. [4]
(b) A steel strip ($E=200$ GPa, $\rho=7800$ kg/m³), 30 mm wide, 10 mm thick and 0.8 m long, is clamped at one end and vibrates in its thickness direction. Find its first two bending natural frequencies. Use $\beta_1L=1.875$, $\beta_2L=4.694$. [4]

Step 1 — (a) Shaft

$\theta_{tt}=c^2\theta_{xx}$ with $c=\sqrt{G/\rho}=3203$ m/s. $\Theta=A\sin\sigma x+B\cos\sigma x$. Fixed at $x=0$: $B=0$. Free at $x=L$ (no torque, $\Theta'=0$): $\cos\sigma L=0$, so $\sigma_n=(2n-1)\pi/2L$.

$\omega_n=\sigma_nc$: $f_1=c/4L=667$ Hz, $f_2=3c/4L=2002$ Hz. (The diameter does not matter.)

Step 2 — (b) Cantilever

$I=bh^3/12=2.5\times10^{-9}$ m⁴, $A=3\times10^{-4}$ m². $\omega_n=(\beta_nL)^2\sqrt{EI/\rho AL^4}$:

$f_1=12.8$ Hz, $f_2=80.1$ Hz.

Answer. (a) 667 Hz and 2002 Hz. (b) 12.8 Hz and 80.1 Hz.

Which way does the strip bend?

Vibrating in the thickness direction, $I=bh^3/12$ with $h=10$ mm. Using the 30 mm dimension as $h$ gives frequencies three times too high.

Computed in qcalc_mock.py; verify.py.

Q M.8Mock paper — signal processing and EMA[8]

An accelerometer signal is sampled at $f_s=1$ kHz and blocks of $N=2048$ points are recorded.

(a) What is the record length, the frequency resolution and the highest frequency that can be analysed? [3]
(b) The structure also vibrates at 1100 Hz, and there is no anti-aliasing filter. Where does this component appear in the spectrum? [1]
(c) What resolution change is needed to resolve 0.25 Hz? [1]
(d) An FRF peak at 50.0 Hz has half-power points at 48.6 and 51.4 Hz. Find $\zeta$. Why would you use $H_1$ rather than $H_2$ when the response channel is noisy? [3]

Step 1 — (a)

$T=N/f_s=2.048$ s, $\Delta f=1/T=0.488$ Hz, $f_{max}=f_s/2=500$ Hz (Nyquist). In practice analysers display up to about $f_s/2.56\approx390$ Hz to allow for the anti-aliasing filter; either answer with its reason earns the mark.

Step 2 — (b)

Aliased to $|1100-1000|=100$ Hz.

Step 3 — (c)

$\Delta f=0.25$ Hz needs $T=4$ s, i.e. $N=4000$ points (4096 in practice) at the same $f_s$.

Step 4 — (d)

$\zeta=(f_b-f_a)/2f_d=2.8/100=0.028$. $H_1=S_{fx}/S_{ff}$ is unbiased by noise on the output, because the uncorrelated noise averages out of the cross-spectrum; $H_2$ is the one to use when the noise is on the input.

Answer. (a) 2.048 s, 0.488 Hz, 500 Hz. (b) 100 Hz. (c) $T=4$ s, $N\approx4000$. (d) $\zeta=0.028$; $H_1$ for output noise.

Computed in qcalc_mock.py; verify.py.

Q M.9Mock paper — condition monitoring[8]

A motor running at 1480 rpm drives a gearbox through a coupling. The pinion on the motor shaft has 32 teeth.

(a) Name the three maintenance philosophies and give one advantage of condition-based maintenance. [3]
(b) The spectrum shows a large peak at 49.3 Hz, strongest in the radial direction. Name the likely fault. [2]
(c) At what frequency would you expect the gear-mesh peak, and what around it would indicate a worn or damaged gear? [2]
(d) Large peaks at 24.7 Hz in the axial direction instead suggest which fault? [1]

Step 1 — (a)

Breakdown (run to failure), time-based (preventive) and condition-based (predictive) maintenance. Advantage: parts are replaced only when needed, and failures are caught before they happen — less downtime and fewer unnecessary replacements.

Step 2 — (b)

Shaft speed $1480/60=24.7$ Hz, so 49.3 Hz is $2\times$. High $2\times$ radial: parallel misalignment. (It is not the 50 Hz mains: the peak sits exactly at $2\times24.67$ Hz and moves with the shaft speed.)

Step 3 — (c)

GMF $=32\times24.67=789$ Hz. Sidebands around the GMF, spaced at the speed of the damaged gear’s shaft (±24.7 Hz for the pinion), indicate wear or a damaged tooth.

Step 4 — (d)

High $1\times$ axial: angular misalignment (a bent shaft is also possible).

Answer. (b) Parallel misalignment. (c) 789 Hz, sidebands at ±24.7 Hz. (d) Angular misalignment.

Fault table from the Week 10 condition-monitoring lecture.

Q M.10Mock paper — sound[8]

(a) Three machines produce 88, 85 and 82 dB at a point. What is the total level? [1]
(b) A pump has sound power level $L_W=105$ dB and acts as a point source on hard ground ($L_P=L_W-20\log r-8$). Find $L_P$ at 10 m, and the distance from the pump at which the level is 85 dB. [3]
(c) A machine measures 78 dB with it running and 74 dB with it off. Is the measurement valid, and what is the machine's own level? [2]
(d) The octave-band levels of a fan are given below with the A-weighting corrections. Find the overall dB(A) and the unweighted total. [2]

Band [Hz]631252505001k2k4k8k
$L$ [dB]8082858483807670
A-weighting [dB]−26.2−16.1−8.6−3.20+1.2+1.0−1.1
Step 1 — (a)

$L=10\log(10^{8.8}+10^{8.5}+10^{8.2})=90.4$ dB.

Step 2 — (b)

$L_P=105-20-8=77$ dB at 10 m. For 85 dB: $20\log r=105-8-85=12$, so $r=3.98$ m.

Step 3 — (c)

The difference is 4 dB, at least 3 dB, so the measurement is valid. $L=10\log(10^{7.8}-10^{7.4})=75.8$ dB.

Step 4 — (d)

A-weighted bands: 53.8, 65.9, 76.4, 80.8, 83.0, 81.2, 77.0, 68.9 dB; energetic sum $=87.5$ dB(A). Unweighted sum $=90.7$ dB. The A-weighting removes mostly low-frequency energy.

Answer. (a) 90.4 dB. (b) 77 dB; 3.98 m. (c) Valid; 75.8 dB. (d) 87.5 dB(A); 90.7 dB unweighted.

Computed in qcalc_mock.py; verify.py.

Appendix A

The formula sheet, derived

Every expression printed on the assessment appendix formula sheet [2], with a pointer to where it is derived in this document. If you can trace each line back to its derivation, you will not misapply it.

SDOF

Exam angle

The typeset formula sheet in the tips deck shows $\frac{X\wnn^2}{f_0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2-(2\zeta r)^2}}$ with a minus sign under the root. That is a typographical error — with a minus, the expression is singular whenever $2\zeta r = |1-r^2|$ and becomes imaginary beyond that, which is not physical. The correct denominator is $\sqrt{(1-r^2)^2+(2\zeta r)^2}$, as used in every past memo and in Lecture 6 [8]. Use the plus sign. If in doubt, check $r=1$: the minus version takes the root of $-4\zeta^2$; the correct one gives $1/(2\zeta)$. (The $r\to0$ limit does not help here: both versions give 1.)
